title: Trial Balance
in30Seconds: A trial balance is a list of all accounts in the general ledger with their balances at a point in time, used to check that total debits equal total credits — the core definition in this lesson comes from OpenStax's Principles of Accounting. Each account's ending balance goes into one of two columns: debits on the left, credits on the right. The two columns are totaled, and the totals must match. Equal totals mean the recording stayed in balance — but they do not prove everything is right.
whyItMatters: The trial balance is the check that runs before the statements. Without it, a recording mistake could ride all the way into the income statement and balance sheet and surface only when someone challenged the final numbers. Because the check runs at the end of every accounting period, it catches the most common mechanical slips — a balance in the wrong column, a transposed pair of digits, an entry that never balanced — while the fix is still cheap. Everyone downstream benefits: lenders, owners, and managers rely on statements that were only as clean as the check that came before them. And knowing what the trial balance cannot catch is as valuable as knowing what it can.
learningObjectives: Define the trial balance as a list of all accounts with their balances at a point in time that checks that total debits equal total credits, using the working definition from OpenStax's Principles of Accounting.
Describe how a trial balance is built: each account's ending balance in one of two columns, debits on the left and credits on the right, with the column totals compared.
Explain what a balanced trial balance does and does not prove — equal totals do not guarantee the books are right.
Name the errors a trial balance cannot catch: missing transactions, wrong accounts, and equal mistakes on both sides.
Apply the two search methods for an unbalanced trial balance — divide the difference by two, and divide it by nine — to a small example.
Distinguish the trial balance from the financial statements, and place it in the accounting cycle between the ledger and the statements.

collegeVersion.heading: What a trial balance is
collegeVersion.body: OpenStax's Principles of Accounting describes the trial balance as a list of all accounts in the general ledger that have balances, and CFI's Trial Balance guide frames the same idea as a report that lists the balances of all general ledger accounts at a certain point in time. Together they give this lesson's working definition: a trial balance is a list of all accounts in the general ledger with their balances at a point in time, used to check that total debits equal total credits. It is a list — a snapshot of ending balances — and a check: collecting every balance in one place confirms the recording stayed in balance. CFI adds one more frame: it is not an official financial statement, but an internal working document, usually kept inside the company.

collegeVersion.heading: How a trial balance is built
collegeVersion.body: Building a trial balance is mostly copying, and the copying follows a rule. OpenStax lays out the format: the page carries the company's name, the label of the trial balance, and the date, and each account's final balance is transferred from the ledger into one of two columns. An account ending with a debit balance goes in the left column; one ending with a credit balance goes in the right. Cash, supplies, equipment, and expenses typically land on the left; liabilities, owner's equity, and revenue on the right. Then the two columns are totaled and compared. A small illustration: Bright Steps Tutoring ends June with Cash $6,500, Accounts Receivable $900, Supplies $400, Equipment $2,000, and Rent Expense $900 on the debit side — $10,700 in all — and Accounts Payable $1,300, Notes Payable $1,500, Common Stock $5,000, and Service Revenue $2,900 on the credit side, also $10,700. As OpenStax puts it, if the two totals are not equal, there is a mistake in at least one of the columns.

collegeVersion.heading: What equal totals do — and do not — prove
collegeVersion.body: A balanced trial balance is good news: account by account, the period's double-entry recording stayed arithmetically consistent — every debit was matched by a credit somewhere. That is real information — and why the check exists. But it is not a verdict. OpenStax makes the honest point twice: equal column totals are no guarantee that a mistake is not present, and a company can have errors and still be mathematically in balance. The trial balance verifies the arithmetic of the recording, not the truth of what was recorded. A sale never written down, a payment posted to the wrong account, an entry with the wrong figure on both sides — all of these leave the columns equal. A check that balances is a green light to continue, not a certificate of correctness.

collegeVersion.heading: What a trial balance cannot catch
collegeVersion.body: CFI names the errors that slip past a balanced trial balance; the three most important are worth knowing by name. An error of omission: a transaction was never entered at all — no debit, no credit, no trace — so nothing exists to unbalance the columns. A commission error: the amount is right, but it was recorded in the wrong account — a repair charged to Equipment instead of Repairs Expense — so the entry still balances, and only its destination is wrong. An error of original entry: the transaction was entered with the wrong amounts on both sides, such as $500 on each side instead of $300, which keeps the columns equal even though both figures are wrong. CFI also lists rarer cases: reversal errors, where the account to be debited is credited instead, and principle errors, where a transaction lands in the wrong type of account. All of these leave the trial balance balanced. That is the honest framing of this lesson: the trial balance is a tripwire, not a verdict — it catches many errors, not all.

collegeVersion.heading: When the columns do not match
collegeVersion.body: An unbalanced trial balance is not a dead end; it is a starting point. OpenStax describes the standard search. First, divide the difference between the totals by two — a $200 gap points to a $100 amount in the wrong column, since moving it raises one column by $100 and lowers the other by $100. Second, divide the difference by nine — if the result is a whole number, suspect a transposed pair of digits, such as $3,500 written as $5,300, because transpositions always produce differences divisible by nine. If neither method lands on the error, trace back step by step: from the trial balance to the ledger, and from the ledger to the journal. The methods turn a vague feeling that something is off into a short checklist.

collegeVersion.heading: The trial balance in the cycle
collegeVersion.body: The trial balance is one step in a longer routine. OpenStax numbers it as the fourth step of the accounting cycle — after transactions are identified, journalized, and posted to the ledger — and CFI's accounting cycle guide places it at the same spot: step four of eight, run at the end of the accounting period — monthly, quarterly, or yearly. Its timing follows from its purpose: prepared after the ledger is complete, because it needs every account's ending balance, and before the financial statements, because the statements are built from balances that passed the check. There is also a second edition: the unadjusted trial balance comes before adjusting entries, and an adjusted trial balance after them, to confirm the totals still balance before the statements are built. The ledger, adjusting entries, the cycle, and the statements each have their own lessons — here, the point is the position: the check between the ledger and the statements.

vocabulary.definition: A list of all accounts in the general ledger with their balances at a point in time, used to check that total debits equal total credits; the core definition in this lesson comes from OpenStax's Principles of Accounting.
A trial balance prepared right after posting, before adjusting entries, showing the accounts as they were recorded during the period.
A second trial balance prepared after adjusting entries, used to confirm that the totals still balance before the financial statements are built.
An account ending on the debit, or left, side — typical of cash, supplies, and expenses — placed in the left column of the trial balance.
An account ending on the credit, or right, side — typical of liabilities, owner's equity, and revenue — placed in the right column of the trial balance.
An error in which a transaction was never entered into the records at all; the trial balance cannot detect it because nothing was recorded.
An error in which the correct amount is recorded in the wrong account; the trial balance can still balance because the entry itself is complete.
An error in which a transaction is entered with wrong amounts on both sides; the columns still match even though both figures are incorrect.
The stretch of time — often a month, quarter, or year — covered by one run of the accounting cycle, at the end of which the trial balance is prepared.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Think of the trial balance as the moment the bookkeeper holds the two halves of the books up against each other. In double-entry bookkeeping, every transaction is written twice — once as a debit, once as a credit — so at the end of the period each account has an ending balance. The trial balance collects all of those balances in one place and adds them up: all the debit balances on one side, all the credit balances on the other. If the two totals match, the double-entry recording stayed consistent. It is a quick, cheap check that runs before anything is turned into a statement, and it exists because even careful people make slips when they record dozens of entries a week.
eli10.analogy: A tripwire. Picture a guard walking a corridor at night, with a wire strung low across the floor near a vault. If the wire is tripped, an alarm rings — something crossed it. But a silent corridor proves nothing: someone could be breaking in on the other side of the building, or a thief could have crossed earlier and reset the wire. The tripwire only reports what happens at its exact spot. The trial balance is the same. It rings the alarm when the columns disagree, and it stays silent when they agree — even when something is wrong elsewhere in the books.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy understates the trial balance's reach: a tripwire guards one point, while the trial balance rechecks every account's balance in a single pass, so it catches a much wider class of errors — wrong columns, transposed digits, entries that never balanced. It also overstates the alarm: a balanced trial balance sounds no bell at all, and the check can only verify what was recorded in the first place. The wire is as good as the recording behind it, and it verifies arithmetic consistency, not the truth of the underlying events.

workedExample: Bright Steps Tutoring is a small tutoring business run by Lena. At the end of June, her bookkeeper lists every account's ending balance: Cash $6,500 debit, Accounts Receivable $900 debit, Supplies $400 debit, Equipment $2,000 debit, and Rent Expense $900 debit — and on the credit side, Accounts Payable $1,300, Notes Payable $1,500, Common Stock $5,000, and Service Revenue $2,900. The debit column totals $10,700 and the credit column totals $10,700, so the trial balance balances. Yet a tutoring session on June 12 worth $200 was never recorded at all — an error of omission. No debit, no credit, no trace — and the columns still match. The check passes, and the mistake rides along inside it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a balanced trial balance as proof that the books are right.
commonMistakes.correction: Equal totals only show the recording stayed arithmetically consistent. As OpenStax puts it, a company can have errors and still be mathematically in balance — a balanced trial balance is a green light to continue, not a certificate of correctness.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the trial balance catches every recording error.
commonMistakes.correction: It cannot see transactions that were never entered, amounts recorded in the wrong account, or entries with wrong figures on both sides — CFI names these as the undetectable errors. The trial balance catches many errors, not all.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating the trial balance as a financial statement to hand to outsiders.
commonMistakes.correction: It is an internal working document, not an official financial statement, and CFI notes it is usually not distributed outside the company.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dismissing a credit balance typed into the debit column as a harmless slip.
commonMistakes.correction: That slip is exactly what makes the columns disagree — and OpenStax's divide-the-difference-by-two method exists precisely to find amounts sitting in the wrong column.

commonMistakes.mistake: Guessing blindly when the trial balance does not balance.
commonMistakes.correction: Use the systematic search first: divide the difference by two to spot a wrong-column amount, divide by nine to spot transposed digits, and if neither works, trace back step by step from the trial balance to the ledger to the journal.

compareContrast.distinction: The ledger shows every transaction, organized by account; the trial balance shows only each account's ending balance at a point in time — a snapshot taken from the ledger.
Both must balance, but the unadjusted one is prepared before adjusting entries and the adjusted one after them; the statements are built from the adjusted balances.
The trial balance is an internal check that the recording stayed in balance; the income statement and balance sheet are formal reports prepared for outsiders from the checked balances.

keyTakeaway: The trial balance is a tripwire, not a verdict: when the columns disagree, it rings the alarm, and when they agree, it confirms only that the books stayed in balance — not that everything is right.

title: Adjusting Entries
in30Seconds: Adjusting entries are journal entries made at the end of an accounting period to record things the books have not yet captured — the definition guiding this lesson comes from OpenStax's Principles of Accounting. Some events happen gradually: supplies get used, prepaid rent runs out, wages are earned but unpaid. At period end, the bookkeeper adjusts the accounts for prepayments used up, accrued expenses, and accrued revenue. Adjustments come after the trial balance and before the statements — and they are how the books tell the truth about the period.
whyItMatters: If a period's books contained only the transactions someone happened to write down, the statements would lie: profit would be overstated when used supplies never became an expense, and understated when wages earned but unpaid never appeared. Adjusting entries close that gap, and every reader of the statements depends on it. A lender sizing up a loan, an owner deciding whether to expand, a manager judging a slow month — all of them need numbers that match what actually happened in the period. Learning when and why adjustments are made is the difference between reading a business's true results and reading its rough draft.
learningObjectives: Define adjusting entries as journal entries made at the end of an accounting period to record transactions not yet captured in the books, using the working definition from OpenStax's Principles of Accounting.
Explain why adjusting entries exist: gradual events like using supplies, consuming prepaid rent, and earning unpaid wages trigger no entry during the period because they produce no source document.
Name the common types of adjusting entries — prepayments used up, accrued expenses, and accrued revenue — with one original example of each.
Describe when adjusting entries happen in the accounting cycle: after the trial balance and before the financial statements.
Distinguish adjusting entries from closing entries: adjusting corrects the period's balances, while closing resets the accounts for the next period.
Explain the honest framing: adjustments are how accountants make the statements tell the truth about a period.

collegeVersion.heading: What adjusting entries are
collegeVersion.body: OpenStax's Principles of Accounting says adjusting entries update accounting records at the end of a period for any transactions that have not yet been recorded. CFI frames the same idea as the entries that record the revenue and expense recognition that belongs to a period, pairing each adjustment with the cash settlement that comes before or after it. In plainer words: adjusting entries are journal entries made at the end of a period to record things the books have not yet captured. Notice what the definition is not. It is not about fixing mistakes — a wrong number typed into the ledger gets a correcting entry, not an adjustment. It is about finishing: capturing activity that genuinely happened but never made it into the journal, because nothing during the period triggered a recording. Adjustments are routine, expected, and made every period.

collegeVersion.heading: Why they exist: the timing problem
collegeVersion.body: Most transactions announce themselves. A sale produces an invoice, a purchase produces a receipt, a loan payment produces a bank statement — the paper trail triggers the journal entry. But some events happen gradually and quietly. A design studio buys $900 of paper and ink; by month end, $300 of it has been used, and no invoice exists for “paper used.” A bakery pays three months of rent in advance; each week that passes consumes part of that prepayment. A shop's employees earn wages every day, but payday falls on the first of next month. OpenStax puts it directly: journal entries are triggered by original source documents, and not every transaction produces one. Using supplies from the supply closet generates no document, and a customer does not send a reminder that revenue has now been earned. Those silent, gradual events are the timing problem, and adjusting entries are the answer.

collegeVersion.heading: The common types
collegeVersion.body: Accountants sort adjusting entries into a few familiar types. Prepayments used up: money paid in advance for something not yet consumed — supplies, rent, insurance. The used portion stops being an asset and becomes an expense; OpenStax's supplies example moves $150 of use out of a $400 supply balance, leaving $250 still on the balance sheet. Unearned revenue, the flip side: a customer pays $300 in advance for a workshop, which is a liability until the workshop happens, and becomes revenue as it happens. Accrued expenses: costs incurred but not yet recorded or paid — wages earned but unpaid, interest that has built up on a loan, a utility bill that has not arrived. Accrued revenue: income earned but not yet recorded or collected — work finished but not yet billed. Each adjustment pairs one income statement account with one balance sheet account, and no adjusting entry touches cash; the cash side was or will be recorded separately. Depreciation, a close cousin, gets its own lesson.

collegeVersion.heading: When they happen
collegeVersion.body: Adjusting entries have a fixed place in the accounting cycle. First the bookkeeper records the period's transactions, posts them to the ledger, and runs an unadjusted trial balance — the first check that debits equal credits. Then come the adjusting entries: after the trial balance and before the financial statements, followed by an adjusted trial balance that reflects them. That position matters. The statements are built from adjusted balances, so an adjustment made after the statements would arrive too late, and an adjustment before the trial balance would defeat the check. The trial balance and the full cycle each have their own lessons; the point here is the slot: adjustments sit between the rough check and the final report, every period, without exception.

collegeVersion.heading: Adjusting versus closing, and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Two end-of-period routines sound alike and do opposite jobs. Adjusting entries update the accounts so the period's statements tell the truth — they add what was missing. Closing entries, which CFI describes as zeroing out revenue and expense accounts, wipe the slate for the next period — they reset what the period produced. Adjustments happen before the statements; closing happens after. Adjusting never resets an account, and closing never corrects a balance. And the honest framing: adjustments are not busywork or a loophole. They are how accountants tell the truth about a period. OpenStax says the entries exist so the income statement and balance sheet present correct, up-to-date numbers, and CFI says the statements end up reflecting a more accurate financial picture of the company. A company that skips adjustments does not save time — it publishes a rough draft as its final report.

vocabulary.definition: Journal entries made at the end of an accounting period to record transactions and events the books have not yet captured; the definition guiding this lesson comes from OpenStax's Principles of Accounting.
The stretch of time — often a month, quarter, or year — over which a business records activity and reports results before the cycle begins again.
An asset created when a business pays for something in advance, such as supplies, rent, or insurance; the used-up portion becomes an expense at period end.
A liability created when a customer pays before the business delivers the goods or service; it becomes revenue as the business performs.
A cost incurred in the period but not yet recorded or paid, such as wages earned but unpaid or interest that has accumulated on a loan.
Income earned in the period but not yet recorded or collected, such as services completed but not yet billed to the customer.
Entries made after the financial statements that zero out revenue and expense accounts so the next accounting period starts fresh.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Adjusting entries are the end-of-period updates that catch the quiet stuff. During the month, the bookkeeper records what arrives with paperwork: sales, purchases, payments. But some things happen without paperwork. The studio used up part of its paper supply. The rent paid in advance got a little more used up with each passing week. Employees earned wages that will not be paid until next month. None of these produced a document, so none were recorded — yet they all happened. At period end, the bookkeeper makes an adjusting entry for each one: the used-up prepayments move from asset to expense, the unpaid wages appear as an expense and a liability, and the unbilled work appears as revenue. Then the statements are built from numbers that match reality.
eli10.analogy: Think of a gym membership. You pay for the whole year in January, but the membership is used up a little every time you walk in. If you tracked it only as one big January purchase, your January would look expensive and your summer would look free. The honest picture comes from spreading the cost across the months you actually use the gym — exactly what an adjusting entry does for prepaid rent or supplies.
eli10.analogyLimits: The gym analogy covers prepayments, but adjustments do more than spread costs: they also add things cash never touched, like wages owed but unpaid or work done but not yet billed. And unlike a gym membership, adjusting entries follow rules about which accounts move and when — not how a person feels about fairness.

workedExample: Maple Row Studio rents its workshop for $1,800 per month, paid quarterly in advance. On April 1 it pays $5,400, recorded as prepaid rent. By April 30, one month — $1,800 — has been used, so the adjusting entry increases rent expense by $1,800 and decreases prepaid rent by $1,800. The studio also owes its two assistants $2,200 in wages for the last week of April, payable May 1: an accrued expense, recorded as wages expense up and wages payable up. And it finished a $950 design job on April 28 without billing yet: accrued revenue, recorded as accounts receivable up and service revenue up. After the three adjustments, April's statements show the real cost of doing business in April — and the rent asset on the balance sheet is down to $3,600, the two months still to come.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating adjusting entries as error corrections.
commonMistakes.correction: Adjustments record real activity that was never captured; a genuine mistake — a wrong amount or a misfiled transaction — gets a correcting entry. Mixing the two hides both problems.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting cash in an adjusting entry.
commonMistakes.correction: Adjusting entries move amounts between income statement and balance sheet accounts; the cash side was recorded when the payment happened. An adjusting entry that touches cash usually means the original transaction was recorded twice.

commonMistakes.mistake: Adjusting only when something looks wrong.
commonMistakes.correction: Adjustments are a matter of routine, not of suspicion: they happen every period, even a quiet one, because gradual events like using supplies and accruing wages never stop.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing adjusting entries with closing entries.
commonMistakes.correction: Adjusting updates the period's balances before the statements; closing zeroes out revenue and expense accounts after the statements so the next period starts fresh. Doing one in place of the other leaves the books either unfinished or reset too early.

compareContrast.distinction: Adjusting entries add missing activity so the current period's statements are accurate; closing entries reset revenue and expense accounts to zero after the statements so the next period starts fresh.

A prepaid expense is an asset for what the business has already paid for and will use; unearned revenue is a liability for what the business still owes customers after being paid in advance. Both are adjusted as time passes.
An accrued expense is a cost incurred but unpaid, creating a payable; accrued revenue is income earned but uncollected, creating a receivable. Both record activity before cash moves.

keyTakeaway: Adjusting entries are how the books tell the truth about a period: they capture the gradual activity that never triggered an entry, so the statements show what really happened.

title: Income Statement
in30Seconds: The income statement is the scoreboard for a period. It reports a business's revenue at the top, its expenses below, and the profit or loss at the bottom — this lesson's definition follows OpenStax's Principles of Accounting. The math is one subtraction: revenue minus expenses. Gross figures come before other items are subtracted; net figures come after. The statement shows earnings, not cash movements, and it answers one question: did the business make money this period?
whyItMatters: Every money decision about a business starts with its income statement. Owners read it to see whether their work made money and how much they can take out or reinvest. Lenders read it to decide whether the business can repay a loan. Investors read it to judge whether profits are growing before they buy or hold shares. It is also the easiest statement to misunderstand: a profitable business can still run short of cash, and a big revenue number can hide a loss. Learn to read the scoreboard — what the lines mean, what the bottom line is, and what it does not tell you — and you can judge any business's performance for yourself.
learningObjectives: Define the income statement using the working definition in this lesson, attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting: a statement that shows the organization's financial performance — its revenues and expenses — for a given period of time, ending in profit or loss.
Describe the shape of the income statement in words: revenue at the top, expenses below, and profit or loss at the bottom.
Compute profit or loss by subtracting expenses from revenue, using an original bakery example.
Distinguish gross from net: gross figures come before other items are subtracted; net figures come after everything is subtracted.
Explain that the income statement shows earnings, not cash movements, and that the statement of cash flows is the sibling topic that tracks cash.
Name who reads the income statement — owners, lenders, and investors — what each looks for, and apply the honest framing: the statement answers one question, did the business make money this period?

collegeVersion.heading: What an income statement is: the scoreboard for a period
collegeVersion.body: The income statement, per OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, shows the organization's financial performance for a given period of time. CFI describes the same document as one of a company's core financial statements, showing profit and loss over a period of time and summarizing all revenues and expenses from operating and non-operating activities. The period matters: it can be a month, a quarter, or a year, and the statement's heading is labeled with the dates it covers — 'for the month ended July 31,' not 'as of July 31.' The scoreboard analogy fits: the statement keeps score for a stretch of play, not for a single moment. A statement that shows a snapshot at one moment — what a business owns and owes — is the balance sheet, a sibling topic referenced here only.

collegeVersion.heading: The shape: revenue at the top, expenses below, profit or loss at the bottom
collegeVersion.body: The statement has a fixed shape, and you can describe it in words without a spreadsheet. Revenue sits at the very top — CFI notes that sales revenue is displayed at the very top of the statement, and it is the first line anyone reads. Below it come the expenses: the direct cost of what was sold first, then operating expenses such as wages and rent, and further down items such as interest and taxes. The bottom line is the profit or loss — net income when revenues and gains are greater than expenses and losses, net loss when the reverse is true, as OpenStax states it. Readers work top to bottom: the top shows how much business happened, the middle shows what it cost, and the bottom shows what was left. That bottom line is the number the whole statement is built to produce.

collegeVersion.heading: The simple arithmetic: revenue minus expenses
collegeVersion.body: The whole statement rests on one subtraction: revenue minus expenses equals net income or net loss. OpenStax writes the income statement as the formula Revenue − Expenses = Net Income/(Loss). Take a small bakery's month. Meadow & Main Bakery sells 2,400 loaves at $3.50 in July, earning $8,400 in revenue. Its expenses for the month — flour and other ingredients, wages for two bakers, rent, utilities, and delivery fuel — come to $6,150. Revenue minus expenses: $8,400 − $6,150 = $2,250 of net income. If expenses had instead reached $9,100, the same subtraction gives $8,400 − $9,100 = −$700, a net loss of $700. One subtraction, two possible endings: profit or loss.

collegeVersion.heading: Gross vs net: before and after
collegeVersion.body: The words gross and net mark where you are in the statement. A gross figure comes before other items are subtracted; a net figure comes after everything is subtracted. CFI's example is gross profit: it is calculated by subtracting the cost of goods sold from sales revenue — for a bakery, the cost of the ingredients that went into the bread — before any rent, wages, or utilities are taken out. Net income, by contrast, is the figure after every expense on the statement has been deducted. For Meadow & Main, the bread line's gross profit is $8,400 − $1,900 = $6,500: the bread money minus what the bread itself cost. The month's net income, $2,250, is what remains after the other $4,250 of expenses come out too. Gross is the earlier, bigger number; net is the final one.

collegeVersion.heading: Profit vs cash: earnings are not banknotes
collegeVersion.body: Here is the honest note of this lesson: the income statement shows earnings, not cash movements. A profitable month does not guarantee a fat bank account, and a loss does not mean the business is out of cash. OpenStax's own opening example makes the point: a landscaping business earned $1,400 and spent $1,150, a $250 gain on paper, while its checking account told a slightly different story depending on when bills were paid. Customers who pay later, purchases made before the month, and loan repayments all move cash without showing up as this month's revenue or expense. The statement that tracks cash movements — operating, investing, and financing — is the statement of cash flows, a sibling topic referenced here only.

collegeVersion.heading: Who reads it: owners, lenders, and investors
collegeVersion.body: Different readers come to the income statement with different questions. Owners read it to see whether the business made money and what they can take out or leave in; OpenStax notes that owners use the financial statements to make decisions about their businesses. Lenders read it to judge whether the business earns more than it spends and can repay what it borrows — OpenStax gives the example of a banker who studies the statements to decide whether to lend. Investors read it to watch whether profits are growing, which is why CFI calls the statement vital to investors and company management. Each reader lands on the same bottom line, but each reads it for a different decision.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing: one question
collegeVersion.body: The honest framing of this lesson: the income statement answers one question — did the business make money this period? It does not answer whether the business is healthy overall, whether it can pay its bills next month, or whether it is a good investment; those questions belong to the balance sheet, the statement of cash flows, and ratio analysis, each a sibling topic. A single loss is not a verdict on a business, any more than one winning month proves it is safe. The statement is a scoreboard for the period it covers: read the dates in the heading, read the subtraction, and you know what the score was.

vocabulary.definition: A financial statement that shows an organization's financial performance for a given period of time, reporting revenue, expenses, and the resulting profit or loss; also called the profit and loss statement.
The stretch of time an income statement covers, such as a month, a quarter, or a year, stated in the heading of the statement.
The value of the goods and services a business provides to its customers, displayed at the top of the income statement.
The costs a business incurs to provide goods and services, listed below revenue on the income statement and subtracted from it.
The profit for the period, which occurs when revenues and gains are greater than expenses and losses.
The loss for the period, which occurs when expenses and losses are greater than revenues and gains.
Revenue minus the direct cost of what was sold, computed before other expenses such as rent and wages are subtracted.
The nickname for the final figure on the income statement, the net income or net loss, because it sits at the bottom.
The sibling statement that reports a business's cash movements from operating, investing, and financing activities; referenced in this lesson only.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: An income statement is the scoreboard for a stretch of business time — a month, a quarter, or a year. It lists what the business earned at the top, what it spent below that, and the profit or loss at the very bottom. The math is one subtraction: earnings minus spending. Gross figures come before other costs are subtracted; net figures come after everything is subtracted. And the scoreboard shows the score, not the cash: a business can show a profit and still be short on cash, because customers may pay later and bills may be due sooner. The income statement answers one question: did the business make money this period?
eli10.analogy: Think of a basketball scoreboard at the end of the quarter. The board shows points scored at the top and the final score at the bottom — the whole game's result on one board. An income statement is that scoreboard for a business's period. The revenue line is the points scored; the expense lines are the points given up; the bottom line is the final score. Fans glance at the final score first, and so do owners, lenders, and investors.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy has limits. A game ends with a final whistle, but a business plays on, period after period, and no single quarter's score is the whole season. The scoreboard also shows points, not the team's bank account: sales made on credit count as revenue before the cash arrives, and the scoreboard says nothing about whether the team can pay its next payroll. Cash movements have their own statement, the statement of cash flows.

workedExample: Meadow & Main Bakery closes its books for July. The month's revenue: 2,400 loaves sold at $3.50 each, $8,400. The month's expenses: ingredients, $1,900; wages for two bakers, $2,400; rent, $1,200; utilities, $450; delivery fuel, $200 — $6,150 in total. The income statement runs top to bottom: revenue $8,400, expenses $6,150, and the bottom line, $2,250 of net income, because $8,400 − $6,150 = $2,250. The bread line alone shows a gross profit of $6,500 — the $8,400 of sales minus the $1,900 of ingredients — before the other $4,250 of expenses are subtracted. None of this says the bakery's bank account grew by $2,250: a wholesale customer pays in August, and the rent check clears before month-end. The statement reports July's earnings; cash is another statement's job.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading the income statement as a snapshot of one moment.
commonMistakes.correction: The statement covers a period — a month, a quarter, or a year — and its heading says so; a point-in-time picture of what a business owns and owes is the balance sheet, a sibling topic.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating net income as cash in the bank.
commonMistakes.correction: Net income is earnings, not cash movements; customers who pay later and bills due sooner can make a profitable period look short on cash, which is why the statement of cash flows exists.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing gross and net.
commonMistakes.correction: Gross figures come before other items are subtracted — gross profit is revenue minus the direct cost of what was sold; net income comes after every expense on the statement.

commonMistakes.mistake: Judging the whole business on one period's bottom line.
commonMistakes.correction: One month's loss is not a verdict on a business; the income statement answers only whether the business made money in the period it covers.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading the bottom line without checking the period.
commonMistakes.correction: A $5,000 profit means very different things over a month and over a year; read the dates in the heading first.

compareContrast.distinction: The income statement covers a period — revenue, expenses, and profit or loss — while the balance sheet is a snapshot at a single moment, showing what a business owns and owes; the balance sheet is a sibling topic.

A gross figure comes before other items are subtracted (gross profit is revenue minus the direct cost of what was sold); a net figure comes after everything is subtracted (net income is revenue minus all expenses).
The income statement reports earnings for the period; the statement of cash flows reports actual cash movements, and the two can differ whenever payments and expenses fall in different periods.

keyTakeaway: The income statement is the scoreboard for a period: revenue at the top, expenses below, and profit or loss at the bottom. It is built on one subtraction — revenue minus expenses — and it answers one question: did the business make money this period? Gross comes before, net comes after, and earnings are not the same as cash.

questionBank.prompt: A bakery's income statement for June lists its sales at the top, its costs below, and one final figure at the bottom. What does that final figure report?

title: Balance Sheet
in30Seconds: A balance sheet is a financial statement that shows what a business owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities), and what is left for its owners (equity) at a single moment in time. It is a snapshot, dated “as of” one specific day, not a report of activity over a period like the income statement. Its items are grouped into current (within one year) and non-current (beyond one year) sections, and the two sides always match: assets equal liabilities plus equity.
whyItMatters: Every serious question about a business starts with where it stands right now: can it pay what it owes soon, how much debt is it carrying, and what would the owners actually take away if it stopped tomorrow? The balance sheet is the report that answers those questions. Lenders read it before approving a loan, suppliers before extending credit, owners to see what their stake is worth, and managers to spot problems early. Reading one correctly also protects you from being impressed by size alone — a big company can sit on a weak balance sheet. It is the foundation for the ratio analysis and lending decisions you will meet in later lessons.
learningObjectives: Define the balance sheet as a snapshot: a financial statement that reports what a business owns, owes, and is worth on a specific date.
Explain the shape of the balance sheet as the accounting equation in statement form, with assets on one side and liabilities plus equity on the other.
Distinguish a point-in-time statement from a period statement, contrasting the balance sheet with the income statement.
Classify balance sheet items into current and non-current sections using the one-year horizon.
Explain what owners and lenders each look for when they read a balance sheet.
Evaluate the honest framing that a balance sheet always balances by construction and that the real question is what the numbers mean.

collegeVersion.heading: What a balance sheet is (the snapshot)
collegeVersion.body: OpenStax’s Principles of Accounting describes the balance sheet as a statement that lists what the organization owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities), and what it is worth (equity) on a specific date. Corporate Finance Institute calls it a snapshot of what a company owns, what it owes, and the value left for the owners. Two words in those definitions carry the whole idea: specific date. The balance sheet is a photograph, not a movie. It shows the financial position of a business at one chosen moment — the close of business on a particular day — and that day is printed at the top of the statement, usually written “as of” a date. Change any transaction after that moment and the picture would be slightly different. This is why the balance sheet is sometimes called the statement of financial position: it answers the question “where does this business stand right now?”, not “how did it get here?”

collegeVersion.heading: The shape: the equation in statement form
collegeVersion.body: The balance sheet has two sides. On one side sit the assets: cash, inventory, equipment, buildings, and everything else the business owns or controls. On the other side sit the liabilities — what the business owes to others — and equity, the owners’ claim on what remains. The two sides always match because the statement is simply the accounting equation written out: assets = liabilities + equity. The equation itself, why it holds, and how transactions keep it in balance are a separate topic covered in its own lesson. What matters here is the shape: the balance sheet is the equation in statement form, with total assets on one side and total liabilities plus total equity on the other, so the bottom lines always agree. A statement that did not balance would mean the accounting records behind it were wrong.

collegeVersion.heading: The moment in time
collegeVersion.body: The most important habit when reading a balance sheet is to notice the date. The income statement reports what happened over a period — a month, a quarter, a year — and OpenStax describes it as a statement of financial performance for a given period of time. The balance sheet works the opposite way: it reports position at the close of business on one specific date, so it is a snapshot, not a period report. A balance sheet dated December 31 shows the business as it stood at that instant; everything that happened in January is invisible to it. Comparing snapshots — last year’s balance sheet against this year’s — is how you see change over time, but any single balance sheet is frozen at one moment.

collegeVersion.heading: Current and non-current sections
collegeVersion.body: Inside each side, items are grouped by time. Current assets are expected to be used up or converted to cash within one year, and current liabilities are expected to be settled within one year. Everything that works on a longer horizon goes into the non-current sections: non-current assets such as buildings, equipment, and land, and non-current liabilities such as long-term loans and mortgages. OpenStax stresses why the split matters: knowing a business owes $750,000 is useful, but knowing that only $125,000 of it is due within a year is far more useful. The current sections show what the business can mobilize soon against what it must pay soon — the near-term pressure point of the whole statement.

collegeVersion.heading: Reading a balance sheet: owners and lenders
collegeVersion.body: Owners and lenders read the same statement for different reasons. Owners look at equity, the value left for them after subtracting what the business owes; it is their stake, built from what they invested plus profit the business kept. Lenders look at the other side of the picture: what the business owes, and especially whether its current assets can cover what comes due in the near term. A lender weighing a one-year loan wants to know whether the borrower will have the cash when the payment lands. CFI summarizes the statement’s purpose as helping investors, lenders, and leaders assess performance, funding needs, and overall financial strength — the same document, three different questions.

collegeVersion.heading: Balance sheet versus income statement, and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: The contrast between the two statements is simple: the income statement is the period report (revenues minus expenses over time), and the balance sheet is the snapshot (position at a moment). The honest framing follows from the shape itself. Because the balance sheet is built from the accounting equation, it always balances — the two sides match by construction, whether the company is thriving or struggling. That means a balanced statement is not praise; it is arithmetic. The real question is what the numbers mean: whether the assets are productive, whether the debt is manageable, and whether the equity is real value or a thin cushion. Analysts use the balance sheet to assess liquidity, financial strength, and leverage — the meaning behind the matching totals.

vocabulary.definition: A financial statement that reports what a business owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities), and what is left for its owners (equity) on a specific date.
Another name for the balance sheet, used because the statement reports a business’s financial position at a single point in time.
The date printed on a balance sheet that marks the exact moment, usually the close of business, whose financial position the statement reports.
An asset expected to be used up or converted to cash within one year, such as cash, accounts receivable, or inventory.
An asset expected to keep serving the business beyond one year, such as equipment, buildings, or land.
An obligation expected to be settled within one year, such as a short-term loan or unpaid supplier bills.
An obligation due more than one year out, such as a long-term loan or a mortgage.
The owners’ claim on the business, equal to what remains of the assets after subtracting what the business owes to others.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: The balance sheet is a photograph of a business taken at one exact moment. The camera catches everything the business owns — its cash, its stock of goods, its machines and buildings — on one side of the picture. On the other side it catches everything the business owes, plus what belongs to the owners. The two sides always match, because every thing the business has was paid for either with borrowed money (a liability) or with the owners’ money (equity). Items that will be used or paid within a year go in the current sections; everything else goes in the non-current sections. A fresh photograph is taken as of each reporting date, so you can compare one snapshot with the next to see how the business is changing.
eli10.analogy: Think of the balance sheet as a weigh station on a highway. A truck pulls in, and the scale records its load at that exact moment — one reading, not a log of the whole trip. The driver’s trip log (the income statement) tells you about the journey; the scale (the balance sheet) tells you how heavy the truck is right now. Owners and lenders both look at the scale reading, though they care about different parts of the load.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks down because a truck’s weight is a fact you simply measure, while a balance sheet’s numbers are judgments made by accountants — what something is worth, how fast it will be used up, and which accounting rules the business chose. Also, a weigh station has one scale, but the same business can produce different snapshots under different rules, which is why comparing statements means knowing the rules behind them.

workedExample: Northgate Print Shop opens on March 1 with $25,000 in cash: $15,000 from owner Priya’s savings and a $10,000 bank loan. Priya buys a $12,000 printing press, $8,000 of paper and ink, and keeps $5,000 in cash. The balance sheet as of March 1 shows assets of $25,000 — the press ($12,000, non-current), inventory ($8,000, current), and cash ($5,000, current) — balanced against liabilities of $10,000 and equity of $15,000. The loan splits into $2,000 due within a year (current liability) and $8,000 due in three years (non-current). A lender reads $13,000 of current assets against $2,000 of current liabilities; Priya reads $15,000 of equity that is hers to keep growing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading the balance sheet as if it covered a period
commonMistakes.correction: A balance sheet shows one moment; activity over time belongs on the income statement. Check the “as of” date and treat the statement as frozen at that instant.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a balanced sheet means a healthy business
commonMistakes.correction: The two sides match by construction for every business that keeps proper records, profitable or not. Balancing is arithmetic; look at what the numbers mean before judging.

commonMistakes.mistake: Sorting items by how long-term they feel instead of using the one-year rule
commonMistakes.correction: A machine headed for sale within a year is current, and a loan payment due in nine months is current even if the rest of the loan runs for years. Apply the one-year horizon to each item.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring the “as of” date
commonMistakes.correction: A balance sheet from six months ago may say nothing about today. Match the statement date to the question you are asking before drawing conclusions.

compareContrast.distinction: A snapshot of financial position at a single date versus a period report of revenues minus expenses over time.
Current items are expected to be used up, converted to cash, or settled within one year; non-current items operate on a horizon beyond one year.
One shows what the business has; the other shows who supplied it — creditors or owners — and the claims each holds.

keyTakeaway: A balance sheet is a snapshot of what a business owns, owes, and is worth on one specific date, with assets on one side and liabilities plus equity on the other — and because it always balances by construction, the real work is judging what the numbers mean.

questionBank.prompt: What does a balance sheet report?
options: A business's assets, liabilities, and equity at a single moment in time
A business's revenues and expenses over a period of time
The cash that flowed in and out during the year
The market value of the business's stock
questionBank.explanation: A balance sheet reports what a business owns (assets), owes (liabilities), and what is left for the owners (equity) on a specific date. Revenues and expenses belong on the income statement, cash flows belong on the cash flow statement, and stock price is a market figure, not a balance sheet line.
questionBank.skill: Identifying what the balance sheet reports

questionBank.prompt: A balance sheet is dated "as of June 30." What does that date tell you?
options: It covers the six months of activity ending June 30
It shows the financial position at the close of business on June 30
The business first opened its doors on June 30
All of the business's debts come due on June 30
questionBank.explanation: The "as of" date marks the exact moment the snapshot was taken: the balance sheet shows financial position at the close of business on that day. It does not summarize activity over time, mark the start of the business, or set a single due date for debts.
questionBank.skill: Interpreting the point-in-time nature of the balance sheet

questionBank.prompt: A delivery company holds $40,000 cash, $60,000 of customer invoices due within 60 days, and two loans: $15,000 due next March and $85,000 due in five years. Which items go in the current sections of its balance sheet?
options: Cash and the customer invoices only
The $15,000 loan due next March only
Cash, the customer invoices, and the $15,000 loan
Cash and the $85,000 five-year loan
questionBank.explanation: The current sections hold items that will be used up, converted to cash, or settled within one year. Cash and the customer invoices are current assets, and the $15,000 loan payment due within a year is a current liability; the $85,000 loan is non-current.
questionBank.skill: Classifying balance sheet items into current and non-current sections

questionBank.prompt: A lender must decide whether to give a bakery a one-year loan. Which reading of the bakery's balance sheet will the lender weigh most heavily?
options: The non-current assets, such as the building and the ovens
The owner's equity line on its own
The total of all long-term loans the bakery already carries
Current assets compared with current liabilities: what the bakery can turn into cash soon versus what it must pay soon
questionBank.explanation: A lender wants to know whether the bakery can pay what comes due within the loan's horizon, so it weighs near-term resources against near-term obligations. Buildings and ovens are long-term assets, equity alone does not show repayment capacity, and long-term loans miss the timing of the question.
questionBank.skill: Reasoning about what a lender looks for in the balance sheet

questionBank.prompt: Why does a balance sheet always balance, even for a business that is losing money?
options: Accountants adjust the numbers until the two sides happen to match
Assets equal liabilities plus equity by the design of the accounting system
Only businesses with balanced records are allowed to publish one
Auditors correct every statement before it is released
questionBank.explanation: The balance sheet is built from the accounting equation, so the two sides match by construction for any business that keeps proper records, profitable or not. No adjustment, permission, or audit is what makes it balance.
questionBank.skill: Explaining why the balance sheet balances by construction

title: Statement of Cash Flows
in30Seconds: The statement of cash flows is a financial report showing the cash coming into a business and going out over a period, organized by activity — the this lesson's definition comes from OpenStax's Principles of Accounting. It has three sections: operating, investing, and financing. Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact. Because a profitable business can still run out of cash, the statement answers the simplest question: can this business pay its bills?
whyItMatters: The income statement reports profit, but profit is not the same as cash in the bank. Businesses pay employees, suppliers, and lenders with cash — and a company can show a healthy profit while its bank account drains. The statement of cash flows is where readers see where cash actually came from and where it went, which is precisely what lenders, owners, and managers need to judge whether the business can keep operating. Learning to read it separates a real sense of a company's health from the impression the income statement alone can give. That skill pays off in any role that watches money move: running a business, lending to one, or investing in one.
learningObjectives: Define the statement of cash flows as a report of cash coming in and going out over a period, organized by activity, using the working definition from OpenStax's Principles of Accounting.
Name the three sections — operating, investing, and financing — and give one original example of each.
Explain why cash matters separately from profit: profit is an opinion, cash is a fact.
Distinguish cash flow from profit, and explain how a profitable business can still run out of cash.
Describe what the statement shows: where cash came from and where it went.
Explain the honest framing: the statement answers the simplest question — can this business pay its bills?

collegeVersion.heading: What the statement of cash flows is
collegeVersion.body: OpenStax's Principles of Accounting defines the statement of cash flows as a financial statement listing the cash inflows and cash outflows for the business for a period of time. CFI describes cash flow in the same spirit: the increase or decrease in the amount of money a business has. Two halves of that definition matter. First, it tracks cash — currency that actually moved, not amounts earned on paper. Second, it covers a period — a month, a quarter, or a year — not a single moment. The statement is one of the four major financial statements; OpenStax's Section 2.1 lists the four in preparation order: income statement, statement of owner's equity, balance sheet, and statement of cash flows last. It is prepared last because it draws on the others. The organizing principle is activity: every cash movement is sorted into one of three sections — operating, investing, or financing.

collegeVersion.heading: The three sections
collegeVersion.body: Operating activities are the day-to-day activities a business uses to produce income. In OpenStax's words, operating cash flows come from sales and go to inventory, salaries, and utilities. One line: the daily business — money collected from customers in, money paid for the stuff of running the shop out. Original example: a bakery's operating section shows cash from bread sales and cash paid for flour, wages, and the electric bill. Investing activities are transactions in long-term assets. One line: buying and selling the big things the business uses for years. Original example: the same bakery pays $18,000 cash for a second oven — that outflow goes in investing; selling its old van for $3,000 puts a cash inflow there. Financing activities are about raising money and paying it back. One line: money from lenders and owners in, repayments and dividends out. Original example: the bakery borrows $20,000 from the bank (an inflow) and repays $5,000 of the loan principal (an outflow). Each section nets to one number, and the three nets add up to the period's total change in cash.

collegeVersion.heading: Why cash matters separately
collegeVersion.body: The income statement reports profit, but profit is built on the accrual basis, not on cash. CFI puts it plainly: income and profit are based on accrual accounting principles, which smooth out expenditures and match revenues to the timing of delivery, so a company's net income can be materially different from its cash flow. OpenStax makes the same point from the other side: accrual accounting creates timing differences between income statement accounts and cash — a revenue can be recorded in a different year than the one its cash arrives. That is why cash deserves its own statement. The honest framing, stated simply: profit is an opinion — a judgment built on rules about when to count revenue and expenses; cash is a fact — the money that actually moved. The income statement is a sibling topic with a lesson of its own; here it appears only as the contrast that explains why the cash flow statement exists.

collegeVersion.heading: Cash flow vs profit
collegeVersion.body: A profitable business can still run out of cash. Here is an original example. Brightside Landscaping finishes $100,000 of work in March and bills its customers, who pay in sixty days — so no cash arrives in March. Meanwhile it pays $65,000 in crew wages and $20,000 for plants and materials, all in cash, during the month. The income statement reports revenue of $100,000, expenses of $85,000, and a profit of $15,000. The bank account tells another story: $0 in, $85,000 out. Brightside started March with $60,000, so it holds less than it owes, and the $25,000 loan installment due at month-end goes unpaid. Profit of $15,000, and the business cannot pay its bills. Nothing in the numbers is wrong: the profit is real, and so is the cash shortage. Only the statement of cash flows shows both at once.

collegeVersion.heading: What the statement shows
collegeVersion.body: OpenStax's Section 16.1 states the read directly: the statement answers two questions — what are the sources of cash, where does the cash come from, and what are the uses of cash, where does the cash go. Sources are the inflows: collections from customers, proceeds from selling equipment, money borrowed. Uses are the outflows: payments to suppliers and staff, purchases of equipment, loan repayments, dividends. The three sections organize the answer, and the bottom line is the net cash flow — positive means cash increased over the period, negative means it decreased. The practical read: run your eye down the sections rather than the total — which activities produced the cash, and which consumed it? A business that generates cash from operating while spending on equipment tells a different story from one that stays afloat by borrowing.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Strip the statement to its simplest question: can this business pay its bills? Profit does not pay suppliers — cash does. That is why OpenStax's Section 2.1 notes that accounting provides cash flow information to potential lenders, and why OpenStax's Section 16.1 says the statement lets users see how well a company's income generates cash and predict its future cash generation. CFI is blunter: cash flow is the lifeblood of a company. The cash flow statement is the reality check because it undoes the accrual estimates — in CFI's phrase, it shows pure cash movements — and reports what actually happened to the money. A lender, an owner, or an employee can ask one question of the statement and get an honest answer: when the bills arrive, will the cash be there?

vocabulary.definition: A financial statement listing the cash inflows and cash outflows for a business over a period of time, organized by operating, investing, and financing activity.
Cash coming into a business, such as collections from customers, proceeds from selling equipment, or money borrowed from a lender.
Cash leaving a business, such as payments for inventory, wages, equipment, loan repayments, or dividends to owners.
The day-to-day activities a business uses to produce income; their cash flows come from sales and go to inventory, salaries, and utilities.
Transactions involving a business's long-term assets, such as buying or selling land, buildings, and equipment.
Transactions that raise money from debt or stock and repay it, including borrowing, issuing stock, paying dividends, and repaying loan principal.
The difference between a period's cash inflows and cash outflows; a positive net cash flow means cash increased and a negative one means it decreased.
The two sides of the statement of cash flows: sources show where cash came from and uses show where cash went.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: The statement of cash flows is a business's cash report card for a stretch of time. It does not ask whether the business earned a profit — the income statement handles that question. It asks a simpler, harder one: did cash actually come in, did cash actually go out, and which kinds of activities moved it? The whole statement is one ledger with three drawers: everyday business in the operating drawer, big purchases and sales in the investing drawer, and borrowed or owner money in the financing drawer. Add up the three drawers and you get the change in cash for the period.
eli10.analogy: Picture the business's cash as water in a tank. Three pipes feed or drain the tank. The operating pipe carries the daily flow: customer payments in, rent and wages out. The investing pipe moves big one-time amounts: buying a delivery van drains the tank, selling an old one tops it up. The financing pipe connects to the bank and the owners: a loan fills the tank, while loan repayments and dividends drain it. The statement of cash flows is the meter reading that shows how much water moved through each pipe over the year — and whether the tank ended higher or lower than it started.
eli10.analogyLimits: Pipes do not make judgment calls, but people classify some transactions, and the rules can place a single payment in a section that surprises you: interest paid, for example, sits in operating activities under U.S. GAAP. The tank level is also just one point in time — the statement covers a period, while the balance sheet captures the level on a single date. And water in a tank can sit there safely, whereas idle cash in a business often earns little, which is a different problem the analogy cannot show.

workedExample: Harbor Coffee runs a single coffee cart, and the owner wants to know where the year's cash went. The statement of cash flows answers it. Operating: customers paid $120,000 for coffee, while rent, wages, and supplies consumed $90,000 — net operating cash, +$30,000. Investing: she bought a second cart for $15,000 and sold the old one for $2,000 — net investing, −$13,000. Financing: she borrowed $20,000 from the bank and repaid $5,000 of the loan principal — net financing, +$15,000. Net change in cash: $30,000 − $13,000 + $15,000 = +$32,000. The year started with $8,000 in the bank and ended with $40,000. The three sections show the story behind the total: the cart's daily business produced the cash, the new cart consumed some of it, and borrowing covered the difference.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating net income as cash in the bank — assuming the profit on the income statement equals the change in cash.
commonMistakes.correction: Profit is measured on the accrual basis and can differ from cash flow in a period; check the statement of cash flows for the actual money movement.

commonMistakes.mistake: Judging a section's sign in isolation — assuming negative investing cash flow is always bad or positive financing cash flow is always good.
commonMistakes.correction: Buying equipment shows up as negative investing cash but may be growth spending; OpenStax notes that investors do not always take negative cash flow as negative, so read the sign with context.

commonMistakes.mistake: Misclassifying activities — putting an equipment purchase in operating or a loan repayment in investing.
commonMistakes.correction: Long-term assets belong in investing, borrowing and repaying debt belong in financing, and the day-to-day business belongs in operating.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading only the bottom line — looking at the net change in cash and skipping the three sections.
commonMistakes.correction: The net number hides which activities produced or consumed the cash; the sections are where the information lives.

compareContrast.distinction: Profit is measured on the accrual basis and can differ materially from cash flow in a period; cash flow is the actual money that moved in and out.
The statement of cash flows covers a period of time and shows cash movements; the balance sheet is a snapshot of assets, liabilities, and equity at one point in time.
Operating activities are the day-to-day business that produces income; financing activities raise money from lenders and owners and pay it back.

keyTakeaway: The statement of cash flows tracks the cash coming in and going out over a period, organized into operating, investing, and financing activity — and it answers the simplest question a business faces: can it pay its bills?

questionBank.prompt: Which three sections make up the statement of cash flows?
options: Operating, investing, and financing
Revenue, expenses, and profit
Assets, liabilities, and equity
Debits, credits, and balances
questionBank.explanation: The statement organizes cash movements into operating, investing, and financing activities. Revenue and expenses belong to the income statement, assets, liabilities, and equity to the balance sheet, and debits and credits to the mechanics of recording.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the three sections of the statement of cash flows

questionBank.prompt: A bakery pays $18,000 cash for a second oven. In which section of its statement of cash flows does that payment appear?
options: Operating, because the oven helps bake the daily sales
Financing, because the bakery will use the oven for years
Investing, because the oven is a long-term asset
It does not appear, because the statement reports only sales and expenses
questionBank.explanation: Cash paid to buy long-term assets such as ovens, buildings, and equipment is an investing cash outflow. Operating covers day-to-day items like inventory and wages, and financing covers raising money and repaying it.
questionBank.skill: Classifying a transaction into the correct section of the statement

questionBank.prompt: Harbor Coffee started the year with $8,000 cash. Over the year it collected $120,000 from customers, paid $90,000 in operating costs, bought a second cart for $15,000, borrowed $20,000, and repaid $5,000 of loan principal. What is its ending cash balance?
questionBank.explanation: $8,000 + $120,000 − $90,000 − $15,000 + $20,000 − $5,000 = $38,000. Each item lands in a section — operating, investing, or financing — and the net change is added to the starting balance.
questionBank.skill: Computing the change in cash from operating, investing, and financing activity

questionBank.prompt: A landscaping company shows a $15,000 profit for the month, yet its cash fell and it missed a loan payment. Which explanation fits best?
options: The profit number must be wrong, because profit and cash always move together
The company's customers paid faster than the company paid its own bills
The company recorded no expenses during the month
The company earned revenue on credit, while wages and supplies were paid in cash during the month
questionBank.explanation: Accrual accounting records revenue when it is earned, so billed work counts as profit before the cash arrives, while the cash statement shows the actual outflows. Profit and cash can diverge, which is why the cash flow statement exists.
questionBank.skill: Explaining why profit and cash flow can diverge in a period

questionBank.prompt: Why does a lender reading a small business's financial statements turn to the statement of cash flows?

It predicts exactly how much profit the business will earn next year
It shows where cash actually came from and went, and loans are repaid in cash
It replaces the income statement and the balance sheet
questionBank.explanation: Lenders care whether the business can pay them back, and repayment happens in cash. The statement answers where cash came from and where it went, while profit alone does not show that.
