title: Accounts Receivable
in30Seconds: Accounts receivable is the money customers owe a business for goods or services already delivered — the working definition here comes from OpenStax's Principles of Accounting. Receivables arise when a business sells on credit: the customer gets the goods now and promises to pay later. Because that promise is expected to turn into cash, the receivable is an asset. The business collects it with invoices and follow-up, while watching the honest risk that some customers never pay.
whyItMatters: Businesses rarely get paid at the cash register. They sell on credit — to other companies, to agencies, to customers with accounts — and the amounts owed sit on their books as accounts receivable. For many businesses, receivables are among the largest assets they hold and the biggest source of the cash they will need next month. Reading them shows how much money is realistically on the way, how well the business collects, and how much risk it carries in customers who may never pay. Understanding receivables separates seeing a sale from seeing the money, which is exactly what lenders, managers, and owners must do.
learningObjectives: Define accounts receivable as money customers owe a business for goods or services already delivered, using the working definition from OpenStax's Principles of Accounting.
Explain how accounts receivable arises from selling on credit, and trace one original credit sale from delivery to payment.
Describe the asset view: a receivable is an asset because the business expects to receive cash for value it has already delivered.
Describe the collection process in general terms — invoices, payment terms, and follow-up.
Explain the honest risk that some customers never pay, and name what that risk is called: bad debts.
Describe aging receivables — sorting what customers owe by how long it has been owed — and explain why a business does it.

collegeVersion.heading: What accounts receivable is
collegeVersion.body: OpenStax's Principles of Accounting gives the working definition this lesson uses: accounts receivable is an outstanding customer debt on a credit sale — money a customer owes the company for goods or services already provided. OpenStax's Section 9.1 puts it directly: when revenue is recognized before cash arrives, the customer still owes the company money, and that money owed is a receivable. Receivables are expected to be paid within the company's operating period (less than a year), and the customer is sent an invoice with credit payment terms. CFI's revenue guide agrees: revenue is recorded when the performance obligation is satisfied whether or not payment has been received, with the unpaid amount recorded as accounts receivable. Two features matter: the goods were delivered, and the cash has not arrived — the customer's promise stands in for it.

collegeVersion.heading: How it arises: selling on credit
collegeVersion.body: Accounts receivable exists because businesses sell on credit — the practice of handing over the goods or the service now and agreeing to be paid later. Credit sales are ordinary practice: one company bills another, a clinic bills after a visit, a contractor sends an invoice after the job. Original example: Northline Print & Design delivers 500 menus to a restaurant group on March 14 and invoices $2,400 with terms of net 30 — payment due within thirty days. Northline has done its part, so under the revenue recognition principle the sale counts in March even though no cash has moved, and the restaurant group's $2,400 is now Northline's account receivable. The principle itself is a sibling topic; the consequence is that a credit sale creates a receivable the moment the business delivers.

collegeVersion.heading: The asset view
collegeVersion.body: Receivables are assets. OpenStax's Section 9.1 states it plainly: accounts receivable is considered an asset. The reason is the expectation of future cash — the business has already delivered value, and the customer's promise means cash should follow within the operating period. Assets are a sibling topic with their own lesson; this lesson only references the classification. On the balance sheet, accounts receivable sits on the asset side of the accounting equation — assets = liabilities + equity — which CFI's accounting-equation guide describes as the balance sheet's structure. An asset does not have to be cash in the bank; it can be a claim to future cash. That is exactly what a receivable is — value already given, payment still expected, only as strong as the customer's promise.

collegeVersion.heading: Collecting: invoices, payment terms, and follow-up
collegeVersion.body: Receivables do not collect themselves. The collection process rests on three named pieces. The invoice is the bill — what was delivered, how much is owed, and when it is due; OpenStax's Section 3.3 notes that the sales invoice is the original source document where transaction analysis begins. Payment terms are the conditions of the credit sale — how long the customer has to pay, commonly written as net 30 or net 60. Follow-up is what happens when a customer is late: a reminder, a second notice, a phone call, sometimes pausing further credit. Original example: when one of Northline's invoices passes its due date, the owner sends a reminder email, then a second notice, and moves the account to a follow-up list.

collegeVersion.heading: The risk: some customers never pay
collegeVersion.body: The honest note: some customers never pay. No matter how careful the business is, a few promises go unkept, and the money is simply not coming. Accounting names the problem: bad debts — receivables the business does not expect to collect. OpenStax's Section 9.2 covers how businesses account for uncollectible accounts: the direct write-off method removes a specific account when it clearly fails, and the allowance method estimates in advance the portion of receivables that will not be collected, using an allowance for doubtful accounts — a contra asset that reduces the receivable total to its net realizable value. The literacy-level point: expect a few losses, estimate them honestly, and keep trying to collect the full amount anyway.

collegeVersion.heading: Aging receivables
collegeVersion.body: Aging is the practice of sorting what customers owe by how long each invoice has been owed — described in words: the business lists every unpaid invoice and files it into a bucket by age, such as current (due within 30 days), 31 to 60 days past due, 61 to 90 days, and more than 90 days. OpenStax's Section 9.2 describes the balance sheet aging of receivables method, which splits accounts receivable into past-due categories and assigns an estimated uncollectible percentage to each. CFI describes the same tool from practice: aging shows who needs a follow-up invoice, which customers may be becoming a credit risk, and which accounts might be uncollectible. The older the bucket, the more follow-up it needs; a business typically runs the aging report monthly.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Strip the topic to its simplest shape: a sale on credit is a promise to pay. The business watches both halves. It watches the sale — the revenue earned when the goods or services are delivered, which belongs on the income statement. And it watches the promise — the receivable, which stays on the books until the cash actually arrives. OpenStax's Section 9.1 makes the point at the moment of creation: when revenue is recognized before cash payment, the customer still owes the company money, and that money owed is a receivable. CFI's revenue guide adds the end of the story: no additional revenue is recorded at collection — collecting only converts the promise into cash. The two halves can drift apart, and the receivable is where accounting watches the gap.

vocabulary.definition: Money customers owe a business for goods or services already delivered on credit; an outstanding customer debt on a credit sale.
A sale in which the customer receives the goods or services now and agrees to pay later, under stated payment terms.
The bill a business sends a customer, listing what was delivered, the amount owed, and when payment is due.
The conditions of a credit sale, including how long the customer has to pay — net 30, for example, means payment is due within thirty days.
Something a business owns or is owed that is expected to bring future value, such as cash, inventory, or a receivable.
A receivable the business does not expect to collect because the customer does not pay.
A listing of unpaid invoices sorted by how long each has been owed, grouped into age buckets such as current, 30, 60, and 90-plus days.
The estimated portion of receivables the business expects will never be collected, subtracted from the receivable total.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: When a business sells on credit, it does not walk away with cash — it walks away with a promise. That promise is a real thing the business owns, called an account receivable: the customer's name, the amount, and the day the money is due. The business keeps a list of every promise, marked by age. Young promises get a gentle reminder when they come due. Older promises get firmer follow-up. A few promises are never kept, and the business has to admit the money is not coming. A sale on credit is really two events: the sale, which is done, and the promise, which is still open. Accounts receivable is the promise waiting to be kept.
eli10.analogy: Think of accounts receivable as a row of IOUs on the business's fridge. Each IOU names a neighbor, an amount, and a payback date. The business trusts most neighbors, so the IOUs are worth something — they are promises of future cash, not scraps of paper. When a neighbor pays, the IOU comes down and cash goes in the drawer. When a neighbor goes quiet, the IOU stays up longer, and the business starts to wonder. A few IOUs will never be honored, and the business knows it. The fridge is the aging report: every IOU hangs in plain sight, sorted by how long it has been waiting.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks down where formality matters. An IOU between neighbors is informal and rarely enforced; a receivable is a formal business record backed by an invoice, agreed payment terms, and legal remedies. Neighbors usually pay; some customers genuinely cannot or will not, and businesses estimate those losses in advance. And one fridge holds a handful of IOUs, while a business can hold thousands of receivables, which is why it groups and ages them instead of eyeballing each one.

workedExample: Cedar & Sage Catering caters a wedding in June for $6,500, with payment terms of net 30. The work is delivered on June 14, and the invoice goes out the same day. Under the revenue recognition principle, Cedar & Sage records the $6,500 as revenue in June — the service is complete — and carries $6,500 in accounts receivable, because the client has not paid yet. On July 8 the client pays in full: cash rises by $6,500 and the receivable falls to zero. No new revenue is recorded at collection; the sale was already counted. Meanwhile, one March invoice — $900 for a corporate lunch — is now 120 days past due after three reminders and a phone call. The owner moves it to the 90-plus bucket on the aging report and, drawing on past experience, treats it as a likely bad debt, trimming the expected collectible amount of receivables. The $6,500 shows how a promise becomes cash; the $900 shows why the business watches its promises.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a credit sale as cash in the bank
commonMistakes.correction: Recording revenue is not the same as receiving money. The sale is counted when the goods or services are delivered, and the unpaid amount is a receivable — the cash arrives later, if at all.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming every receivable will be paid
commonMistakes.correction: Some customers never pay. Businesses estimate bad debts in advance rather than treating every dollar owed as certain cash.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing accounts receivable with accounts payable
commonMistakes.correction: Accounts receivable is money owed to the business — an asset. Accounts payable is money the business owes its suppliers — a liability. They are mirror images of the same kind of credit transaction.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting old invoices sit without follow-up
commonMistakes.correction: Receivables do not collect themselves. An aging report that nobody acts on is just a list; following up on overdue invoices is what turns promises into cash.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating an aging report as a death sentence for old invoices
commonMistakes.correction: An old invoice is riskier, but not automatically lost. Aging guides follow-up and estimation; it does not write off accounts by itself.

compareContrast.distinction: A receivable is money customers owe the business — an asset. A payable is money the business owes its suppliers — a liability. One credit sale is the same promise seen from two sides.
Cash is money in hand; a receivable is a promise expected to become cash. Both are assets, but only cash is already collected, so the receivable carries the risk of nonpayment.
A cash sale records revenue and receives cash at the same moment. A credit sale records revenue at delivery and receives cash later, holding the difference as accounts receivable.

keyTakeaway: Accounts receivable is the money customers owe for goods or services already delivered — an asset that becomes cash only when customers pay, which is why a business watches both the sale and the promise.

questionBank.prompt: A bakery finds three unpaid invoices: one 12 days past due, one 45 days past due, and one 80 days past due. Where does each fall on its aging report?

Only the 80-day invoice is listed, because the others are still recent
The 12-day invoice in the current bucket, the 45-day in the 31-to-60 bucket, and the 80-day in the 61-to-90 bucket
The 12-day invoice in the over-90 bucket and the other two in the current bucket
questionBank.explanation: Aging sorts invoices by how long each has been owed: current covers roughly the first 30 days, then 31-to-60, 61-to-90, and over 90. The 12-day invoice is current, the 45-day falls in the 31-to-60 bucket, and the 80-day falls in the 61-to-90 bucket.

questionBank.explanation: Money the restaurant owes its supplier is an accounts payable, a liability; money a customer owes the restaurant is an accounts receivable, an asset. They are mirror images of the same kind of credit transaction.

As a likely bad debt — money that may never be collected — flagged by the aging report and estimated for losses
questionBank.explanation: A receivable past 90 days with no response is a likely bad debt: the business expects not to collect it and estimates such losses rather than counting every dollar as certain cash. The revenue was already recorded when the work was delivered; the question now is whether the promise becomes cash.

title: Accounts Payable
in30Seconds: Accounts payable is the money a business owes to suppliers for goods or services it has already received. It arises when a business buys on credit — the supplier delivers now and the payment comes later, usually within 30 days. Payables are liabilities: promises to pay that sit on the balance sheet. Paying them on time keeps supplier trust and keeps credit flowing. When a business owes a supplier, that is accounts payable; when customers owe the business, that is accounts receivable.
whyItMatters: Nearly every business buys something before it can pay for it — ingredients, parts, software, office space — and that makes accounts payable one of the most common obligations on a balance sheet. Understanding payables matters because they are real promises with real deadlines: a business that misses them loses supplier trust, and a supplier that stops shipping can stop a business overnight. Payables also matter for reading financial health, since the total owed to suppliers shows how much cash a business will need soon. And the contrast with accounts receivable — what you owe versus what you are owed — is where many people first learn to tell a balance sheet from a wish list.
learningObjectives: Define accounts payable as money a business owes to suppliers for goods or services it has already received, and explain how buying on credit creates it.
Explain why accounts payable is a liability — an obligation to pay — and where it sits on the balance sheet.
Read common payment terms such as net 30 and explain what they require of the business.
Distinguish accounts payable, money the business owes, from accounts receivable, money owed to the business.
Evaluate how paying suppliers on time builds trust and keeps credit available.

collegeVersion.heading: What accounts payable is
collegeVersion.body: Accounts payable is the money a business owes to suppliers for goods or services it has already received. The working definition used in this lesson comes from standard accounting texts: OpenStax's Principles of Accounting describes accounts payable as the financial obligations owed to suppliers after purchasing products or services on credit. Three features matter. The goods or services have already arrived — the business is not paying for a promise, it is paying for something in hand. The payment has not happened yet. And the amount is specific — an invoice, not a guess. A bakery that receives flour on Tuesday and pays the mill on Friday has accounts payable between those two moments. Once the payment goes out, the payable is gone. What remains is the everyday engine of supplier credit: receive now, pay later, record the obligation the whole time.

collegeVersion.heading: How accounts payable arises: buying on credit
collegeVersion.body: Accounts payable is born the moment a business buys on credit from a supplier. Buying on credit means the supplier delivers the goods or service now and agrees to be paid later, usually within a set number of days. The supplier documents the arrangement with an invoice that lists what was purchased, the amount owed, the invoice date, and the payment terms. Take an original example: Riverline Cycling Supply ships 40 inner tubes and 12 helmets to Harbor Bikes, a repair shop, and sends an invoice for $1,860 with net 30 terms. Harbor Bikes now has the parts on its shelves and a $1,860 obligation on its books. The supplier extended credit because it expects to be paid; the shop accepted the obligation because it needs parts before it has the cash to spare. That trade — inventory now, payment later — is how payables appear in nearly every business.

collegeVersion.heading: Payables are liabilities
collegeVersion.body: Every accounts payable is a liability: an obligation to pay, created by something the business has already done. A liability is a present obligation that will be settled in the future, and the full treatment belongs to the sibling topic accounting:foundations:liabilities; this lesson references it rather than covering it. Here the point is placement. Because payables are due within a year — typically within 30 or 60 days — they are current liabilities, and they sit on the balance sheet among the obligations the business must settle soon. Lenders and investors read that number to see how much cash the business will need in the near term. An unpaid supplier bill is not a vague intention; it is a promise with a deadline, and accounting records it the moment the goods arrive, not the moment cash leaves.

collegeVersion.heading: Payment terms: net 30 and friends
collegeVersion.body: Suppliers and buyers agree on payment terms, and the invoice states them. The most common is net 30: the full amount is due 30 days after the invoice date. Relatives include net 60 and net 90 for larger or slower-moving orders. A common variant adds an early-payment discount: 2/10, n/30 means the buyer may subtract 2% if it pays within 10 days, otherwise the net amount is due in 30. OpenStax explains the notation — the 2 is the discount rate, the 10 is the discount period in days, and n/30 means the payment period without the discount. Paying inside the discount window saves real money, and paying within the net window keeps the relationship clean. Missing the deadline entirely changes the relationship: suppliers may add late fees, tighten terms, or demand cash on delivery.

collegeVersion.heading: Managing payables: paying on time, keeping trust
collegeVersion.body: Managing payables is mostly calendar discipline. A business knows every invoice's amount and due date, schedules payments so nothing slips, and watches its cash so the money is there when the date arrives. The reward for paying on time is trust, and trust is the currency of supplier credit. Suppliers who are paid on time keep offering good terms, keep shipping, and may extend more credit as the relationship grows. The risk of paying late is compounding: a supplier that gets burned once may tighten terms; a supplier burned twice may stop shipping or demand payment upfront. Because payables are usually the largest short-term obligation on a small business's books, late payments can ripple — a single missed deadline can break a supply line that took years to build. Recorded carefully and paid on schedule, payables are a routine, manageable part of running a business.

collegeVersion.heading: Payable versus receivable, and the honest view
collegeVersion.body: Accounts payable and accounts receivable are mirror images, and the difference is a matter of direction. Accounts payable is what the business owes its suppliers — money leaving later for goods already received. Accounts receivable is what customers owe the business — money arriving later for goods already delivered; that is the sibling topic accounting:foundations:accounts-receivable, referenced here only. A print shop that owes its paper supplier $800 for last month's order has $800 in accounts payable; the same shop waiting on a $300 payment from a customer for a wedding album has $300 in accounts receivable. Confusing the two turns a balance sheet backwards. The honest framing, finally, is that payables are promises — obligations the business made and must keep. They are tracked as carefully as sales because a promise, once made, does not quietly go away. Suppliers, lenders, and investors all read those promises, and the business that keeps them keeps the credit flowing.

vocabulary.definition: Money a business owes to suppliers for goods or services it has already received on credit.
A business or person that sells goods or services to another business.
An arrangement in which a buyer receives goods or services now and promises to pay later.
The supplier's bill listing what was purchased, the amount owed, and the payment terms.
The agreed conditions for paying an invoice, including the deadline for full payment.
A payment term meaning the full amount is due 30 days after the invoice date.
An obligation due within one year, such as an unpaid supplier bill.
Money customers owe the business for goods or services already delivered.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Accounts payable is the tab a business runs with its suppliers. When a supplier delivers flour, bike parts, or software and the business does not pay on the spot, the unpaid amount becomes accounts payable. The goods are already in the door — only the payment is waiting. The business has promised to pay, and accounting treats that promise as a real obligation, not an option.
eli10.analogy: Think of a corner shop that lets you take a loaf of bread today and put it on your tab. You have the bread; the shop does not. The promise to pay is the tab. A business runs the same tab with its suppliers, except the tab has a name — accounts payable — and the shop keeps the record straight with an invoice saying exactly what is owed and when.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy stops where scale begins. A corner shop's tab is informal and small, while a business's payables are tracked in ledgers, carry written terms, and can reach thousands or millions. A neighborly shopkeeper may shrug at a late loaf; a supplier may charge interest, stop shipping, or demand cash on delivery. And unlike a friendly tab, payables appear on financial statements where lenders and investors can see every promise.

workedExample: Marco owns Harbor Bikes, a repair shop that also sells parts. On June 3, he ordered 40 inner tubes and 12 helmets from Riverline Cycling Supply on credit. Riverline shipped the order and invoiced him for $1,860 with terms of net 30. On June 8 he ordered a $410 box of brake pads from the same supplier under the same terms. By June 30, Harbor Bikes owed Riverline $2,270 across two unpaid invoices — its accounts payable balance. The first invoice is due July 3, the second July 8. Marco's bookkeeper records the total as a current liability on the balance sheet and schedules both payments so neither goes past its deadline. If he paid late, Riverline could tighten his terms to cash on delivery, which would force him to tie up his own cash.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling any unpaid bill accounts payable.
commonMistakes.correction: Only goods or services already received count. A purchase order for next month's parts is a plan, not a payable.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating accounts payable as an expense.
commonMistakes.correction: The flour used in today's bread is an expense; the unpaid flour bill is a liability. An unpaid cost can be both, but they are different ideas — and the payable is settled by paying, not by using the goods.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting what the payment terms say.
commonMistakes.correction: Net 30 is not 'sometime next month'; it is 30 days from the invoice date. Miss the date and suppliers may charge late fees, tighten terms, or stop shipping.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing payable with receivable.
commonMistakes.correction: Accounts payable is what the business owes suppliers; accounts receivable is what customers owe the business. Flipping them makes a balance sheet read backwards.

compareContrast: **Accounts payable vs. accounts receivable** — Payable is money the business owes its suppliers for goods already received; receivable is money customers owe the business for goods already delivered. One is an outflow waiting to happen, the other an inflow.

**A payable vs. an expense** — A payable is an amount owed; an expense is a cost incurred. They overlap when a cost is incurred but not yet paid — that amount is both — but paying the bill settles the payable, it does not create the expense. (Expenses have their own lesson in this course.)
**Net 30 vs. 2/10, n/30** — Net 30 is a plain deadline: full payment in 30 days. The discount variant rewards speed: pay within 10 days and take 2% off; otherwise the net amount is due in 30.
keyTakeaway: Accounts payable is the money a business owes to suppliers for goods and services it has already received — a promise to pay, tracked as carefully as any sale. Pay it on time, and suppliers keep extending credit; ignore it, and the promise — and the supply — can disappear.

title: Inventory
in30Seconds: Inventory is the stock of goods a business holds to sell to customers in the normal course of its operations: raw materials, work in progress, and finished goods. Unsold inventory is an asset that sits on the balance sheet. When goods sell, their cost leaves inventory and becomes cost of goods sold on the income statement. Businesses count what is on hand and attach costs using methods like FIFO, LIFO, or weighted average. The honest truth: inventory is money sitting on shelves, and a business wants neither too much nor too little.
whyItMatters: Inventory is where most businesses keep a large share of their money, so getting it right touches everything: reported profit, the balance sheet, and the cash available to pay bills. A company that overstocks can look healthy on paper while running short of cash; one that understocks loses sales it can never get back. Learning how inventory is counted and valued also unlocks the rest of accounting: cost of goods sold feeds the income statement, inventory feeds the balance sheet, and both feed the ratios analysts use to judge a business. Whether you run a shop, read financial statements, or invest, understanding inventory tells you where a company's money is actually sitting.
learningObjectives: Define inventory using the working definition: goods held for sale in the normal course of business, plus goods in production for that sale and the materials that go into them.
Name the three main types of inventory — raw materials, work in progress, and finished goods — and give an original example of each.
Explain why unsold inventory is an asset and what happens to its cost when goods are sold.
Describe how businesses count and value inventory, including the cost-flow methods FIFO, LIFO, and weighted average.
Analyze the costs of carrying inventory — holding costs, obsolescence, and tied-up cash — and apply the framing that a business wants neither too much nor too little.

collegeVersion.heading: What inventory is
collegeVersion.body: Inventory is the stock of goods a business holds to sell to customers in the normal course of its operations. The working definition used across accounting standards: goods held for sale in the ordinary course of business, plus goods being made for that sale and the materials that will go into them. The international standard IAS 2 defines inventories that way, and U.S. accounting under GAAP describes the same idea: goods the company means to sell. A bookstore's shelves of novels are inventory; the delivery truck that brings them is not. The word covers what a business has bought or made with the clear intention of selling it, not the tools and equipment it uses to run itself.

collegeVersion.heading: The three types of inventory
collegeVersion.body: Manufacturers typically hold three types of inventory, one for each stage of production. Raw materials are the basic inputs before any work touches them: the flour in a bakery's storeroom, the steel coils waiting at a factory gate. Work in progress is partly finished product, such as a bicycle frame with wheels fitted but no handlebars yet. Finished goods are complete and ready for sale, like the bikes lined up on a shop floor. Retailers, which buy goods to resell, usually hold only the finished-goods stage; a grocery store's entire inventory is finished goods in this sense. Each type sits at a different stage, so each carries a different value: a raw bolt is worth less than the finished chair it will become.

collegeVersion.heading: Inventory as an asset
collegeVersion.body: Until goods are sold, they are an asset — a resource the business owns that is expected to deliver future value. OpenStax's Principles of Accounting puts it plainly: the unsold inventory at period end is an asset and appears on the balance sheet. Assets are their own topic; what matters here is where inventory sits. Accountants classify it as a current asset, because the business expects to sell it within a year, and for many companies it is one of the largest current assets of all — OpenStax notes that in 2018, Walmart's inventory was roughly 70 percent of its current assets. A box of goods awaiting sale is therefore part of what the business owns, right up until the sale happens.

collegeVersion.heading: Counting and valuing inventory
collegeVersion.body: How does a business know what it has? It counts. The general practice is a physical count of what is on hand, taken at least at the end of each period, then matched against the records. The matching matters because records drift: goods spoil, get damaged, are stolen, or are simply miscounted, and accountants call that gap shrinkage. Once the units are counted, the business attaches a cost to them. Because identical goods are often bought at different prices, accountants use cost-flow methods to decide which purchase price goes with which unit. FIFO (first-in, first-out) assumes the earliest purchases are sold first. LIFO (last-in, first-out) assumes the latest purchases are sold first. The weighted-average method values every unit at the average cost of all units on hand. All three are costing assumptions, not descriptions of how goods physically move through the warehouse. U.S. GAAP permits all of them; under IFRS, LIFO is not permitted.

collegeVersion.heading: The costs of holding inventory
collegeVersion.body: Inventory is not free to keep. Holding costs are the running expenses of storage: warehouse space, insurance, utilities, and the labor that handles the goods. Obsolescence is the quieter risk — products that sit too long go stale, out of fashion, or technically outdated, and a box nobody will buy is worth less than what the business paid for it. Then there is tied-up cash: every dollar sitting on a shelf is a dollar that cannot pay the rent, cover payroll, or fund the next order. OpenStax's introduction to business text summarizes the trade-off: large inventories meet customer demand and earn quantity discounts, but they tie up money, cost money to store, and can become obsolete.

collegeVersion.heading: Inventory and the income statement
collegeVersion.body: Inventory connects the balance sheet to the income statement through one simple mechanism. Unsold goods stay on the balance sheet as an asset. Sold goods leave inventory, and their cost becomes cost of goods sold, an expense on the income statement. Accountants track the flow with a simple identity: goods available for sale equals beginning inventory plus everything purchased during the period. What the business sold becomes cost of goods sold; what remains is ending inventory, and the two always add back to goods available for sale. That is why an accurate count matters: if the ending count is wrong, cost of goods sold — and therefore reported profit — is wrong too. The income statement is its own topic; the mechanism to remember is that a sale moves value from the balance-sheet asset into an income-statement expense.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Here is the honest way to think about inventory: it is money sitting on shelves. A box of goods is cash converted into a promise — the promise that a customer will buy it later, usually at a price above what it cost. The business wants neither too much nor too little. Too little means empty shelves, lost sales, and customers who walk to a competitor. Too much means cash trapped in a warehouse, storage bills that keep arriving, and goods that may never sell at full price. Inventory management is the art of guessing right: enough to serve customers, never so much that the money stops working.

vocabulary.definition: The stock of goods a business holds to sell to customers in the normal course of its operations, including items still being made and the materials that go into them.
The basic materials a business buys to make its products, before any work has been done on them.
Partly finished goods that are still moving through production and are not yet ready to sell.
Completed products that are ready to be sold to customers.
The cost of the inventory a business actually sold during a period, reported as an expense on the income statement.
First-in, first-out: a cost-flow method that assumes the earliest purchased items are the first ones sold.
Last-in, first-out: a cost-flow method that assumes the latest purchased items are the first ones sold.
A cost-flow method that values items at the average cost of all units on hand, dividing total cost by total units.
The ongoing expenses of keeping inventory, such as storage space, insurance, and the risk of damage or spoilage.
The loss of inventory through theft, damage, spoilage, or miscounting that makes the physical count lower than the records.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Inventory is the stuff a business bought or made so it can sell it later. Until the customer buys it, that stuff is an asset: it sits on the balance sheet as something the business owns. The moment it sells, its cost stops being an asset and becomes an expense on the income statement, called cost of goods sold. Three questions matter for any box in the warehouse: how many are there? (count it), what did it cost? (pick a cost-flow method), and is it still worth that? (if it is obsolete, the honest answer is no). Businesses that answer those three questions well keep customers fed without burying their cash in stock.
eli10.analogy: Think of inventory as a household pantry. You keep enough food to feed the family for the week and restock before the shelves go bare. If you overbuy, the cans gather dust, the bread goes stale, and your grocery money sits stuck in the cupboard instead of doing anything useful. If you underbuy, dinner is late and someone goes hungry. A business runs its inventory the same way, stocking what it expects to sell at a price that covers what it paid.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks down in a few places. A pantry feeds one household; a business's inventory is valued in dollars, counted against its records, and reported to investors and lenders. Families do not put a price on last week's pasta and argue about which costing method to use, but businesses must, because the number changes reported profit. A pantry can hold food for months with little harm, while business inventory starts costing money the moment it is bought: storage, insurance, and the risk of obsolescence. And a household never has to explain an empty shelf to a shareholder; a business that runs out of goods has lost sales it may never recover.

workedExample: Riverside Cycles opens January with no bikes on hand. In January it buys 10 bikes at $200 each ($2,000), and in February another 10 at $220 each ($2,200), so goods available for sale total $4,200. February's physical count finds 8 bikes left, meaning 12 were sold at $300 each — $3,600 of revenue. Under FIFO, the 12 sold bikes are costed as the 10 earliest at $200 plus 2 at $220: cost of goods sold is $2,440, and the 8 remaining bikes are valued at $1,760. Under weighted average, each bike costs $210 ($4,200 divided by 20), so cost of goods sold is $2,520 and ending inventory $1,680. Same shelves, same count, two defensible profit figures — which is why the chosen method matters.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating unsold inventory as an expense already paid.
commonMistakes.correction: Unsold goods are an asset while they await sale; the expense appears only when the goods are sold, as cost of goods sold.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking FIFO and LIFO describe how goods physically move.
commonMistakes.correction: They are costing assumptions about which purchase price goes with which sale; the actual boxes may leave the shelf in any order.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading a full warehouse as a sign of health.
commonMistakes.correction: A full warehouse can be a warning: cash tied up, storage bills growing, and goods aging toward obsolescence.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trusting the records without ever counting.
commonMistakes.correction: Physical counts catch shrinkage — theft, damage, spoilage, and miscounting — that the records never show.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing the three types of inventory.
commonMistakes.correction: Raw materials, work in progress, and finished goods are different stages with different values; mixing them up distorts what the business actually has.

compareContrast.distinction: FIFO assumes the earliest-purchased goods are sold first; LIFO assumes the latest-purchased goods are sold first. Both are costing assumptions, and neither describes how the goods physically leave the shelf.

A periodic physical count values inventory at the end of a period; perpetual systems update the value after every purchase and sale. The physical count stays important either way, because records drift.

Inventory is the unsold portion of goods available for sale, an asset on the balance sheet; cost of goods sold is the sold portion, an expense on the income statement. The same purchases split between the two.

keyTakeaway: Inventory is an asset while it sits unsold, becomes cost of goods sold the moment it is sold, and is really money sitting on shelves — enough to serve customers, never so much that cash is trapped.

questionBank.prompt: Under the FIFO cost-flow method, which items does the business assume it sells first?
options: The most recently purchased items
The earliest purchased items
The most expensive items on hand
A random sample of the items on hand
questionBank.explanation: FIFO stands for first-in, first-out: the business assumes the earliest purchased items are sold first, so the latest purchases remain in ending inventory. The other options describe LIFO, a different rule, or no rule at all.
questionBank.skill: Recalling what FIFO assumes about the order of sale

questionBank.prompt: A bakery buys 100 bags of flour at $10 each, then another 100 bags at $12 each, and uses 120 bags. Under FIFO, what total cost is assigned to the flour used?
questionBank.explanation: Under FIFO the earliest purchase is used first: 100 bags at $10 ($1,000) plus the next 20 bags at $12 ($240) totals $1,240. The $1,200 option prices all bags at $10, $1,320 prices all 120 at the $11 average, and $1,160 matches no cost-flow rule.
questionBank.skill: Applying FIFO to a two-lot purchase scenario

questionBank.prompt: Where do unsold goods appear on a company's financial statements?
options: As an asset on the balance sheet
As an expense on the income statement
As a liability on the balance sheet
As revenue on the income statement
questionBank.explanation: Unsold inventory is an asset, so it is reported on the balance sheet; only when goods are sold does their cost become the expense called cost of goods sold. Revenue records the selling price, not the goods themselves, and a liability is something the business owes.
questionBank.skill: Explaining where unsold inventory is reported

questionBank.prompt: A clothing store's winter coats are still unsold in April. Which cost of inventory does this situation most directly illustrate?
options: Holding costs
Tied-up cash
Cost of goods sold
Obsolescence
questionBank.explanation: Coats sitting past their season are aging toward obsolescence: goods that may soon sell only at a markdown or not at all. Holding costs and tied-up cash also accompany stored goods, but the seasonal mismatch is the clearest sign of the obsolescence risk, and cost of goods sold arises only when goods actually sell.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing a scenario to identify which inventory cost dominates

questionBank.prompt: At year end, a hardware store physically counts 340 hammers, but its records say 350 should be on hand. What does the difference most likely represent?
options: A profit the store can report immediately
Inventory shrinkage — goods lost to theft, damage, or miscounting
A debt the store owes its suppliers
A discount the store earned from its supplier
questionBank.explanation: When the physical count falls short of the records, the gap is shrinkage: goods lost to theft, damage, spoilage, or errors in counting and recording. The difference is a loss of goods, not revenue, not a debt, and not a purchase discount.
questionBank.skill: Applying the physical-count concept to interpret a count-versus-records gap

title: Depreciation
in30Seconds: Depreciation spreads the cost of a long-lived asset, like a delivery van or a piece of machinery, over the years it serves the business, instead of charging the whole price in the purchase year. Each year, part of the cost becomes an expense, matched to the revenue the asset helps earn. The straight-line method charges an equal amount every year: cost minus salvage value, divided by useful life.
whyItMatters: Depreciation sits behind the numbers of almost every business that owns equipment, vehicles, or buildings. It keeps one year's income statement from being crushed by a big purchase, and it keeps the balance sheet honest about how much of an asset's cost is still waiting to be used up. Understanding the idea lets you read terms like book value, accumulated depreciation, and net income with real comprehension. It also sets you up for later topics, from adjusting entries and financial statements to the difference between accounting rules and tax rules, where the same spreading idea keeps showing up.
learningObjectives: Define depreciation as spreading the cost of a long-lived asset over its useful life.
Explain why depreciation exists: an asset serves many periods, so its cost is matched to the revenue it helps produce.
Apply the straight-line method to compute annual depreciation, accumulated depreciation, and book value with simple arithmetic.
Distinguish book value from market value, and book depreciation from tax depreciation.
Analyze common depreciation mistakes, such as treating depreciation as cash set aside or as a market-value adjustment.

collegeVersion.heading: What depreciation is
collegeVersion.body: Depreciation is the accounting practice of spreading the cost of a long-lived asset over the periods it serves, rather than treating the full purchase price as an expense of a single year. A delivery van that will carry goods for five years is not "used up" in the year it is bought: it keeps producing benefit year after year, so accountants spread its cost across those years. The amount spread each period is the depreciation expense, reported on the income statement. The part of the cost not yet spread remains on the balance sheet as the asset's book value, alongside accumulated depreciation, the running total of the expense taken so far.

collegeVersion.heading: Why it exists: the matching idea
collegeVersion.body: Depreciation exists because of matching: costs should be reported in the same periods as the revenue they help generate. If a bakery bought a $30,000 van and charged the entire amount in the purchase year, that year's income statement would show a huge expense and every later year would show none, even though the van helps earn delivery revenue in all of them. Spreading the cost puts a fair slice of expense in each year of service, so profits are not distorted by the timing of big purchases. This is part of the broader accrual-accounting approach, where revenue and expenses are recorded when they are earned and incurred, not only when cash changes hands.

collegeVersion.heading: The straight-line method
collegeVersion.body: The straight-line method is the simplest and most widely used way to spread an asset's cost, and it is the one to master first. It charges the same dollar amount of depreciation every year. Three pieces of information go in: the asset's cost, its salvage value (the estimated amount it will be worth, as a sale or trade-in, when its useful life ends), and its useful life (how long the business expects to use it productively). The formula is: (cost − salvage value) ÷ useful life. For a van that cost $30,000, will be worth $5,000 after five years, the depreciable base is $30,000 − $5,000 = $25,000, and the annual expense is $25,000 ÷ 5 = $5,000. The same $5,000 appears as an expense each year, and the van's book value falls by $5,000 each year: $25,000 after year one, $20,000 after year two, and so on, down to the $5,000 salvage value.

collegeVersion.heading: Other methods, book value, and market value
collegeVersion.body: Two other common methods deserve a mention. Declining balance charges more depreciation in the early years and less later, which suits assets that lose usefulness quickly. Units of production charges depreciation based on how much the asset is actually used, such as miles driven or units made. Both spread the same total cost; only the timing differs. A separate idea matters more for reading statements: book value is the un-depreciated portion of original cost, not a guess at what the asset could sell for. Depreciation is a spreading rule, and the calculation is not based on changes in the asset's market value. A van with a $15,000 book value might sell for $12,000 or $18,000 on the open market; the accounts do not chase that number.

collegeVersion.heading: Depreciation and taxes, plus the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: The depreciation a company reports in its financial statements is book depreciation, computed under accounting rules. The depreciation it claims on its tax return is tax depreciation, computed under tax rules, which in the United States follow a separate system called MACRS. The two are different numbers for the same asset, and that is expected; nothing in this lesson is tax advice. The honest framing to carry away: depreciation is a spreading rule, not a valuation. It decides when a cost shows up in the income statement; it does not say what an asset is worth today, and it does not put cash aside for a replacement. Two related details follow from the definition: land is never depreciated, because it is assumed to have an unlimited useful life, and a fully depreciated asset stays on the books at its salvage value until it is sold or scrapped.

vocabulary.definition: The accounting practice of spreading a long-lived asset's cost over the years it is used, instead of charging the full cost in the purchase year.
The length of time a business expects to use an asset productively before it is worn out or obsolete.
The estimated amount an asset will be worth, as a sale or trade-in, when its useful life ends; also called residual value.
The simplest depreciation method: cost minus salvage value divided by useful life, giving the same expense every year.
The portion of an asset's cost that gets spread into expense: the cost minus the salvage value.
An asset's original cost minus the depreciation taken on it so far, also called net book value.
The running total of all depreciation expense charged on an asset since it was bought.
The price an asset could actually be sold for today, which can differ from its book value.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: When a business buys something that will last for years, a van, a machine, a building, it does not treat the whole purchase as an expense of just one year. The van will help earn money for five years, so its cost is spread over five years. That spreading is depreciation. The straight-line method is the simplest version: figure out how much of the cost will be used up (cost minus what it will still be worth at the end), then divide by the number of years. Same amount every year, like a steady monthly payment the asset makes to the income statement.
eli10.analogy: Think of a shop that buys a year's supply of 120 boxes of packing tape at once. It would not call the whole delivery an expense of that single day. It counts a few boxes each month as they are used. Depreciation does the same for a van: the van is a box of usefulness that gets consumed a little each year, and each year's slice becomes that year's expense.
eli10.analogyLimits: The tape-box analogy suggests the asset is used up at a perfectly steady rate. Real assets often lose usefulness unevenly, and straight-line ignores that by design, which is why other methods exist. The analogy also implies physical wear, but depreciation is about spreading recorded cost, not measuring wear, and it never sets aside cash for a replacement.

workedExample: Bella's Bakery buys a delivery van for $30,000. The van is expected to serve deliveries for five years, after which Bella estimates it can be sold for $5,000. The depreciable base is $30,000 − $5,000 = $25,000. Straight-line depreciation: $25,000 ÷ 5 = $5,000 per year. After year one, the income statement shows $5,000 of depreciation expense, accumulated depreciation is $5,000, and the van's book value is $30,000 − $5,000 = $25,000. After year three, accumulated depreciation is $15,000 and book value is $15,000. At the end of year five the van is fully depreciated to its $5,000 salvage value. Each year's $5,000 slice is matched to the delivery revenue the van helped earn.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking depreciation measures how much an asset's market value has dropped.
commonMistakes.correction: Depreciation is a cost-spreading rule, not a valuation. Book value is the un-depreciated part of original cost, not what the asset would sell for.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to subtract salvage value in the straight-line formula.
commonMistakes.correction: Only the depreciable base, cost minus salvage, is spread into expense; the salvage value is expected to remain at the end of the asset's life.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing depreciation sets aside cash to replace the asset.
commonMistakes.correction: Depreciation is a bookkeeping allocation; no cash moves when it is recorded, and it does not create a cash fund.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing one year's depreciation with accumulated depreciation.
commonMistakes.correction: Annual depreciation is a single year's slice; accumulated depreciation is the running total since purchase, and it is the number subtracted from cost to get book value.

commonMistakes.mistake: Depreciating land along with the building on it.
commonMistakes.correction: Land is not depreciated, because it is assumed to have an unlimited useful life; only the building wears out over a measurable life.

compareContrast.distinction: Book value is the un-depreciated portion of original cost; market value is what the asset could sell for today. They measure different things and usually differ.
Straight-line charges the same amount each year; declining balance charges more in the early years and less later. Both spread the same total cost, just on different schedules.
Book depreciation follows accounting rules and appears in financial statements; tax depreciation follows tax rules, such as MACRS in the United States, and is used on tax returns.

keyTakeaway: Depreciation is a spreading rule, not a valuation: it moves a long-lived asset's cost into expense over its useful life. The straight-line method divides cost minus salvage value by the years of service.

questionBank.prompt: What does depreciation do in accounting?
options: Spreads the cost of a long-lived asset over its useful life
Records how much the asset could be sold for each year
Sets aside cash to replace the asset when it wears out
Shows the total amount the business paid in cash for the asset
questionBank.explanation: Depreciation allocates an asset's cost across the periods it serves. It is not a market-value estimate, a cash reserve, or a record of the purchase payment.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the working definition of depreciation

questionBank.prompt: Why does a business spread an asset's cost over several years instead of charging the full cost in the purchase year?
options: Because the purchase was paid for in installments over several years
Because accounting rules require cash to be saved before an asset is replaced
Because the asset's market value changes every year
Because the asset serves the business for several periods, and matching pairs its cost with the revenue those periods earn
questionBank.explanation: The matching idea: an asset that helps earn revenue over many periods has its cost spread over those same periods, so no single year carries the whole cost.
questionBank.skill: Explaining the matching reason behind depreciation

questionBank.prompt: Bella's Bakery buys a delivery van for $30,000. It will last 5 years and be worth $5,000 at the end. Using straight-line depreciation, what is the annual depreciation expense?
questionBank.explanation: The depreciable base is cost minus salvage value: $30,000 − $5,000 = $25,000. Divided by 5 years of useful life: $25,000 ÷ 5 = $5,000 per year. $6,000 ignores the salvage value, and $25,000 is the total to spread, not the yearly amount.
questionBank.skill: Applying the straight-line formula with simple arithmetic

questionBank.prompt: After three years of straight-line depreciation at $5,000 per year on a van that cost $30,000, what is the van's book value?
questionBank.explanation: Accumulated depreciation after three years is 3 × $5,000 = $15,000. Book value is original cost minus accumulated depreciation: $30,000 − $15,000 = $15,000. That is the un-depreciated cost, not a selling price.
questionBank.skill: Computing book value as cost less accumulated depreciation

questionBank.prompt: A van has a book value of $15,000, and a dealer offers $12,000 for it. Which statement is correct?
options: Book value is the un-depreciated part of the van's original cost, and the $12,000 offer is its market value; the two can differ
The van's book value must be adjusted down to the $12,000 offer
Depreciation is no longer needed because the market value fell
The $3,000 difference is a loss recorded when depreciation was taken
questionBank.explanation: Depreciation does not track market value: book value is simply original cost minus depreciation taken so far, while market value is what a buyer would pay today. The two often differ, and the difference is not an accounting loss.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing the difference between book value and market value

title: Accrual Accounting
in30Seconds: Accrual accounting records revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, no matter when cash changes hands — this lesson anchors its definition on OpenStax's Principles of Accounting. A painter who finishes a job in September records the revenue in September even if the customer pays in October, and the matching principle pairs that revenue with the costs that produced it. GAAP requires accrual accounting because it gives a truer picture of performance — and it is also more complicated.
whyItMatters: Readers of financial statements need to know what a business actually accomplished in a period, not just when money happened to move. If revenue were recorded only when cash arrived, a December full of work would look empty and a January with no work would look busy. Accrual accounting fixes that: each period's statements show the work done and the costs that went with it. Lenders, investors, and managers depend on that honest picture, and U.S. accounting standards (GAAP) require it for most businesses. Understanding accrual accounting also unlocks the difference between profit and cash — a distinction behind almost every real business decision, from hiring to borrowing.
learningObjectives: Define accrual accounting as recording revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of cash movement, using the working definition from OpenStax's Principles of Accounting and corroborated by CFI.
Explain the revenue recognition principle: revenue is recorded in the period it is earned, not the period it is paid.
Explain the matching principle: expenses are recorded in the same period as the revenues they helped produce.
Distinguish accrual accounting from cash accounting: when things count versus when money moves.
Explain why accrual accounting is the standard under GAAP: it matches revenues and expenses to the right periods and makes statements comparable.
Describe the honest framing: accrual accounting is more accurate and also more complicated.

collegeVersion.heading: What accrual accounting is
collegeVersion.body: OpenStax's Principles of Accounting states the rule directly: accrual basis accounting prescribes that revenues and expenses are recorded in the accounting period in which they were earned or incurred, no matter when cash receipts or payments occur. CFI's Accrual Accounting guide opens with the same idea — recording earned revenues or incurred expenses regardless of whether cash is exchanged. In plainer words, accrual accounting records things when they happen, not when money moves. The rule has two halves. Revenue is recorded when it is earned: the business has delivered the product or service, so the customer owes for it. Expenses are recorded when they are incurred: the business has used up something of value, so it owes for that too. Cash is not ignored — it is tracked carefully — but it is tracked separately. Whether the customer has paid yet, or the business has paid its suppliers yet, does not decide when the event enters the books.

collegeVersion.heading: Revenue recognition: earned, not paid
collegeVersion.body: The revenue recognition principle tells a business to record revenue in the period it earns it, and revenue counts as earned only once a product or service has been provided. OpenStax adds that there does not have to be a correlation between when cash is collected and when revenue is recognized: a customer may not pay on the day of the service, yet the company records the revenue as earned because the work happened. Here is an original example. Harborview Painting finishes painting a house on September 24 and sends a bill for $4,800; the homeowner pays on October 9. The revenue belongs in September, because that is when the painting was done. A system that waited for cash would show no revenue in September for work actually completed, and $4,800 in October for a month in which no painting happened.

collegeVersion.heading: The matching principle
collegeVersion.body: The expense recognition principle, also called the matching principle, states that expenses must be matched with the associated revenues in the period in which those revenues were earned. OpenStax warns that a mismatch makes statements unreliable: expenses recorded separately from the revenues they generated would understate net income in one period and overstate it in another. Return to Harborview Painting. The September job used $1,100 of paint and materials bought on credit in August, and the crew's wages of $1,650 were paid on October 1. Both are September expenses: the paint helped produce September's revenue, and the crew worked in September. The $4,800 of revenue and the $2,750 of expenses land on the same September income statement, which is what makes September's profit of $2,050 meaningful.

collegeVersion.heading: Accrual versus cash: when things count versus when money moves
collegeVersion.body: Cash basis accounting is the simpler alternative: transactions are not recorded until there is an exchange of cash. OpenStax notes that this method can delay or accelerate revenue and expense reporting until cash receipts or outlays occur, and that it can be simpler to track. Take Riverbend Tutoring. In December, Marisol finishes ten sessions for a school district and bills $1,500, paid in January; she also receives the December electricity bill for $180, paid in January. Accrual books show December revenue of $1,500 and December expense of $180, because the work and the electricity use both happened in December. Cash books show nothing for December, because no cash moved; January would show both amounts, making a month with no tutoring look like the busy one. The contrast in one line: accrual records when things count; cash records when money moves. Cash accounting has its own lesson; here it serves as the contrast that shows what accrual is for.

collegeVersion.heading: Why accrual is the standard
collegeVersion.body: Companies, public or private, that use US GAAP or IFRS prepare their financial statements using the rules of accrual accounting, as OpenStax states. The reason is that the accrual method is considered to better match revenues and expenses, and it standardizes reporting information for comparability — which matters to external users trying to make investment or lending decisions, and to internal users making decisions about performance, budgeting, and growth. CFI puts the same argument in plainer terms: accrual accounting provides a more accurate picture of a company's true financial position, while cash accounting can offer a misleading picture when unpaid expenses and outstanding receivables are missing from the statements. The SEC's Investor.gov glossary defines GAAP as the accounting standards, conventions, and rules companies use to measure their financial results. The point of the standard is trust: statements prepared on the same rules, with each period's results matched to the activity that produced them, can be compared and relied on.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing: more accurate, and more complicated
collegeVersion.body: Accrual accounting wins because it is truer, and the honest framing is that truer costs more. OpenStax itself notes that cash basis accounting can be simpler to track, and CFI observes that accrual accounting becomes especially valuable in large and complex businesses — precisely because it asks more of the people keeping the books. Deciding when revenue is earned, which costs belong to which period, and what to do when amounts are uncertain all require judgment. No receipt announces 'this expense belongs to March.' The trade-off is plain: accrual accounting gives readers a more accurate picture of performance, and it demands more care, more estimates, and more decisions. That is not a flaw to hide; it is the reason the work exists.

vocabulary.definition: A method of accounting that records revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash is received or paid; this lesson anchors its definition on OpenStax's Principles of Accounting.
The rule that revenue is recorded in the period it is earned, when the product or service has been provided, even if the customer has not yet paid.
The rule, also called the expense recognition principle, that expenses are recorded in the same period as the revenues they helped produce.
Revenue that has been earned but not yet collected, such as work completed and billed but still unpaid at period end.
A cost that has been incurred but not yet paid, such as electricity used in December but paid for in January.
A method of accounting that records transactions only when cash is received or paid out.
Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, the accounting standards, conventions, and rules that U.S. companies use to measure and report their financial results.
The stretch of time, often a month, quarter, or year, over which a business measures and reports its results.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Accrual accounting means recording things when they happen, not when money moves. If you tutor a student in December but get paid in January, December is when the revenue counts — you did the work in December. If you use electricity all December but pay the bill in January, December is when the cost counts. Cash accounting, by contrast, waits for the money: it would show the revenue in January and the electricity bill in January too, making January look like the month you did all your work. Accrual keeps each month's report honest: work in December, costs in December, results in December.
eli10.analogy: Think of a scoreboard at a basketball game. Points count the moment the ball goes through the hoop, not when the tickets are sold or the players are paid. The score at halftime tells you what happened on the court in the first half. Accrual accounting keeps the same kind of score for a business: revenue and expenses are recorded when the game — the work — happens, so each period's score reflects what the business actually did in that period.
eli10.analogyLimits: The scoreboard analogy has limits. In basketball, scoring is exact and instant; in accrual accounting, deciding when revenue is earned and which expenses belong to a period often takes judgment and estimates. And the score accrual produces — profit — is not cash you can spend. A team can win on the scoreboard and still have an empty wallet, just as a profitable business can run short of cash.

workedExample: Riverbend Tutoring is a small business run by Marisol. On December 20 she finishes ten tutoring sessions for a school district and bills $1,500; the district pays on January 12. On December 28 she receives the December electricity bill for $180 and pays it on January 5. Under accrual accounting, December shows revenue of $1,500 — the work was done in December — and electricity expense of $180 — the power was used in December — for a December profit of $1,320. Under cash accounting, December shows no revenue and no expense, because no cash moved; January would show both, making a month with no tutoring look like the profitable one.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking revenue is recorded when payment arrives.
commonMistakes.correction: Revenue is recorded when it is earned — when the product or service has been provided — even if the customer pays weeks later. Waiting for cash is cash accounting, not accrual accounting.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking the matching principle is about paying bills on time.
commonMistakes.correction: Matching is about recording an expense in the same period as the revenue it helped produce, not about when the bill is paid.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating accrual profit as cash in the bank.
commonMistakes.correction: Accrual profit measures performance; the cash may arrive or leave later. A business can show a profit and still be short of cash.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming any method is fine for financial statements.
commonMistakes.correction: Statements prepared under GAAP use accrual accounting. Cash basis is a simpler alternative that some nonpublic companies may use, and it can give a misleading picture of performance.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing accrual accounting is just adding things up.
commonMistakes.correction: Accrual accounting also involves judgment — deciding when revenue is earned and which costs belong to a period. More accurate does not mean simpler.

compareContrast.distinction: Accrual records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred; cash accounting records transactions only when cash changes hands. One tracks what happened, the other tracks money movement.
Accrued revenue is income earned but not yet collected; an accrued expense is a cost incurred but not yet paid. Both are accrual accounting's way of recording activity before cash moves.
Profit is the period's revenues minus the expenses matched to them; the cash balance is what the business can actually spend. They differ precisely because of timing.

keyTakeaway: Accrual accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, so each period's statements match the work actually done — a truer picture of performance than cash accounting, and a more demanding one.
