title: Cash Accounting
in30Seconds: Cash accounting records revenue when cash arrives and expenses when cash leaves — the this lesson's central definition comes from OpenStax's Principles of Accounting. No money, no record: a sale on credit is not counted until the customer pays, and a bill is not an expense until it is paid. The method is simple, obvious, and mirrors the bank account, which makes it a natural fit for small businesses with simple operations. The honest trade-off: it is fuzzy about a period's true performance.
whyItMatters: Every business faces one question: does the money I can spend match the money I earned? Cash accounting answers with the simplest rule — record when money moves — which keeps the books in step with the bank balance, the number that actually pays the rent. That makes bookkeeping approachable for a small business owner who has never taken an accounting class. But the same simplicity has a cost: when customers owe money or bills are unpaid at month-end, the records can flatter or punish a period unfairly. Understanding that trade-off — honest about cash, fuzzy about performance — is what lets you read a small business's numbers without being misled.
learningObjectives: Define cash accounting as recording revenue when cash arrives and expenses when cash leaves, attributing the working definition to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting.
Explain the mechanics of cash accounting — no money, no record — using an original example.
Identify the kind of business cash accounting typically fits: small businesses with simple operations.
Contrast cash accounting with accrual accounting: when things count versus when money moves.
Name the three strengths of cash accounting — simple, obvious, and in step with the bank account — and explain each.
Evaluate the honest framing: cash accounting is honest about the bank balance and fuzzy about a period's true performance.

collegeVersion.heading: What cash accounting is
collegeVersion.body: OpenStax's Principles of Accounting describes cash basis accounting as a method in which transactions are not recorded in the financial statements until there is an exchange of cash. CFI's Accrual Accounting guide states the working version in one line: under cash accounting, income and expenses are recorded when cash is received and paid. Two halves matter. Revenue counts when cash arrives — a sale made today is recorded today only if the customer paid today. An expense counts when the cash leaves — a bill sitting on the desk is not an expense until it is paid. What it does not do is match effort to reward: it never asks when work was done or when a cost was used up, only whether money moved.

collegeVersion.heading: How it works: no money, no record
collegeVersion.body: The mechanics are thin. A transaction enters the books when cash actually moves, and not before. Original example: Rivertown Bike Repair. The owner fixes a commuter's flat tire on Tuesday and the customer pays $40 cash on the spot — revenue of $40 is recorded Tuesday. On Thursday he repairs a delivery van's brakes for $260 and the fleet company will pay in thirty days — nothing is recorded on Thursday; the $260 appears in the books only when the check arrives. The same rule applies to expenses: the shop orders $120 of brake pads on credit, and the $120 is not an expense until the owner pays the bill. Every entry is a deposit or a withdrawal, and the period's profit is simply cash received minus cash paid.

collegeVersion.heading: Who uses it
collegeVersion.body: OpenStax notes that cash basis accounting is permitted for nonprofit entities and small businesses that elect to use it, and CFI states the general fit in the same spirit: cash accounting is allowed for sole proprietorships and small businesses, whereas large businesses will typically use accrual accounting. The pattern is a fit, not a rule. Cash accounting suits small businesses with simple operations — a food truck that takes payment at the counter, a tutoring service paid per session, a solo landscaper who buys supplies and sells jobs within weeks. When sales are paid on the spot and bills are paid soon after, the cash register and the books barely differ. One caution: this lesson states only the general fit — no universal tax rule is asserted.

collegeVersion.heading: Cash vs accrual
collegeVersion.body: The contrast that defines the method: accrual books revenue at earning and expenses at incurring — in the period the transactions affect — regardless of when cash moves. OpenStax's Section 4.1 ties accrual accounting to the revenue recognition and expense recognition (matching) principles. Cash accounting, by contrast, records when money moves. One line: accrual asks “when did the business do the work?” and cash asks “when did the money show up?” The two can disagree sharply in a single month — heavy billing with slow collections looks strong on accrual and weak on cash — and they tend to agree once the money settles. Accrual accounting is a sibling topic taught in its own lesson; here it appears only as the contrast.

collegeVersion.heading: The strengths
collegeVersion.body: Three strengths, each worth naming. Simple: every entry is a deposit or a withdrawal, with no adjusting entries and no estimates — OpenStax notes the cash basis can be simpler to track than accrual. Obvious: the rule is transparent; anyone can look at a recorded number and see the cash movement behind it, and no one has to explain a judgment call about when a cost was used up. In step with the bank account: OpenStax's illustration walks a summer landscaping business through its checking account, and the cash-basis income statement mirrors that balance, because every recorded item moved through it. What the books say the business has, the bank says it has — for an owner who lives by the bank balance, that alignment is the point.

collegeVersion.heading: The weakness
collegeVersion.body: The honest note comes from CFI: a potential flaw with cash accounting is that it can offer a misleading picture of an entity's financial health, especially when transactions like unpaid expenses or outstanding receivables are not represented in the financial statements. Original example: Hearthstone Cafe does $9,000 of catering in June, but its two biggest clients pay in July, and it pays $7,000 of expenses in June. Cash accounting reports June revenue of $0, expenses of $7,000, and a loss of $7,000 — even though the cafe is owed $9,000. In July the checks land, so July reports $9,000 of revenue against a light month of bills — a windfall. Neither month tells the truth; only the two months together do. Nothing in the records is wrong — but each period's number misstates the cafe's performance.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing
collegeVersion.body: The trade-off, stated plainly: cash accounting is honest about the bank balance and fuzzy about a period's true performance. If the question is “how much cash do I have?” the answer is exact — the books and the bank agree. If the question is “how well did the business do this period?” the answer can mislead, because work done but unpaid and bills owed but unpaid are invisible until money moves. That is why the method fits small businesses with simple operations, where the two questions nearly coincide, and why businesses move toward accrual accounting as they grow more complex. And the statement of cash flows, a sibling topic, is the report that shows cash movement even for accrual-based businesses — not the same thing as cash accounting.

vocabulary.definition: A method of recording revenue when cash is received and expenses when cash is paid, so nothing enters the books until money actually moves.
Money actually received by a business; under cash accounting, the event that triggers recording revenue.
Money actually paid out by a business; under cash accounting, the event that triggers recording an expense.
The alternative method that records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash moves; a sibling topic with its own lesson.
The span of time, such as a month, a quarter, or a year, over which a business measures its results.
How well a business did in a period as judged by its income; cash accounting can misstate it when money and work fall in different periods.
The amount of cash a business holds in its bank account; the number that cash accounting mirrors most directly.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Cash accounting is the money-diary way of keeping books: you write an entry only when money actually moves. Cash lands from a customer — that is revenue, recorded that day. Cash leaves to pay a supplier — that is an expense, recorded that day. A promise to pay later is not an entry yet, and neither is a bill you have not paid. At the end of the month, cash in minus cash out is your profit, and it should match what your bank account says. That is the whole method — there is no second layer of estimates or adjustments.
eli10.analogy: Think of cash accounting as the way a kid runs a lemonade stand with a shoebox. A quarter lands in the box when a cup is sold — that is the day's revenue. Coins leave the box when the kid buys more lemons — that is the day's expense. At sunset the kid dumps the box and counts: what came in minus what went out is the day's take, and it is exactly what is in the box. No ledger, no guessing, no counting cups that customers promised to pay for later.
eli10.analogyLimits: The shoebox only shows coins that are physically inside it. A neighbor who drank a cup and promised to pay tomorrow is not in the box at all, and the lemon bill that arrives next week is not in the box either — both are real claims on the business that the shoebox cannot see until money moves. A real business has the same blind spots: unpaid customer invoices and unpaid supplier bills are invisible under cash accounting, which is exactly the weakness the method trades for its simplicity.

workedExample: Riverside Dog Walks is a one-person business using cash accounting. In March, Maya bills $2,200 of walks but collects $1,800 of it; the remaining $400 is still owed. She pays $80 cash for leashes, $350 cash to a part-time helper, and $120 for phone and insurance — $550 of cash payments in all. Cash accounting records: revenue $1,800, expenses $550, net income $1,250. Her bank balance rises by exactly $1,250, from $2,000 to $3,250, because every recorded item moved through the account. But the $400 her clients owe is not recorded anywhere, so March's books show $1,250 of profit and say nothing about the money still coming. Both statements are true at once: the bank balance is exactly right, and the performance number is incomplete.

commonMistakes.mistake: Recording a sale when the work is done instead of when the cash arrives.
commonMistakes.correction: Under cash accounting a job that is billed but unpaid is not revenue until the customer's money lands — no exchange of cash, no record.

commonMistakes.mistake: Recording an expense when the invoice arrives instead of when it is paid.
commonMistakes.correction: The bill itself is not an entry; the payment is. An unpaid invoice stays out of the books until cash leaves.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading a cash-accounting profit as the full measure of performance.
commonMistakes.correction: When customers owe money or bills are unpaid, the period's profit can flatter or punish unfairly; check what is still owed before trusting the number.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming cash accounting is the required method for all small businesses everywhere.
commonMistakes.correction: The fit is general — small businesses with simple operations — and what any tax authority permits varies by jurisdiction; this lesson states no universal tax rule.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing cash accounting with the statement of cash flows.
commonMistakes.correction: Cash accounting is a way of recording transactions; the statement of cash flows is a report that shows cash movement even for accrual-based businesses.

compareContrast.distinction: Cash accounting records revenue when cash arrives and expenses when cash leaves; accrual accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash moves.
Cash accounting is a method of recording transactions; the statement of cash flows is a report showing cash movement that accrual-based businesses prepare too.
Cash-basis profit is exact about the bank account but can misstate performance when work done but unpaid and bills owed but unpaid fall across period boundaries.

keyTakeaway: Cash accounting records revenue when cash arrives and expenses when cash leaves — simple, obvious, and in step with the bank account, but fuzzy about a period's true performance; that trade-off is exactly why it fits small businesses with simple operations.

title: Financial Ratios
in30Seconds: Financial ratios are simple divisions between two numbers on a company's financial statements. They turn large figures into comparable measurements: profit per sales dollar, assets per liability dollar, debt per equity dollar. Four families — profitability, liquidity, leverage, and efficiency — each answer one question about how the business runs. Four classics do most of the work: current ratio, profit margin, return on equity, and debt-to-equity. A single ratio says little on its own; ratios earn their meaning when compared over time and against similar companies.
whyItMatters: Ratios convert statement numbers into the questions people actually ask about a business: Can it pay its bills? How much of each sales dollar stays as profit? How much of the company is financed by debt? Lenders use ratios to size up repayment risk before lending, investors use them to judge profitability before buying shares, and managers use them to spot weaknesses early. Because a ratio divides one number by another, it strips out size: the same measurement works for a corner bakery and a national chain, and for this year compared with last. The four classics are the shared language of that conversation.
learningObjectives: Define a financial ratio as a relationship between two numbers drawn from a company's financial statements.
Explain what each of the four ratio families — profitability, liquidity, leverage, and efficiency — shows about a business.
Calculate the current ratio, profit margin, return on equity, and debt-to-equity from simple statement numbers.
Analyze what a higher or lower value of each classic ratio tends to mean for a company.
Analyze why a single ratio means little until it is compared over time and against peers.
Distinguish what ratios can show — the past as reported — from what they cannot: a prediction of the future.

collegeVersion.heading: What a financial ratio is: the statements turned into questions
collegeVersion.body: A financial ratio is a relationship between two numbers from a company's financial statements: one figure divided by another, expressed as a single number. The working definition used across the profession is that ratios are calculations that compare two or more figures from the financial statements to measure performance and financial health. Why divide at all? Because raw numbers carry scale: a national chain earns $40 million and a neighborhood bakery earns $40 thousand, and those figures cannot be compared directly. Dividing by another statement number removes the size difference, so both businesses can be measured on the same scale. The current ratio divides current assets by current liabilities — both balance-sheet numbers — and the result is a measurement that works whether the company is tiny or enormous. Ratios pull their inputs from whichever statement holds the numbers they need: the income statement provides revenue and profit figures, the balance sheet provides asset, liability, and equity figures, and the statement of cash flows provides cash figures.

collegeVersion.heading: The families: four questions, four sets of ratios
collegeVersion.body: Ratios are grouped into families, and each family answers one question about the business. Profitability ratios show profit relative to sales, assets, or equity — how much of what flows in stays as earnings. Liquidity ratios show short-term payment ability — whether the company can cover the bills coming due within about a year. Leverage ratios show debt and capital structure — how much of the company is funded by borrowing rather than by owners' money. Efficiency ratios show asset use and productivity — how hard the assets work to generate sales. The families overlap in practice: a healthy company needs reasonable numbers in more than one, and analysts typically use combinations of ratios rather than any single one.

collegeVersion.heading: The four classics: formulas and what the numbers tend to mean
collegeVersion.body: Four ratios appear so often in real analysis that they are worth knowing by heart. The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. It measures how well current assets can cover short-term obligations: a ratio of 2.0 means two dollars of current assets for every dollar of bills due within the year, and a higher number means more cushion. Profit margin is net income divided by revenue. It shows the share of each sales dollar left as profit after all expenses — 10% means ten cents of every sales dollar became net income — and a falling margin can signal costs rising faster than prices. Return on equity is net income divided by shareholders' equity. It measures profit relative to the owners' stake: how effectively the company turns owners' capital into earnings, where higher means the owners' money is working harder. Debt-to-equity is total debt divided by shareholders' equity. It shows the financing mix: a higher number means more debt in the mix, a lower number means the company leans more on owners' money. These tendencies are factual, not verdicts: what counts as a good level for any of them depends on the industry and on the company's own history.

collegeVersion.heading: Ratios in context: time and peers
collegeVersion.body: A single ratio means little alone. Analysts rarely rely on one number; they track a company's ratios over time — is this year's margin better than last year's? — and they benchmark them against peers — is this company more or less leveraged than its competitors? The same current ratio of 1.5 can look like a strength for a stable utility and a warning sign for a startup burning cash. Ratios make comparison possible precisely because they strip out size, and the comparison itself is where the meaning comes from.

collegeVersion.heading: Who uses them, and the limits
collegeVersion.body: Lenders and creditors use ratios to judge whether a borrower can meet its obligations. Investors use them to monitor financial performance and evaluate whether their capital is earning a decent return. Managers use them to run the business: spotting weak spots and measuring the effect of their own decisions. External and internal users apply the same numbers to different questions. The limits are real. Ratios are computed from reported figures, which describe what already happened. They summarize the past; they do not predict the future. A strong current ratio does not guarantee next year's bills get paid, and last year's good margin says nothing certain about next year's demand.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing: a lens, not a verdict
collegeVersion.body: The honest way to hold a ratio is as a lens for looking at the statements, not a verdict on the company. A lens brings one relationship into focus — profit per dollar of sales, assets per dollar of bills — while the rest of the picture stays outside the frame. Read a ratio as a question to investigate (why did this move?) rather than a sentence to accept (this company is good or bad). Combined with history, peers, and the rest of the statements, ratios are among the most useful tools in finance. Alone, they are just division.

vocabulary.definition: A calculation that compares two or more figures from a company's financial statements, used to measure performance and financial health.
The family of ratios that shows earnings relative to sales, assets, or owners' equity — how much of what a company earns stays as profit.
The family of ratios that shows short-term payment ability — whether a company can cover obligations due within about a year.
The family of ratios that shows debt and capital structure — how much of a company's financing comes from borrowing rather than owners' money.
The family of ratios that shows asset use and productivity — how effectively a company's assets generate sales.
A liquidity ratio computed as current assets divided by current liabilities, measuring the ability of current assets to cover short-term obligations.
A profitability ratio computed as net income divided by revenue, showing the share of each sales dollar that ends up as earnings.
A profitability ratio computed as net income divided by shareholders' equity, measuring how effectively owners' capital generates earnings.
A leverage ratio computed as total debt divided by shareholders' equity, showing how much financing comes from debt relative to owners' money.
A reference point used to interpret a ratio, such as the company's own past ratios or the ratios of similar companies.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: A financial ratio is one statement number divided by another — a way of putting companies of different sizes on the same scale. The bakery's $40,000 profit and the chain's $40 million profit are hard to compare directly, but 'ten cents of profit per dollar of sales' is a measurement both can be judged by. The four families ask four questions: Are we making money? (profitability) Can we pay the bills coming due? (liquidity) How much debt are we carrying? (leverage) Are our assets working hard? (efficiency). The four classic ratios — current ratio, profit margin, return on equity, and debt-to-equity — are the most common answers to those questions.
eli10.analogy: A ratio is like a blood-pressure reading. One number is a compressed summary of something important about the body. On its own, a single reading tells you little: you want your history, and you want to know how you compare with people of your age and build. A company's ratios work the same way — a compressed summary of financial health that only means something in comparison, over time and against similar companies.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks down in an important way. Blood pressure has standard healthy ranges that apply to nearly everyone, but ratios have no universal 'normal'. A current ratio that suits a grocery store can look wrong for a software firm, and no single ratio — or even a handful — captures the whole financial picture the way a full checkup combines many measurements.

workedExample: Harbor & Pine Cafe ends its year with these numbers. Income statement: revenue of $240,000 and net income of $24,000. Balance sheet: current assets of $60,000 (cash $12,000, customer receivables $8,000, inventory $40,000), current liabilities of $30,000, total liabilities of $90,000, and shareholders' equity of $60,000. Profit margin = $24,000 / $240,000 = 10%, so ten cents of every sales dollar stayed as profit. Current ratio = $60,000 / $30,000 = 2.0, so two dollars of current assets stand behind each dollar of bills due within the year. Return on equity = $24,000 / $60,000 = 40%, or forty cents of profit for every dollar of owners' capital. Debt-to-equity = $90,000 / $60,000 = 1.5, a dollar and a half of debt for every dollar of equity. Now the context step: last year's margin was 8%, so 10% is an improvement; the cafe across town runs 12%, so there is still ground to gain.

commonMistakes.mistake: Judging a company from a single year's ratio.
commonMistakes.correction: A ratio earns meaning in comparison: track it over time and against peers before drawing any conclusion.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pulling the wrong statement's numbers into a ratio.
commonMistakes.correction: The current ratio uses balance-sheet figures (current assets, current liabilities); profit margin uses income-statement figures (net income, revenue). Check which statement a number comes from.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading a ratio like 2.0 as a percentage.
commonMistakes.correction: A ratio of 2.0 is a comparison — two dollars per dollar — not 2%. Percentages appear only when a ratio is multiplied by 100, as in a 10% profit margin.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a higher number is always better.
commonMistakes.correction: Context decides. Cash behind a very high current ratio can be sitting idle instead of working, and a high debt-to-equity can be routine in capital-heavy industries. Ask what the level means for this company in this industry.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating ratios as predictions.
commonMistakes.correction: Ratios describe the reported past. They can flag strengths and risks, but they do not forecast what will happen next.

compareContrast.distinction: Both divide balance-sheet numbers, but they answer different questions: the current ratio is about short-term bill-paying ability (liquidity), while debt-to-equity is about the long-term financing mix (leverage).
Both are profitability ratios with different denominators: profit margin measures profit per dollar of sales, while return on equity measures profit per dollar of owners' capital.

A raw number shows scale — the chain earned $40 million — while a ratio shows a relationship, such as ten cents of profit per sales dollar, which stays comparable as the business grows or across companies of different sizes.

keyTakeaway: A financial ratio is a lens for reading the statements, not a verdict on the company: it summarizes one relationship between numbers, and it earns meaning only when compared over time and against peers.

title: Managerial Accounting
in30Seconds: Managerial accounting prepares financial information for managers to make decisions inside the business — the lesson's working definition is drawn from OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, Volume 2. It produces budgets, cost analyses, and performance reports. Where financial accounting looks back at what already happened for outsiders, managerial accounting looks forward, helping managers plan. It follows no external standard like GAAP — the reports are built for the business's own needs. It is the business's internal compass.
whyItMatters: Managers make decisions every day that hinge on numbers: whether to add a product, how to price it, where to cut costs, when to hire. Financial statements alone cannot answer those questions — they summarize the whole company for outsiders and arrive after the fact. Managerial accounting builds the detailed, timely information managers actually decide with: a budget for next quarter, a cost breakdown of one product line, a report comparing the plan to what really happened. Understanding it changes how you read any business: you stop looking only at the public reports and start seeing the decisions behind them.
learningObjectives: Define managerial accounting using the working definition from OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, Volume 2: preparing financial information for managers to make decisions inside the business.
Contrast managerial accounting with financial accounting — internal decisions versus external reports — with the purpose of accounting referenced as the sibling topic.
Name what managerial accounting produces — budgets, cost analyses, and performance reports — and give one original example of each.
Explain the future orientation: plans and forecasts, not just history.
Identify the internal users: managers at every level of the business.
State the honest framing: managerial accounting is not governed by GAAP, and it is the business's internal compass.

collegeVersion.heading: What managerial accounting is
collegeVersion.body: OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, Volume 2 defines managerial accounting as the process that allows decision makers to set and evaluate business goals by determining what information they need to make a particular decision and how to analyze and communicate that information. CFI describes the same work in fewer words: the identification, measurement, analysis, and interpretation of accounting information for internal decision-making. In plain terms, managerial accounting prepares financial information for managers to make decisions inside the business. Notice what is missing from that definition: no outsiders, no required format, no single report. The point is not to publish results — it is to give the people running the business the numbers they need before they choose.

collegeVersion.heading: Managerial versus financial accounting
collegeVersion.body: The cleanest way to separate the two is by who reads the report. Financial accounting produces standardized financial statements — income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement — for external users: investors, creditors, and regulators. Managerial accounting serves internal users: the managers who run the business. OpenStax puts the timing difference bluntly: financial accounting focuses on reporting what has already happened, while managerial accounting focuses more on the future. The formats differ as much as the audiences. Financial statements follow a common set of rules called GAAP, so an investor can compare one company with another; managerial reports follow no such standard and are customized for the decision at hand. The purpose of accounting as a whole is a sibling topic covered in its own lesson; here it appears only to place managerial accounting in context.

collegeVersion.heading: What it produces: budgets, cost analyses, performance reports
collegeVersion.body: Three products carry most of the work. A budget is a plan expressed in numbers — expected sales and expected costs for a coming period. A cost analysis breaks a product or job into its parts — materials, labor, overhead — to reveal what something really costs to make. A performance report compares the plan with what actually happened, showing variances: budgeted $38,000 for materials, spent $41,000, so $3,000 over. OpenStax's examples of managerial reports run from budget variance analyses to production reports and job order cost sheets; each exists because a manager needs that specific information to act. Original example: Pine & Post, a furniture workshop, budgets next quarter at $90,000 in sales, runs a cost analysis showing each $700 table uses $455 in wood, hardware, and labor, and closes the quarter with a performance report flagging where actuals drifted from the plan.

collegeVersion.heading: The future orientation
collegeVersion.body: The biggest difference in spirit: financial accounting reports history; managerial accounting plans the future. OpenStax is direct — managerial accountants regularly calculate and manage what-if scenarios to help managers make decisions and plan for future business needs. A budget is a forecast of a period that has not happened yet. A cost analysis of a proposed product answers should-we-make-it before the money is spent. Even a performance report, which compares actuals to plan, exists to feed the next plan: the variance tells the manager what to change going forward. Original example: the owner of Pine & Post wants to know what happens to profit if she raises table prices by 5 percent — a what-if question with no place on any financial statement, and a routine one for managerial accounting.

collegeVersion.heading: Internal users: managers at every level
collegeVersion.body: OpenStax names the audience plainly: managerial accounting information is gathered for internal users — management at all levels in all departments, owners, and other employees. That is broader than a single finance office. The shift supervisor who decides whether to run a second shift, the store manager who chooses which products to reorder, the department head who must cut costs, the executive weighing a new location — all use managerial accounting information, and each needs a different level of detail. Original example: at a three-store bakery chain, the regional manager uses a budget for each store, each store manager tracks a daily sales report against it, and the owner uses both to decide whether to open a fourth location.

collegeVersion.heading: No external standards
collegeVersion.body: Because the reports stay inside the business, no outside authority dictates their form. OpenStax is explicit: managerial accounting is not governed by GAAP, and each organization is free to structure its reports in the format that organizes its information best. That is a freedom and a responsibility. The numbers need not follow GAAP, but the report's creator must state the assumptions used — a budget built on a guessed sales figure is only useful if everyone knows it is a guess. And because these reports are not published, a business can keep its plans and cost details private from competitors, which is one reason companies guard them closely.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Strip managerial accounting to its simplest job: it is the business's internal compass. Financial accounting tells outsiders where the company has been; managerial accounting points the people inside toward where to go next. It does not make decisions — managers do — and it cannot guarantee the future, because forecasts are only as good as their assumptions. What it does is replace guessing with information: the numbers behind a pricing decision, a hiring decision, an expansion decision. The reality check, stated simply: managerial accounting is decision support, not decision-making — and that is exactly why it exists.

vocabulary.definition: Preparing financial information for managers to make decisions inside the business; the process that lets decision makers set and evaluate goals by determining what information they need and how to analyze and communicate it.
The branch that produces standardized financial statements for external users — investors, creditors, and regulators — following rules such as GAAP.
A plan expressed in numbers: expected sales and expected costs for a coming period.
A breakdown of what a product, job, or service really costs, by materials, labor, and overhead.
A report comparing planned results with actual results, highlighting the variances between them.
The difference between a budgeted amount and the actual amount; spending $41,000 against a $38,000 budget is a $3,000 unfavorable variance.
The people inside a business who use managerial accounting information: managers at all levels, owners, and other employees.
People outside a business who read its financial statements: investors, creditors, tax authorities, and regulators.
Generally accepted accounting principles, the common set of rules and procedures that publicly traded companies must follow when preparing their financial statements.
An estimate of future results, such as next quarter's sales, used in planning.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Managerial accounting is the accounting that works inside the business. It gathers the numbers managers need to make decisions: how much a product really costs, what next quarter might bring in, and whether the plan is working. It is the difference between a report card and a roadmap. Financial accounting writes the report card — standardized, for outsiders, about what already happened. Managerial accounting draws the roadmap — custom-made, for the people driving, pointing at what comes next. Its main tools are simple to name: budgets plan the future, cost analyses reveal true costs, and performance reports compare the plan with reality. It follows no outside rulebook; the business shapes the reports to fit its own decisions, and it keeps them private.
eli10.analogy: Picture the business as a ship and managerial accounting as its compass. The financial statements are the logbook — a careful record of where the ship has been, written in a standard format for the harbor masters, owners, and insurers ashore. The compass lives on the bridge, in the hands of the captain and crew, and it points forward. A budget is the planned course; a cost analysis shows how much fuel each leg of the journey truly burns; a performance report checks whether the ship drifted off course and by how much. No harbor master requires the compass — the crew does, because steering happens on the bridge, not in the logbook.
eli10.analogyLimits: A compass points true north no matter what, but a managerial report is only as good as its assumptions — if the budget guessed sales wrong, the true north is wrong too. A compass cannot choose the route; it informs the navigator, who decides. And unlike a compass, which reveals direction to anyone who reads it, managerial reports are deliberately kept private — the business's plans and costs are its own secret.

workedExample: Pine & Post builds custom furniture. The owner, Priya, sets the quarterly budget: $90,000 in sales, $38,000 for materials, $24,000 for shop wages. At quarter's end, the performance report shows actuals of $87,000 in sales, $41,000 in materials, and $23,500 in wages. The variances: sales $3,000 under budget, materials $3,000 over, wages $500 under. Priya investigates the material variance first — lumber prices rose, and one table order needed more wood than estimated — and decides to quote a small materials surcharge on future custom orders. Separately, a cost analysis shows each $700 table uses $455 in materials, hardware, and labor, while each $420 chair uses $310, so the table contributes $245 and the chair $110 per unit. With that comparison, Priya shifts shop time toward tables next quarter, which the new budget reflects. One set of numbers, three reports, one decision each.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing managerial and financial accounting — assuming every accounting report follows GAAP and goes to outsiders.
commonMistakes.correction: Managerial reports are internal, customized, and not governed by GAAP; financial statements are standardized for external users.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating managerial accounting as history — thinking it is just record-keeping of what already happened.
commonMistakes.correction: Its signature is the forward look: budgets, forecasts, and what-if scenarios for decisions not yet made.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting managerial reports to look like financial statements.
commonMistakes.correction: Each business formats its reports the way it wants, because no external standard dictates the form. The requirements are usefulness and stated assumptions, not a fixed format.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming internal means informal.
commonMistakes.correction: Managerial reports still demand care: OpenStax notes the creator must disclose all assumptions, because a report without stated assumptions can mislead the very managers it is meant to serve.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring nonfinancial information.
commonMistakes.correction: Managerial accounting uses nonfinancial data too, such as customer counts and quality measures, while financial accounting relies on financial data alone.

compareContrast.distinction: Managerial accounting prepares information for internal decisions and looks forward; financial accounting produces standardized reports of the past for external users.
A budget plans expected results for a coming period; a performance report compares actual results against that plan and highlights the variances.

Internal users (managers at every level, owners, employees) decide with managerial reports; external users (investors, creditors, regulators) evaluate the business through published financial statements.
Managerial reports are customized, private, and free of GAAP; financial statements follow a common set of rules so outsiders can compare companies.

keyTakeaway: Managerial accounting prepares financial information for managers to make decisions inside the business — budgets, cost analyses, and performance reports built for the business's own needs, looking forward rather than back.

The audited financial statements
A cost analysis of materials, hardware, and labor per chair
A bank loan statement

Materials ran $3,000 under budget
Materials matched the budget exactly

questionBank.prompt: Why are a company's managerial reports usually kept inside the business, while its financial statements go out to investors and lenders?

Because managers prefer to work without any written information
Because the reports are too short to be worth sharing
Because they hold the company's plans and cost details, and no external standard requires them to be published
questionBank.explanation: Managerial reports are internal by design: they contain plans and proprietary cost details, and because they are not governed by GAAP or any publication requirement, the company keeps them private. There is no law requiring secrecy, and managers rely heavily on these reports.

questionBank.prompt: Nadia manages a juice bar and must decide whether to open a second location next year. Which use of managerial accounting helps her most?
options: A budget and forecast of the new location's expected sales and costs
Last year's audited financial statements
The tax forms filed for the current location
A credit check on her suppliers
questionBank.explanation: The decision is about the future, and managerial accounting's forward-looking tools — budgets and forecasts — estimate the new location's expected sales and costs. Audited statements and tax forms report the past, and a supplier credit check answers a different question entirely.

title: Cost Behavior
in30Seconds: Cost behavior is the study of how a business's costs change as its activity changes — bake more loaves, and the flour bill climbs while the rent stays put. The definition this lesson builds on comes from CFI and OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, Volume 2. Most costs follow one of three patterns: fixed, variable, or mixed. Fixed costs hold steady in total; variable costs move with activity; mixed costs combine a fixed base with a variable part. Managers study these patterns to plan, price, and predict.
whyItMatters: Every business faces a mix of bills: some arrive the same size no matter what, others swell exactly when business is booming. Managers who cannot tell the two apart make guesses — how much will next month cost, what price covers this product, can we afford a bigger order. Cost behavior replaces those guesses with a pattern. Once you see that rent is fixed and materials are variable, you can predict how costs respond to growth, price a product with confidence, and spot the mixed costs that hide a fixed base inside a variable bill. It is the difference between budgeting with a map and budgeting blind.
learningObjectives: Define cost behavior as how a business's costs change as its activity changes, attributing the working definition to CFI and OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, Volume 2.
Name the three cost behavior patterns — fixed, variable, and mixed — and give one original example of each.
Explain the per-unit flip side: fixed costs stay the same in total but fall per unit as activity rises, while variable costs stay the same per unit but change in total.
Explain why managers study cost behavior: it drives planning, pricing, and cost prediction, with managerial accounting referenced as the sibling topic.
State the honest framing: real costs rarely behave perfectly as one type, and classification depends on the decision at hand.

collegeVersion.heading: What cost behavior is
collegeVersion.body: Cost behavior is how a cost responds to changes in business activity. CFI puts the working definition plainly: cost behavior analysis is management's attempt to understand how operating costs change in relation to a change in the organization's level of activity. OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, Volume 2 makes the same point from the other end: most costs are classified in one of three ways — fixed, variable, or mixed — because different decisions need costs sorted differently. The activity in the definition is the thing the business does that drives costs: loaves baked, bikes repaired, rooms rented. The core question of cost behavior is always the same: when activity rises or falls, what happens to this cost?

collegeVersion.heading: The three patterns at a glance
collegeVersion.body: Nearly every cost falls into one of three patterns. Fixed costs stay the same in total over a range of activity — a bakery's monthly rent does not care how many loaves come out of the oven. Variable costs move with activity — every extra loaf needs more flour. Mixed costs do both: a delivery van's monthly lease is a fixed base, and the fuel it burns per mile is a variable part. OpenStax calls these the major cost behavior patterns and treats everything else as a variation on them.

collegeVersion.heading: Fixed costs: the total that doesn't move
collegeVersion.body: A fixed cost is an operating expense that does not change in total over the short term, even when activity varies. Rent, salaries, insurance, and equipment leases are the standard examples. Original example: Mara pays $2,400 a month to lease the storefront for her candle studio; she owes that amount whether she pours 100 candles or 1,000. The flip side is the part people miss: fixed costs are fixed in total, not per unit. At 100 candles, the lease costs $24 per candle; at 1,000 candles, $2.40. The total bill never moves, but the cost per unit falls as activity spreads the same bill over more units — and rises when activity shrinks.

collegeVersion.heading: Variable costs: moving with activity
collegeVersion.body: A variable cost changes in total in direct proportion to activity. Raw materials and hourly labor are the standard examples. Original example: Mara's candle studio buys soy wax at $0.80 per candle. Pour 500 candles and the wax bill is $400; pour 1,200 and it is $960. Note the mirror image of the fixed-cost rule: variable costs stay the same per unit — $0.80 a candle, every time — but change in total as activity changes. The activity that drives a variable cost has a name: a cost driver, such as units produced, hours worked, or miles driven.

collegeVersion.heading: Mixed costs: a fixed base plus a variable part
collegeVersion.body: Some costs refuse to be one or the other, and those are mixed costs: a fixed base that must be paid regardless, plus a variable part that grows with activity. OpenStax's example is a hotel occupancy tax with a $2,000 monthly base plus $5 per rented room. Original example: Tarek leases a delivery van for his spice business for $350 a month and pays $0.28 per mile driven. The $350 is there in a slow month with 200 miles, and the per-mile charge rides on top. Total mixed cost is simply the fixed base plus the variable part times the activity — no mystery, just two behaviors in one bill.

collegeVersion.heading: Why managers care
collegeVersion.body: Cost behavior is a managerial-accounting idea — that field, which has its own lesson, prepares financial information for managers' decisions inside the business, and cost behavior is one of its core tools. Managers care because the pattern tells them what the future costs. Planning: if next quarter's orders double, which costs double with them? Pricing: a product's price must cover the variable cost of each unit and still contribute something to the fixed costs that will arrive regardless. OpenStax says it directly: organizations classify costs as fixed or variable in order to control costs, make decisions, and plan for the future.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing
collegeVersion.body: The three patterns are a model, not a law of nature. Real costs are rarely perfectly one type: a fixed rent steps up when the lease expires on a bigger space, salaried staff can earn overtime, and materials prices move for reasons that have nothing to do with activity. CFI notes that in real life cost functions are not always linear and are not explained by a single driver, and OpenStax reminds us that the same cost — rent, say — can be classified differently by different companies for different decisions. The honest framing, stated simply: cost behavior gives managers a reliable map of how costs respond to activity within a normal range, and the map needs redrawing when the range changes.

vocabulary.definition: How a cost responds to changes in business activity; the study of whether a cost changes, and how, when activity rises or falls.
The level of business operations that drives costs, such as units produced, hours worked, or miles driven.
A cost that stays the same in total over a range of activity, such as monthly rent or salaries.
A cost that changes in total in direct proportion to activity, such as raw materials or hourly labor.
A cost with a fixed base that is paid regardless of activity plus a variable part that grows with activity.
The total of a cost divided by the number of units of activity; fixed costs fall per unit as activity rises.
The activity that causes a variable cost to change, such as units produced or miles driven.
The range of activity over which a cost's behavior holds, bounded by a minimum and a maximum amount.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Cost behavior is about the personality of a bill. Some bills are steady friends — the rent arrives the same size every month whether business is great or quiet. Some bills are followers — the more you produce, the bigger they get, dollar for dollar with your activity. And some bills are split personalities — a phone plan with a monthly line fee plus a charge per call. Once you know a bill's personality, you can predict what it will do next month, which is exactly what managers do before they set prices or approve a big order. You do not need to predict the future; you just need to know which costs move with your activity and which do not.
eli10.analogy: Picture a pizzeria's wood-fired oven. The oven lease is the fixed cost: the pizzeria pays it whether the oven bakes 10 pizzas a day or 300. The dough and cheese are variable: every extra pizza needs its own dough and cheese, so the ingredient bill grows one pizza's worth at a time. The delivery scooters are mixed: a scooter lease costs the same every month, but fuel and wear climb with every mile the couriers ride. The pizzeria's whole cost picture is just these three personalities stacked together — the oven that ignores the crowd, the ingredients that follow it, and the scooters that do a bit of both.
eli10.analogyLimits: Where the analogy breaks down: an oven's lease truly never changes, but real fixed costs eventually step up — bake enough pizzas and the shop needs a second oven, or a bigger lease. Real costs also refuse to stay in one lane: a salaried baker who earns overtime becomes partly variable, and ingredient prices can climb for reasons unrelated to how many pizzas you sell. The analogy treats activity as the only force moving costs, which is true enough for planning, but not the whole story.

workedExample: Golden Loaf Bakery rents its storefront for $2,800 a month and pays $6,000 a month in baker salaries — fixed costs of $8,800 that do not change with output. Its flour and butter cost $1.20 per loaf — a variable cost. In a 5,000-loaf month, the fixed costs work out to $1.76 per loaf ($8,800 divided by 5,000) on top of the $1.20 variable cost, so the bakery's cost per loaf is $2.96. In an 8,000-loaf month, fixed costs fall to $1.10 per loaf, and total cost per loaf drops to $2.30. Owner Sana uses both numbers: the per-loaf cost at expected volume sets her $3.50 shelf price, and she knows a bulk order can be priced lower because each extra loaf only adds the $1.20 variable cost. The bakery's delivery van is mixed — $400 a month plus $0.35 per mile — so she tracks miles on big catering runs rather than treating the whole bill as fixed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking fixed costs are fixed per unit
commonMistakes.correction: Rent stays the same in total, but the rent per unit falls as activity rises; treating it as fixed per unit makes costs look wrong at every volume.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking variable means unpredictable
commonMistakes.correction: Variable costs are the most predictable per unit — $0.80 of wax per candle, every time; what varies is the total, not the unit rate.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting every cost to be clearly one type
commonMistakes.correction: Many costs are mixed, and even fixed costs step up when activity leaves the normal range; the three patterns are a model, not a label printed on the invoice.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using only the total and ignoring the per-unit view
commonMistakes.correction: Pricing decisions run on per-unit costs, so a cost that is small in total can be decisive per unit — and the reverse.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming cost behavior is permanent
commonMistakes.correction: When the business outgrows its relevant range — a second oven, a bigger lease — the old pattern stops holding and the map needs redrawing.

compareContrast.distinction: A fixed cost stays the same in total as activity changes; a variable cost changes in total as activity changes.
Fixed costs are constant in total and falling per unit; variable costs are constant per unit and rising in total.
A fixed cost has one behavior; a mixed cost contains a fixed base and a variable part, so it moves with activity but never from zero.
Activity is the general level of operations; the cost driver is the specific activity that moves a particular variable cost, such as miles driven moving fuel cost.

keyTakeaway: Cost behavior is how costs respond to activity: fixed costs hold steady in total, variable costs move with activity, and mixed costs do both — and managers read those patterns to plan, price, and predict.

questionBank.prompt: What does cost behavior describe?
options: How a business records its daily sales
How costs change as business activity changes
How a company's prices compare with competitors'
How managers report costs to outside investors
questionBank.explanation: Cost behavior is the study of how costs respond to changes in activity — whether a cost changes, and how, when the business does more or less. Sales recording, price comparison, and investor reporting are different jobs.

questionBank.prompt: Marisol runs a bike repair shop and pays $1,800 a month in rent whether she repairs 20 bikes or 200. Which statement about the rent is correct?
options: Rent is a fixed cost: the total stays $1,800, and the rent per bike falls as she repairs more bikes
Rent is a fixed cost, so the rent per bike never changes
Rent is a variable cost because it must be paid every month
Rent is a variable cost because more repairs use more of the shop
questionBank.explanation: The rent is fixed in total — $1,800 regardless of repairs — and the per-unit flip side applies: at 20 bikes the rent is $90 per bike, at 200 bikes it is $9 per bike. Fixed costs are fixed in total, not per unit.
questionBank.skill: Applying the per-unit flip side of a fixed cost

questionBank.prompt: A bakery's flour costs $1.20 per loaf baked. One month it bakes 3,000 loaves and the next 5,000. What happens to the flour cost?
options: The total flour cost stays the same, but the cost per loaf falls
Both the total and the per-loaf cost rise
The total flour cost rises from $3,600 to $6,000, while the cost per loaf stays $1.20
Flour is a fixed cost, so neither the total nor the per-loaf cost changes
questionBank.explanation: Flour is a variable cost: $1.20 times 3,000 loaves is $3,600, and $1.20 times 5,000 is $6,000. The total moves with activity while the per-unit rate stays the same — the mirror image of a fixed cost.
questionBank.skill: Computing a variable cost in total and per unit

questionBank.prompt: A bakery's phone bill is $60 a month for the line plus $0.10 per call. Calls rise from 300 one month to 900 the next. What happens to the bill?
options: It stays $60, because the line fee is fixed
It rises by $30
It rises from $60 to $120
It rises from $90 to $150
questionBank.explanation: The bill is mixed: $60 plus $0.10 times 300 calls is $90, and $60 plus $0.10 times 900 is $150 — a $60 rise. The fixed base never moves; the variable part grows with the calls.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing a mixed cost as a fixed base plus a variable part

questionBank.prompt: Why does understanding cost behavior help a manager price a product?
options: Because fixed costs disappear once volume gets high enough
Because it shows which costs rise with each extra unit sold, so the price can cover those costs and still contribute to the fixed costs
Because it reveals exactly what competitors will charge
Because it makes every cost variable, so pricing becomes automatic
questionBank.explanation: A price must cover the variable cost of each unit and contribute toward the fixed costs that arrive regardless of volume. Seeing which costs move with each sale is what lets a manager set a price that works. Fixed costs do not disappear, competitors are a separate question, and costs do not become variable.

title: Fixed and Variable Costs
in30Seconds: Fixed costs stay the same in total as a business's activity changes — rent and insurance do not budge when output doubles. Variable costs move with activity: every extra batch needs more materials. The key twist is per unit: fixed cost per unit falls as volume rises, while variable cost per unit holds steady. Those patterns hold only within the relevant range, a bounded activity band. The split underpins pricing, break-even, and profit planning — a tool, not a law.
whyItMatters: Every pricing decision, profit forecast, and break-even calculation starts with the same question: which costs move with activity, and which do not? A manager who treats rent as if it varied with every sale — or treats materials as if they were fixed — will misprice products, misread profit, and plan on numbers that cannot come true. The fixed/variable split is how managers see that difference clearly: it shows what a unit really costs to make, how profit behaves as volume changes, and where a business starts losing money. Get the split right, and pricing, planning, and break-even analysis all start from a sound base.
learningObjectives: Define fixed costs using the working definition from OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, Volume 2: an operating expense that holds steady in total for a time, even when activity varies.
Define variable costs as costs that vary in direct proportion to the level of activity in the business.
Explain the per-unit flip with original arithmetic: fixed cost per unit falls as volume rises, while variable cost per unit stays constant.
Describe the relevant range as the bounded activity band within which the fixed/variable pattern holds.
Apply the fixed/variable split to a pricing or profit-planning decision, with break-even analysis referenced as a sibling topic.
State the honest framing: the fixed/variable split is a decision tool, not a law.

collegeVersion.heading: Fixed costs: the bill that does not move
collegeVersion.body: OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, Volume 2 supplies the working definition: a fixed cost is an operating expense that holds steady in total for a time, even if activity varies. The words "in total" and "over the short term" do the heavy lifting. The textbook's own examples span business types: rent, insurance, and managers' salaries for merchandisers; property taxes, insurance, and equipment leases for manufacturers; rent, straight-line depreciation, and administrative salaries for service firms. The roastery's $1,800 monthly rent is the same whether Diego roasts 500 pounds of coffee or 2,000. He cannot avoid it by roasting less, and it does not grow when he roasts more. What makes a cost fixed is not that it is small or unimportant — it is that its total does not respond to activity.

collegeVersion.heading: Variable costs: the bill that rides along
collegeVersion.body: A variable cost is one that varies in direct proportion to the level of activity within the business, again per OpenStax, and CFI describes the same pattern: costs that fluctuate with the volume of production. The cost driver is the activity that causes the cost to move: pounds of coffee roasted, units produced, miles driven, rooms rented. For Diego, green coffee beans are the clearest variable cost — about $1.50 per pound, so 100 pounds costs $150 and 1,000 pounds costs $1,500. Direct materials generally, direct labor hours, and fuel behave the same way. Notice the direction: variable costs scale with activity, but the per-unit rate itself does not change.

collegeVersion.heading: The per-unit flip: the key insight
collegeVersion.body: Here is the insight that makes the whole classification useful. Fixed costs are fixed in total but change per unit: $2,400 of monthly fixed costs (rent plus the roaster lease) works out to $3.00 per pound at 800 pounds and falls to $1.50 per pound at 1,600. Variable costs flip it: they change in total but stay constant per unit — beans remain $1.50 per pound whether Diego roasts 800 or 1,600 pounds. One spread, one constant. Managers lean on this every day: more volume dilutes fixed costs, while variable costs ride along at a steady per-unit rate.

collegeVersion.heading: Relevant range: where the pattern holds
collegeVersion.body: The pattern is not unlimited. The relevant range is a specific activity band, bounded by a minimum and a maximum, within which managers can predict revenue or cost levels. Diego's roaster handles up to 2,000 pounds a month. Inside that band, the $2,400 of fixed costs holds. Push past it — say a wholesale contract demands 2,400 pounds — and he needs a second roaster, so fixed costs step up to a new level. OpenStax shows the same stair-step behavior when a quality inspector's 80-unit shift limit is exceeded. The honest caveat: outside the relevant range, the flat lines turn into stairs.

collegeVersion.heading: Why the split matters
collegeVersion.body: Pricing starts here: to price a bag of coffee, Diego needs his variable cost per unit, plus a fair share of fixed costs, plus profit. Profit planning starts here too: knowing which costs move with volume tells him how profit responds when sales rise or fall. The classification even steers investment choices — CFI notes that a company with high direct labor costs may trade them for machinery, swapping variable costs for stable fixed ones when volume is high enough. Break-even analysis — a sibling topic with its own lesson — builds directly on this split, finding the volume at which revenue covers fixed and variable costs combined. Cost behavior is likewise a sibling topic. This lesson names them only; each gets its own lesson.

collegeVersion.heading: Mixed costs and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Not every cost is purely one or the other. Mixed costs carry both a fixed and a variable component — a phone plan with a flat monthly fee plus a per-minute charge, or a base fee plus a per-unit tax. Separating the two components belongs to the cost-behavior topic. And the honest framing: the fixed/variable split is a tool, not a law. Costs get reclassified as leases are renegotiated, capacity is added, or a business changes how it operates. The classification works within the relevant range and over the short term; beyond that, treat it as a useful approximation.

vocabulary.definition: An unavoidable operating expense whose total stays the same over the short term even when business activity changes (OpenStax working definition).
A cost that changes in direct proportion to the level of activity, such as materials that grow with each unit produced.
The full sum of all fixed costs in a period, a total that does not move when activity changes.
The full sum of all variable costs, a total that rises and falls with the level of activity.
A cost containing both a fixed component and a variable component, such as a flat fee plus a per-unit charge.
The bounded activity band, with a minimum and a maximum, within which a business's cost patterns hold as described.
Any activity, such as units produced or labor hours, that causes a variable cost to rise or fall.
The amount of work a business does in a period, measured in units, hours, miles, or rooms, that costs respond to.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Every business has two kinds of bills. Some bills are the same every month no matter how much the business produces — rent, insurance, the lease on the oven. Others grow with the work — the flour in each loaf, the coffee beans in each batch. The surprising part is what happens per unit: the fixed bill gets cheaper per loaf when you bake more, because you are spreading the same total over more loaves. The variable bill stays the same per loaf but grows in total. Knowing which bill is which is the first step in pricing anything.
eli10.analogy: A moving van is a good picture. The daily rental fee is the same whether you drive 5 miles or 50 — a fixed cost that gets cheaper per mile the more you drive. The gasoline is different: each mile burns fuel, so the gas bill grows mile by mile while the cost per mile stays roughly constant. You plan the move by keeping the flat fee in mind and budgeting fuel per mile.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy ends where real businesses start: the van rental does not stay flat forever — rent a bigger van or a second one and the fee jumps, just as fixed costs step up beyond the relevant range. And some real costs mix both patterns, like a phone plan with a monthly fee plus a per-minute charge.

workedExample: Roast & Ember is Diego's coffee roastery. Each month he pays $1,800 rent and $600 for the roaster lease — $2,400 in total fixed costs, no matter what. In March he roasts 800 pounds; in April, 1,600. The fixed cost per pound: March, $2,400 ÷ 800 = $3.00 per pound; April, $2,400 ÷ 1,600 = $1.50. The rent bill never changed, yet its per-pound share halved. Now the variable side: green beans cost $1.50 per pound roasted. March's beans: 800 × $1.50 = $1,200; April's: 1,600 × $1.50 = $2,400. Total bean cost doubled with output, but the $1.50 per pound never moved. Same activity, two opposite behaviors: fixed costs spread thinner per unit as volume grows; variable costs hold their per-unit rate and grow in total. That contrast is the lesson.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a fixed cost as if it were fixed per unit.
commonMistakes.correction: Fixed costs are fixed in total, not per unit. As volume rises, the per-unit share falls — $2,400 spread over 800 pounds is $3.00 per pound; over 1,600 pounds it is $1.50.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a variable cost as if it varied per unit.
commonMistakes.correction: Variable costs vary in total while the per-unit rate holds. Beans at $1.50 per pound cost $1,200 at 800 pounds and $2,400 at 1,600 — same rate, different totals.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing a fixed cost is fixed forever.
commonMistakes.correction: The pattern holds over the short term and within the relevant range. When capacity is added — a second roaster, a bigger space — fixed costs step up to a new level.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming labor is always a variable cost.
commonMistakes.correction: It depends on the arrangement: hourly production labor grows with output, while salaried staff stay fixed in total. Classify by how the cost actually behaves.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forcing every cost into one of two boxes.
commonMistakes.correction: Many costs are mixed — a fixed base plus a variable component. Mixed costs are named here; separating them belongs to the cost-behavior topic.

compareContrast.distinction: Fixed costs stay constant in total as activity changes; variable costs change in total with activity. Per unit, the fixed share falls while the variable share holds.
Fixed cost per unit falls as volume rises; variable cost per unit stays the same regardless of volume.
Inside the band, cost patterns hold as described; outside it, fixed costs step up to new levels and the old predictions break.
Pure costs behave one way; mixed costs combine a fixed component and a variable component, so they must be split before analysis.

keyTakeaway: Fixed costs stay flat in total but thin out per unit as volume grows; variable costs grow in total while holding steady per unit. The pattern holds within the relevant range — a tool, not a law.

It rises from $1.50 to $3.00 per pound

questionBank.explanation: $2,400 ÷ 800 = $3.00 per pound in March, and $2,400 ÷ 1,600 = $1.50 in April. The fixed total never moved, so spreading it over more pounds cut the per-unit share in half.
questionBank.skill: Computing fixed cost per unit at two activity levels

questionBank.prompt: Diego's roaster handles up to 2,000 pounds a month. If orders climb past that, he must lease a second roaster and his fixed costs jump. What does this illustrate?
options: Variable costs always stay constant per unit
Fixed costs never change under any circumstances
The relevant range — cost patterns hold only within a bounded activity band
Mixed costs contain a fixed and a variable component
questionBank.explanation: The relevant range is the bounded activity band within which the fixed-cost pattern holds. Beyond 2,000 pounds the range is exceeded, and fixed costs step up to a new level — the pattern, not the costs, is what changes.
questionBank.skill: Explaining the relevant range with a capacity example

questionBank.prompt: Diego lands a catering order for 400 extra pounds next month. Which statement about his costs is correct?
options: His fixed costs will rise with the order
His variable cost per pound will rise with the order
His fixed cost per pound will stay exactly the same
His total variable cost will rise while fixed cost per pound falls
questionBank.explanation: The extra batch needs more beans, so total variable cost rises, while the per-pound bean rate holds. His fixed total stays at $2,400, so spreading it over more pounds makes the fixed cost per pound fall.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing how an order changes total and per-unit costs

quickCheck.prompt: Diego's roastery pays $1,800 a month in rent whether it roasts 500 pounds of coffee or 2,000. What kind of cost is the rent?
options: A variable cost
A fixed cost
A mixed cost
A step cost
quickCheck.explanation: The rent stays the same in total as activity changes, which is the working definition of a fixed cost. Variable costs move with activity, mixed costs carry both components, and step costs jump at thresholds — the rent does none of those.
quickCheck.skill: Identifying a fixed cost from its total-behavior definition

quickCheck.prompt: Which of these is a variable cost for Diego's roastery?
options: The monthly roaster lease
The annual equipment insurance
The counter staff's fixed salaries
The green coffee beans used in each batch
quickCheck.explanation: Green beans vary in direct proportion to pounds roasted — the defining behavior of a variable cost. The lease, the insurance, and the salaries stay the same in total as output changes.
quickCheck.skill: Recognizing a variable cost among fixed-cost examples

quickCheck.prompt: Roast & Ember pays $2,400 a month in total fixed costs. In March it roasts 800 pounds; in April, 1,600. What happens to the fixed cost per pound?
options: It falls from $3.00 to $1.50 per pound
It stays at $3.00 per pound both months
It rises from $1.50 to $3.00 per pound
It doubles to $6.00 per pound
quickCheck.explanation: $2,400 ÷ 800 = $3.00 per pound in March, and $2,400 ÷ 1,600 = $1.50 in April. The fixed total never moved, so spreading it over more pounds cut the per-unit share in half.
