title: Decision-Making
in30Seconds: Decision making is choosing among options: this lesson’s working definition comes from OpenStax's Principles of Management, which calls it the action or process of thinking through possible options and selecting one. Managers face routine decisions that can run on rules and novel decisions that need a full process — define the problem, gather information, weigh options, choose, act, and review. Because time and information are limited, a good process raises the odds but never guarantees the outcome.
whyItMatters: Every day, managers choose: whom to hire, what to stock, where to spend. Those small choices add up to the organization's direction and survival — a good decision can help a business thrive, while a poor one can push it toward failure. Knowing which decisions are routine and which are novel tells you when rules will do and when to slow down. Knowing the common traps — anchoring, confirmation bias, groupthink — helps you catch your own blind spots before they grow expensive. And the honest part matters most: no process guarantees the outcome, so the goal is to decide well, review honestly, and adjust when reality disagrees.
learningObjectives: State the working definition of decision making, attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Management: the action or process of thinking through possible options and selecting one.
Describe the six-step rational process — define the problem, gather information, weigh options, choose, act, and review — with one line and an original example for each step.
Distinguish programmed from nonprogrammed decisions, each with an original example, and explain why the distinction matters.
Explain bounded rationality — the idea that managers decide with limited time and information — and attribute the concept to Herbert Simon.
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of group decisions, noting that how teams work together is its own topic.
Identify anchoring, confirmation bias, and groupthink in a short scenario, one line each.

collegeVersion.heading: What decision making is: choosing among options
collegeVersion.body: Decision making is choosing among options. This lesson's working definition comes from OpenStax's Principles of Management: decision making is the action or process of thinking through possible options and selecting one. That means two things: options exist, and someone selects one. Managers at every level decide — a supervisor schedules workers, a top team chooses whether to pursue a new product line. OpenStax notes that these choices affect stakeholders, everyone touched by the organization, from customers to employees to owners, and that a good decision can help a business thrive while a poor one can push it toward failure. A management decision is not like a multiple-choice test: sometimes several options look good; sometimes all of them look bad and the task is to minimize harm.

collegeVersion.heading: The rational process: six steps
collegeVersion.body: A rational process walks a decision through six steps. Define the problem: know what you are really deciding — weekend attendance at a neighborhood cinema has slid for three months, not just one bad week. Gather information: collect what is relevant — ticket sales by showtime, a survey of regulars, the projectionist's experience at her previous theater. Weigh the options: compare alternatives on cost, effort, and likely payoff — late shows, earlier matinees, and themed double features. Choose: commit to one option — one 9:30 p.m. showing on Fridays and Saturdays. Act: carry the choice into the world — update the schedule, hire two part-time staff, and post the new times. Review: check the result and adjust — after six weeks, Fridays draw well and Saturdays barely break even, so Saturdays are dropped. OpenStax's version runs the same spine: recognize that a decision is needed, generate multiple alternatives, analyze them, select one, implement it, and evaluate its effectiveness. Real managers rarely walk the steps in a clean line — new information sends them back — but the process is an ideal that raises the odds of a good outcome.

collegeVersion.heading: Programmed and nonprogrammed decisions
collegeVersion.body: OpenStax draws a clean line between two kinds of decisions. Programmed decisions are repeated over time, and an existing set of rules can guide them because the criteria are known or can be estimated. The cinema's weekly popcorn and soda reorder is programmed: last week's sales, current stock, and the supplier's delivery time settle it. So is the weekly staff rota — complex, but built from known facts. These decisions can run on heuristics, mental shortcuts that produce an adequate answer quickly. Nonprogrammed decisions are novel and unstructured: the criteria are not well defined, the information is ambiguous or incomplete, and judgment and creative thinking are required. Whether to replace the aging projector with digital is nonprogrammed — no one can fully know the cost, the lifespan, or whether audiences will care. The distinction matters because routine decisions should run on rules and shortcuts to save time, while novel decisions earn the full six-step process.

collegeVersion.heading: Bounded rationality: the honest limit
collegeVersion.body: Textbook rational choice assumes complete information, but managers never have it. Bounded rationality is the idea that decision makers cannot be fully rational because they cannot grasp every possible alternative or every implication of each one; brains process a limited amount of information, and managers often must decide before all the data arrives. The name belongs to Herbert Simon, the American social scientist who won the 1978 Nobel Prize in economics for his pioneering research into decision making within organizations and whom Britannica calls an influential proponent of bounded rationality. Simon also promoted satisficing — choosing the first acceptable option rather than hunting for the perfect one. Bounded rationality is not an excuse to skip the process; it is the reason the process exists. Under real limits, the goal is a good decision, made deliberately, not a perfect one, made eventually.

collegeVersion.heading: Group decisions: more heads, same traps
collegeVersion.body: OpenStax lists genuine advantages of group decisions: members bring different knowledge and perspectives, more options get generated, individual biases can cancel out — a mixed hiring committee is less likely to hire only people like themselves — and people who helped make a decision commit to it more. The disadvantages are real too. Groups are slower, conflict can bog them down, and groupthink can set in: members choose not to voice concerns because they would rather keep the peace, so dissent is suppressed and the group agrees without real analysis. OpenStax's remedies include diverse membership, encouraging everyone to speak, and assigning a devil's advocate to challenge the group's thinking. How teams form and work together is its own topic; the point here is that deciding together has measurable costs and benefits, and agreement alone is not evidence of a good decision.

collegeVersion.heading: Common traps and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Three traps deserve a name. Anchoring: the first number or option you encounter pulls later judgments toward it — a vendor's $20,000 opening quote makes $14,000 feel fair even when the same equipment sells for $9,000 elsewhere. Confirmation bias: you pay more attention to evidence that supports what you already believe — the manager who has decided a candidate is excellent notices the compliments and skims the complaints. Groupthink: people stay quiet to keep the peace, so the group agrees without analysis. The psychology subject owns the depth of these biases; here they are named as hazards. The honest framing of this lesson is simple: a good process raises the odds; it cannot guarantee the outcome. Decisions are made under uncertainty — you never learn what the road not taken would have delivered — and sometimes every option is bad and the best you can do is minimize harm. What a good process buys you is early detection: review catches a bad call sooner, and changing course is a sign of good management, not weakness.

vocabulary.definition: Choosing among options: the action or process of thinking through possible options and selecting one; this lesson’s working definition comes from OpenStax's Principles of Management.
Anyone affected by an organization's decisions, such as customers, employees, suppliers, or owners.
A decision repeated over time that an existing set of rules can guide, because its criteria are known or can be estimated.
A novel, unstructured decision whose criteria are not well defined and whose information is often ambiguous or incomplete.
A mental shortcut that produces an adequate solution quickly, commonly used for routine programmed decisions.
The idea, associated with Herbert Simon, that decision makers cannot be fully rational because time, information, and processing power are limited.
Choosing the first acceptable option rather than continuing to search for the best possible one; a term promoted by Herbert Simon.
The tendency for a first number or reference point to pull later judgments toward it, so later estimates stay close to the anchor.
The tendency to notice information that supports existing beliefs and to downplay information that challenges them.
A pattern in which group members stay quiet about their objections to keep the peace, producing agreement without real analysis.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Decision making is choosing among options: you see more than one way forward, and you pick one. Managers do it all day. Some choices are so routine they can run on rules; others are brand new and need real thinking. The reliable way to handle the new ones is a loop: figure out what the problem is, gather information, compare your options, choose, act, and then check how it went. Two honest warnings. You will never have all the time or information you want — that limit has a name, bounded rationality. And your own mind plays tricks: the first number you hear pulls you toward it, you notice evidence that agrees with you, and in a group people stay quiet to keep the peace. A good process raises your odds; it does not guarantee the outcome.
eli10.analogy: Choosing where to eat with a hungry friend. You read the menus online (gather information), compare price and distance (weigh options), pick a place (choose), walk over (act), and while you eat you decide whether to come back (review). The first glowing review you read can blind you to the bad ones — anchoring and confirmation bias in action. And if your friend keeps saying whatever you want, you may pick somewhere you both secretly dislike rather than argue — groupthink at a table for two.
eli10.analogyLimits: A meal choice is small and reversible; a business decision can commit money and people's livelihoods, and the menu is never complete — no one hands a manager the full list of options. A diner also gets feedback in one evening, while a manager must actively check results for weeks. The analogy shows the loop and the traps, but not the stakes or the scale.

workedExample: Watch the full process at Priya's cinema, a neighborhood theater with one screen. Define the problem: Friday and Saturday attendance has dropped for three straight months. Gather information: Priya pulls ticket sales by showtime, asks twenty regulars what would bring them back, and calls two other cinema owners about their late shows. Weigh the options: late-night showings, cheaper matinees, and themed double features — she compares staffing costs, marketing effort, and likely demand for each. Choose: one 9:30 p.m. showing on Fridays and Saturdays. Act: she updates the schedule, hires two part-time staff, and posts the new times online. Review: six weeks in, Fridays are nearly full and Saturdays barely cover the extra staff cost, so she drops Saturdays and keeps Fridays. The process did not guarantee success — it caught the miss early and let her adjust.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running every decision through the full six-step process.
commonMistakes.correction: Routine, repeated decisions are programmed: they can run on rules and shortcuts (heuristics) that save time. OpenStax reserves the full process for nonprogrammed decisions, where the quality of the choice matters more than the speed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating the first option as the best option.
commonMistakes.correction: That is anchoring: the first number or alternative you meet pulls later judgments toward it. A $20,000 opening quote makes $14,000 feel fair even when $9,000 is the real market price. Generate and compare alternatives before you commit.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading agreement as analysis.
commonMistakes.correction: Groupthink happens when members stay quiet to keep the peace, so unanimous support can hide real doubts. Encourage dissent — or assign a devil's advocate — and treat silence as a question, not a vote.

commonMistakes.mistake: Deciding before gathering information.
commonMistakes.correction: The rational process starts by defining the problem and gathering information. Choosing from instinct alone is a gamble; even a quick check of the facts narrows the odds.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting the process to guarantee the outcome.
commonMistakes.correction: A good process raises the odds but cannot remove uncertainty — every option carries unknown results. The honest habit is to review the outcome and change course when reality disagrees.

compareContrast.distinction: A programmed decision repeats and can be guided by an existing set of rules with known criteria, like a weekly reorder; a nonprogrammed decision is novel and unstructured with ambiguous information, like adopting a new technology. Routine decisions deserve speed; novel ones deserve the full process.

An individual decision is fast and clearly accountable but carries one person's blind spots; a group decision brings more knowledge, options, and commitment but is slower and can fall into groupthink. How teams work together is its own topic.

The rational ideal assumes complete information and unlimited processing; bounded rationality, associated with Herbert Simon, accepts that time, information, and brainpower are limited, so managers satisfice — pick the first acceptable option — and use process to raise the odds.

keyTakeaway: Decision making is choosing among options. A clear process — define the problem, gather information, weigh options, choose, act, and review — raises the odds of a good outcome, but limited time and information mean no process can guarantee it.

questionBank.prompt: A coffee shop manager reorders beans every Monday using the same formula: last week's sales, current stock, and the supplier's delivery time. What kind of decision is this?
options: A programmed decision, because it repeats and follows known criteria
A nonprogrammed decision, because it involves judgment under uncertainty
A group decision, because the supplier is part of the process
An anchoring trap, because the formula fixes on last week's sales
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax defines programmed decisions as those repeated over time for which an existing set of rules can guide the process; a routine reorder built on known criteria fits that description. Nonprogrammed decisions are novel and unstructured, the supplier is not deciding with the manager, and anchoring is a bias, not a type of decision.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing a programmed decision

questionBank.prompt: A food truck owner wants to know whether to add a second truck. She lists three options — a downtown lunch route, a weekend park circuit, and catering — then compares startup costs and likely demand for each before picking the downtown route. Which step of the rational process is she in?
options: Define the problem
Gather information
Weigh the options
Review the outcome
questionBank.explanation: Weighing the options means comparing alternatives on cost, effort, and likely payoff before choosing, which is exactly what she does with the three routes. She has already defined the problem and gathered information, and she has not yet acted or reviewed the outcome.
questionBank.skill: Applying the rational decision process to a scenario

questionBank.prompt: A manager has already decided that the first job candidate she interviewed is the best. In the final round she notices every compliment the candidate receives and plays down the stronger reviews of the other finalists. Which decision trap is at work?
options: Anchoring
Groupthink
Satisficing
Confirmation bias
questionBank.explanation: Confirmation bias is paying more attention to information that supports an existing belief and less to information that challenges it — precisely what the manager does with the candidate's reviews. Anchoring is a first reference point pulling later judgments, groupthink is staying quiet to keep peace in a group, and satisficing is accepting the first workable option.
questionBank.skill: Diagnosing confirmation bias in a hiring scenario

questionBank.prompt: An equipment vendor opens a negotiation by quoting $20,000. The buyer later learns the same equipment sells for $9,000 elsewhere, yet she still thinks $14,000 is a fair counteroffer. What trap is at work?
options: Groupthink
Anchoring
Confirmation bias
Bounded rationality
questionBank.explanation: Anchoring is the tendency for a first number — the $20,000 quote — to pull later judgments toward it, so $14,000 feels reasonable next to the opening price. Groupthink involves silence in a group, confirmation bias involves favoring supporting evidence, and bounded rationality is the general limit of time and information rather than this specific pull.
questionBank.skill: Identifying anchoring in a negotiation

questionBank.prompt: A store team unanimously approves a new display plan in a five-minute meeting. Two employees privately think the plan will fail but say nothing because they do not want to sour the mood. What is this?
options: Groupthink
Anchoring
Confirmation bias
The review step of the rational process
questionBank.explanation: Groupthink occurs when members choose not to voice their objections to keep the peace, so the group agrees without real analysis — the display plan gets unanimous but hollow support. Anchoring, confirmation bias, and the review step describe different phenomena: reference points, selective attention, and checking results after acting.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing groupthink in a group decision

She lists three options — a downtown lunch route, a weekend park circuit, and catering — then compares startup costs and likely demand for each before picking the downtown route. Which step of the rational process is she in?
options: Define the problem
Gather information
Weigh the options
Review the outcome
quickCheck.explanation: Weighing the options means comparing alternatives on cost, effort, and likely payoff before choosing, which is exactly what she does with the three routes. She has already defined the problem and gathered information, and she has not yet acted or reviewed the outcome.
quickCheck.skill: Applying the rational decision process to a scenario

quickCheck.prompt: A manager has already decided that the first job candidate she interviewed is the best. In the final round she notices every compliment the candidate receives and plays down the stronger reviews of the other finalists. Which decision trap is at work?
options: Anchoring
Groupthink
Satisficing
Confirmation bias
quickCheck.explanation: Confirmation bias is paying more attention to information that supports an existing belief and less to information that challenges it — precisely what the manager does with the candidate's reviews. Anchoring is a first reference point pulling later judgments, groupthink is staying quiet to keep peace in a group, and satisficing is accepting the first workable option.
quickCheck.skill: Diagnosing confirmation bias in a hiring scenario

title: Delegation
in30Seconds: Delegation is handing work down with trust: assigning responsibility and authority to another person to carry out a task. The working definition adopted in this lesson comes from OpenStax's Introduction to Business — managers delegate, or assign, some degree of authority and responsibility to others below them in the chain of command. Managers delegate to scale the work, develop people, and keep focus. Delegate tasks others can do, with the right support. Responsibility is the task; authority is the power to complete it. Final accountability never moves.
whyItMatters: A manager who does everything personally becomes the bottleneck: work queues behind one person, and nobody else learns. Delegation is how managers multiply themselves. It lets an organization carry more work than any one person could (scale), gives people the chance to build skills through real responsibility (development), and protects the manager's attention for decisions only they can make (focus). It is also the honest part of leadership: you stay accountable for what you hand down. Understanding delegation — the task, the authority, and who answers for the outcome — matters whether you run a store, a club, or a team project, because every organization runs on work that flows through other people's hands.
learningObjectives: State the working definition of delegation, attributed to OpenStax's Introduction to Business: managers delegate, or assign, some degree of authority and responsibility to others below them in the chain of command.
Name three reasons managers delegate — scale, development, and focus — with one line of explanation for each.
Describe what to delegate: tasks another person can carry out, matched to their skills and supported with instructions, resources, and availability.
Distinguish responsibility (the task) from authority (the power to complete it), and explain where accountability sits when work is delegated.
List the four delegation steps in order: choose the person, explain the task, grant authority, and check in.
Explain what is never delegated — final accountability for the outcome — and why delegation is not dumping.

collegeVersion.heading: What delegation is: the working definition
collegeVersion.body: Delegation is handing work down with trust: assigning responsibility and authority to another person to carry out a task. The working definition adopted in this lesson comes from OpenStax's Introduction to Business, which explains that most managers delegate, or assign, some degree of authority and responsibility to others below them in the chain of command. Corporate Finance Institute (CFI) describes the same move as assigning tasks, duties, and decision-making authority to others in an organizational team. Two details in that definition do the real work. First, delegation transfers the task — the specific work to be done. Second, it transfers the authority to complete that work — the power to make the decisions the task requires. What never transfers is final accountability, which we will come back to. Delegation is a routine part of management, not an occasional favor: managers cannot personally perform every task their organization depends on, so they distribute work through the people they lead.

collegeVersion.heading: Why delegate: scale, development, and focus
collegeVersion.body: Managers delegate for three reasons, each worth one line. Scale: one person can only do so much, and delegation lets an organization carry more work than any single manager could — CFI calls this enhanced productivity, work allocated across people who can each focus on what they do well. Development: handing real work to people grows their skills, experience, and confidence, so the team gets stronger over time instead of depending on one person. Focus: when well-understood work moves to other hands, the manager's time is freed for the higher-value decisions, planning, and judgment that only the manager can supply. All three reasons are about the organization working better, not about the manager getting rid of work.

collegeVersion.heading: What to delegate: tasks others can do, with the right support
collegeVersion.body: The general practice is simple: delegate tasks another person can perform, matched to their skills, and support them while they do it. CFI's guidelines capture the practice in three parts. Match skills and expertise: choose the person who has — or is ready to build — the knowledge the task requires. Clearly define the task: say what the expected result looks like, the deadline, and any instructions or resources needed. Provide adequate support: stay available for questions and offer help rather than vanishing after the handoff. An original example: Priya manages the kitchen of a campus catering company. She delegates the weekly storeroom inventory to Marcus, a line cook who knows the stock system. She explains that the count happens every Thursday, gets logged in the shared sheet, and must be finished before the Friday order. Marcus may reorder staples up to a set dollar limit on his own, and Priya promises to answer questions at the morning meeting. That is a delegable task: Marcus can do it, he knows what done looks like, and he has support.

collegeVersion.heading: Responsibility, authority, and accountability: the three-way split
collegeVersion.body: Delegation hands down two things and keeps one. Responsibility is the task itself: the duty assigned to the person who will carry it out. Authority is the power to complete it — OpenStax defines authority as legitimate power, granted by the organization and acknowledged by employees, that allows an individual to request action and expect compliance. If you hand someone a task but keep all the authority, you have not delegated; you have assigned homework that needs your signature at every step. OpenStax explains the flow this way: authority and responsibility move downward through the organization as managers assign activities and share decision-making, while accountability — responsibility for outcomes — moves upward, because managers at each level answer for the actions of the people below them. So the delegator keeps the accountability even after the task and the authority move down.

collegeVersion.heading: The delegation steps — and what never gets delegated
collegeVersion.body: Delegation runs in four steps, one line each. Choose the person: pick someone whose skills — or growth needs — fit the task. Explain the task: say what the result should look like, why it matters, and when it is due. Grant authority: give the person the power to make the decisions the task requires, within agreed limits. Check in: review progress at sensible points and stay available for questions — checking in is not hovering, and skipping it turns delegation into abandonment. The honest note: final accountability is never delegated. If the delegated report is late, the manager answers for it — that is what OpenStax means when it says accountability moves upward. The reality check: delegation is not dumping. Dumping is offloading work you do not want, to whoever is closest, with no instructions, no support, and no follow-through. CFI flags the failure modes: delegating without trust or oversight, unclear communication about expectations, and overloading people beyond their capacity, which leads to burnout. Real delegation keeps the outcome on the delegator's shoulders, gives the doer the task, the authority, and the support, and checks in along the way. That is handing work down with trust.

vocabulary.definition: Assigning responsibility and authority to another person to carry out work; the working definition in this lesson draws from OpenStax's Introduction to Business.
The task or duty assigned to a person; in delegation, the work that moves down to the person who will carry it out.
The legitimate power to make decisions and request action; in delegation, the power to complete the assigned task.
Responsibility for outcomes; in delegation, it stays with the delegator even after the task and the authority move down.
The line of authority running from the top of an organization down through its levels, showing who reports to whom.
Giving a person ownership and the authority to make decisions within their assigned work.
Offloading work without matching skills, giving instructions, providing support, or checking in — the failure mode that delegation is not.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Delegation is handing a piece of your work to someone else — with the power to actually do it — while staying answerable for how it turns out. You are not getting rid of the work; you are sharing it. Managers delegate for three reasons: one person can only do so much (scale), people grow by taking on real tasks (development), and the manager's attention is freed for the work only they can do (focus). Hand over tasks the other person can handle, explain what done looks like, give them the authority to decide, and check in along the way. The part you never hand over is the final accountability: if it goes wrong, you still answer for it. That is why delegation is not dumping — dumping is tossing work over the fence with no instructions, no support, and no follow-through.
eli10.analogy: Think of a family recipe. When you teach someone to cook the Sunday stew, you hand over the recipe card and the stove — the authority to cook it — and you trust them to season it their way. You stay in the kitchen doorway for questions, and you check the pot before dinner. If the stew comes out too salty, you still apologize to the guests: it came from your kitchen. Delegation is exactly that: the recipe and the stove go down, the pride and the apology stay with you.
eli10.analogyLimits: The kitchen analogy stops short in two ways. In an organization, authority is formal: it is granted by the organization and runs through the chain of command, not through personal trust alone. And the stakes are larger — a delegated project can involve many people, budgets, and deadlines, so check-ins are structured and repeated, not a single glance at a pot.

workedExample: Watch delegation run in a campus catering company. Priya, the kitchen manager, is stretched thin: between the new menu, supplier calls, and Thursday's banquet, she has no time left. She delegates the weekly storeroom inventory to Marcus, a line cook who already knows the stock system. Step one, choose the person: Marcus fits. Step two, explain the task: count everything by Thursday, log it in the shared sheet, and flag anything below reorder level. Step three, grant authority: Marcus may reorder staples up to $300 without asking, and he schedules the count around his shift. Step four, check in: Priya reviews the sheet Friday morning and answers questions at the daily meeting. The inventory happens on time, Marcus learns the ordering side of the kitchen, and Priya finishes the banquet menu. When a case of tomatoes arrives short, Priya handles the supplier call herself — the accountability stayed with her.

commonMistakes.mistake: Delegating the task but keeping all the authority, so the person must ask permission for every decision.
commonMistakes.correction: Grant the authority the task requires, within agreed limits; otherwise you have assigned homework, not delegated.

commonMistakes.mistake: Delegating and disappearing — no check-in and no availability.
commonMistakes.correction: Schedule check-ins at sensible points and stay available for questions; checking in is oversight, not hovering.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dumping the undesirable work — handing every unpleasant task to whoever is closest, with no support.
commonMistakes.correction: Match the task to skills and development goals, explain it, and support it; dumping teaches people that delegation means getting the garbage.

commonMistakes.mistake: Overloading the most capable person because they never say no.
commonMistakes.correction: Spread the work; CFI warns that piling responsibilities beyond a person's capacity leads to burnout and worse performance.

commonMistakes.mistake: Snatching the task back at the first stumble.
commonMistakes.correction: Treat stumbles as coaching moments and keep the check-ins going; taking work back teaches people that effort is pointless — and the task boomerangs straight back onto your plate.

compareContrast.distinction: Delegation matches the task to the person, explains it, grants authority, and checks in; dumping offloads work without support or follow-through. Delegation keeps the accountability; dumping tries to leave it behind.

Responsibility is the task you are assigned; authority is the power to make the decisions the task requires. Delegation hands down both — keeping one without the other produces homework without the ability to finish it.

A delegator grants authority but keeps accountability and checks in; an abdicator walks away from the outcome entirely. That is the difference between handing work down with trust and letting it fall.

keyTakeaway: Delegation hands the task and the authority to another person but keeps the accountability with you: choose the person, explain the task, grant authority, and check in — because delegation is handing work down with trust, not dumping it.

questionBank.prompt: What happens, per this lesson’s working definition, when a manager delegates?
options: The manager assigns some degree of authority and responsibility to another person to carry out the work
The manager transfers all accountability for the outcome to the other person
The manager permanently reassigns one of the employee's own duties
The manager reviews the employee's work after it is finished

Accountability
Authority
A deadline

questionBank.prompt: A team lead delegates the customer-refund process to a new hire, walks through the refund policy, and sets a fifteen-minute review for Friday afternoon. Which delegation step is the Friday meeting?
options: Choosing the person
Explaining the task
Granting authority
Checking in
questionBank.explanation: The Friday meeting is the check-in: a scheduled point to review progress and answer questions. The lead chose the person and explained the task before the handoff, and authority was granted when the task was assigned — the review is the follow-through.
questionBank.skill: Applying the delegation steps to identify the check-in

questionBank.prompt: A manager delegates a data-entry cleanup to an intern, gives no instructions, and never mentions it again until the report is due. The intern delivers it late and full of errors. Who is accountable to the manager's own boss for the late report?
options: The manager
The intern
The intern's coworkers
No one, because the work was delegated
questionBank.explanation: Accountability moves upward: the manager remains responsible for outcomes of work done by people below them. The manager also skipped the explain and check-in steps — but even so, the final accountability for the report sits with the manager, not the intern.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing where accountability sits when delegated work fails

questionBank.prompt: A department head wants to free up time. Which of the following is an example of delegating rather than dumping?
options: Handing every undesirable task to whichever employee is closest
Giving a capable employee a routine reporting task with clear instructions, a deadline, and a weekly check-in
Assigning a task the employee lacks the skills and resources to complete
Telling an employee to handle something without saying what done looks like
questionBank.explanation: Delegation matches the task to the person, explains the expected result, provides support, and checks in — the second option does all four. The other options are dumping: no matching, no support, and no clarity, which CFI lists among delegation's failure modes.

title: Teams
in30Seconds: More than a group, a team is a set of people with complementary skills who work toward a shared goal and hold themselves mutually accountable — the definition this lesson follows Katzenbach and Smith, as presented in OpenStax's Principles of Management. Organizations use teams because complex work needs many hands and minds. The main team types are functional, cross-functional, and self-managed. Teams work best with a clear goal, clear roles, trust, and communication — but building one takes coordination time, and conflict happens.
whyItMatters: Organizations keep assigning work to teams because complex work needs many hands and minds — and because a well-tuned team can produce results no single member could. But teams fail as often as they succeed, and the difference is rarely talent. It is structure: a shared goal, defined roles, trust, and honest communication. Understanding what a team is — and is not — lets you see when a 'team' is only a collection of people wearing a label, and why some teams click while others stall. The same test applies whether you join a study group, a volunteer committee, or a workplace project: complementary skills, a shared goal, and mutual accountability.
learningObjectives: State the working definition of a team — a group of people with complementary skills working toward a shared goal with mutual accountability — attributed to Katzenbach and Smith as presented in OpenStax's Principles of Management.
Distinguish a team from a group, applying the shared-goal and mutual-accountability test to workplace examples.
Explain why organizations use teams: complex work needs many hands and minds working together.
Name the three team types — functional, cross-functional, and self-managed — each with an original example.
Identify what makes teams work (a clear goal, roles, trust, and communication) and name the honest costs (coordination takes time; conflict happens).

collegeVersion.heading: More than a group: the working definition
collegeVersion.body: Few words in management get used as loosely as 'team.' A company's directory calls every department a team; a project that never meets calls itself one. This lesson needs a working definition, and it follows Katzenbach and Smith, whose Harvard Business Review article 'The Discipline of Teams' is the classic account, as presented in OpenStax's Principles of Management. OpenStax lists the five elements that make a team function: a common commitment and purpose, specific performance goals, complementary skills, commitment to how the work gets done, and mutual accountability. This lesson condenses those five into three that carry the same meaning: complementary skills, a shared goal, and mutual accountability. Consider the night shift at Northgate Bakery: a baker, a decorator, a packer, and a delivery driver. Each brings a different skill; all four share the goal of getting the morning shipment out; and if the shipment fails, all four answer for it together. That is a team. Members discuss, decide, and do real work together, and they measure success by their collective output.

collegeVersion.heading: Team versus group: the distinction
collegeVersion.body: The test for 'team' is whether the people share a goal and hold themselves mutually accountable — not whether they share a room, a shift, or a label. OpenStax contrasts a team with the classic working group: a working group has a focused leader, individual accountabilities, and individual work products, and its purpose is whatever slice of the broader mission it was handed. Katzenbach and Smith put the distinction sharply: in an ordinary working group, performance is a function of what members do as individuals, while a team's performance calls for both individual and mutual accountability. Two examples make it concrete. The five nurses on the 7 a.m. shift at Riverside Clinic each care for their own patients, report to their own supervisors, and share nothing but a break room — a collection of people, a group. The hospital's discharge-improvement committee — a nurse, a pharmacist, a surgeon, and an administrator — shares one goal, depends on one another's expertise, and answers together for the result. Same building, different animal. One honest corollary from Katzenbach and Smith: if a task does not demand joint work, a working group is often the more effective choice.

collegeVersion.heading: Why teams: many hands and many minds
collegeVersion.body: Organizations form teams because the work outgrew the individual. Building a new store, launching an app, or redesigning a patient discharge draws on skills no one person holds — design, finance, operations, marketing — and on more hours than one person has. OpenStax opens its chapter on teams with the old saying, credited to Aristotle, that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts: a team creates a synergy that the members alone cannot produce. OpenStax's Introduction to Business makes the same point about project teams built from different functions: pooling the skills of various specialists increases creativity and innovation and lets an organization tackle more complex tasks. Teams also multiply minds on a problem — more perspectives, more chances to catch a flaw before it ships. That is the core argument, and it is simple: when the work is complex, many hands and minds beat one.

collegeVersion.heading: The team types: functional, cross-functional, and self-managed
collegeVersion.body: Management practice recognizes three common shapes of teams. A functional team is made of people from the same department doing that department's work together — the four loan officers at Meridian Credit Union who share a supervisor, process the same portfolio of applications, and cover for one another in busy weeks. A cross-functional team draws members from different departments to work on one shared project. OpenStax's Introduction to Business describes the matrix structure this way: it brings together people from different functional areas — manufacturing, finance, marketing — to work on a special project. Summit General's discharge committee is cross-functional: a nurse, a pharmacist, a surgeon, and an administrator, each from a different function, all on one project. A self-managed team organizes its own work — schedules, task rotation, quality checks — without a traditional supervisor. OpenStax's Principles of Management mentions self-directed work teams on manufacturing floors; the four-person assembly crew at Alder Appliance, which divides its own tasks and calls the plant manager only about supplies, is one. These three are the common shapes, not an exhaustive catalog — organizations also spin up temporary project teams and virtual teams as needed.

collegeVersion.heading: What makes teams work — and what it costs
collegeVersion.body: The research OpenStax reports points to four conditions that make teams work, each sayable in one line. A clear goal: teams work best when they have a compelling reason for being, with demanding performance standards and direction. Roles: members should be chosen for their skill and skill potential, and everyone should know who does what — role clarity was among the strongest collaboration factors in the Gratton and Erickson research OpenStax cites. Trust: OpenStax notes that time spent together builds camaraderie and trust, and Patrick Lencioni's The Five Dysfunctions of a Team, quoted in OpenStax, puts absence of trust first — without it, members fear conflict and never debate honestly. Communication: teams need explicit rules of behavior, fresh facts, and positive feedback; the mechanics of communication get their own topic. Then the honest costs. Coordination takes time: agreeing on schedules, rules, and how decisions get made is real work, and OpenStax quotes a turnaround manager saying that building an environment for teamwork takes time. Conflict happens: OpenStax lists communication breakdowns, competing goals, power struggles, and personality clashes as routine sources, and badly handled conflict breeds distrust and stalls progress. The reality check: a team is a machine that needs tuning, not magic. Five talented people in a room do not form a team by themselves — the goal, roles, trust, and communication have to be built, and maintained.

vocabulary.definition: A group of people with complementary skills who work toward a shared goal and hold themselves mutually accountable; the definition this lesson follows Katzenbach and Smith as presented by OpenStax.
A collection of individuals who share a setting but do not share a goal or mutual accountability; the label applies to any gathering, team or not.
The condition in which each member answers for the team's collective results, not only for their own piece of the work.
A team whose members all come from the same department or function and do that department's work together.
A team that draws its members from different departments or functions to work on one shared project.
A team that organizes its own work — schedules, task division, and quality checks — without a traditional supervisor.
A set of individuals under a leader whose performance is the sum of separate individual efforts, with no collective work product.
The interpersonal bond among team members that keeps them motivated and committed to the team's goals.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: A team is more than a bunch of people in the same room. It is a group that shares a goal, brings different skills, and answers for results together. Teams exist because complicated work — a new product, a big event, a hospital process — needs more skills and more minds than any one person has. There are three common kinds: functional teams (same department), cross-functional teams (different departments on one project), and self-managed teams (the team runs itself). A team works when it has a clear goal, clear roles, trust, and communication. The honest part: building a team takes time — meetings, rules, arguments — and conflict happens even in good teams. Five talented people do not make a team by themselves; the team has to be built.
eli10.analogy: Think of a rowing crew: eight rowers and a coxswain. Each rower has a position and a skill; they share one goal — crossing the finish line first — and if one rower stops pulling, the whole boat slows, so everyone answers for the boat's result. They practice together until the stroke is smooth. A crew that simply put eight strong athletes in a boat and pushed off would lose.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy has limits. A rowing crew is picked for one purpose, trains for months, and rows one kind of race, while workplace teams form around changing problems, with members coming and going. A crew's success is measured by a single finish line; a work team is judged by many interdependent results over time. And a coxswain steers from outside the work — most teams must coordinate themselves, with leadership shared.

workedExample: Watch one team form at Solstice Gear, an outdoor-equipment maker. Management wants a new backpack line in stores in eight months — complex work spanning fabric sourcing, design, costing, and marketing. The company assembles a cross-functional team: a designer, a materials buyer, a cost analyst, and a brand marketer. First they agree on the goal: a $120 pack, 30,000 units, shipped by March. Then roles: the designer owns samples, the buyer owns fabric, the analyst owns pricing, the marketer owns the launch. Early meetings move slowly — that is the coordination cost. When the designer and the buyer clash over a fabric, they settle it with a prototype test instead of an argument. Small milestones build trust. The line ships on time — not because the four were brilliant, but because the machine got tuned.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling any collection of people a team.
commonMistakes.correction: A label does not make a team. Test for the definition: complementary skills, a shared goal, and mutual accountability. People who merely share a shift or a department are a group.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming talent is enough.
commonMistakes.correction: Five strong employees in a room do not form a team by themselves. Katzenbach and Smith's practices — a compelling purpose, skill-based roles, rules of behavior — have to be put in place deliberately.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting teams to be free.
commonMistakes.correction: Coordination takes time: agreeing on schedules, roles, and how decisions get made is real work. OpenStax quotes a manager who says building an environment for teamwork takes time.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating conflict as proof the team is broken.
commonMistakes.correction: Conflict is a normal cost of teamwork — OpenStax lists competing goals and personality clashes as routine sources. Handled constructively, conflict can strengthen a team; avoiding it entirely erodes trust.

compareContrast.distinction: A group is a collection of individuals who share a setting; a team shares a goal, complementary skills, and mutual accountability. The Riverside nurses are a group; the discharge committee is a team.
A functional team's members all come from one department; a cross-functional team pulls members from different departments to work on one shared project — like Summit General's discharge committee.

keyTakeaway: A team is more than a collection of people: it is a group with complementary skills, a shared goal, and mutual accountability — and like any machine, it needs a clear goal, roles, trust, and communication, plus regular tuning, to perform.

questionBank.prompt: What makes a group of people a team, per the definition used in this lesson?
options: Complementary skills, a shared goal, and mutual accountability
Similar backgrounds, a shared office, and the same manager
A large budget, a clear hierarchy, and formal titles
Individual targets, a supervisor, and personal rewards
questionBank.explanation: The working definition, following Katzenbach and Smith as presented in OpenStax, combines complementary skills, a common purpose or goal, and mutual accountability. Shared offices, budgets, or hierarchy can exist without any of these.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the working definition of a team

questionBank.prompt: Five nurses at Riverside Clinic work the same shift and share a break room, but each cares only for her own patients and reports to her own supervisor. The clinic calls them 'the day team.' Why is the label inaccurate?
options: Five people are too few to form a team
Hospitals rely on groups, not teams
They share no goal or mutual accountability — they are a collection, not a team
Teams must include members from several departments
questionBank.explanation: A team is defined by a shared goal and mutual accountability, not by sharing a shift or a room. These nurses work side by side but do not share a goal or answer for one another's results, so they are a group wearing a team label.
questionBank.skill: Applying the team-versus-group distinction to a workplace scenario

questionBank.prompt: Summit General Hospital forms a committee to redesign patient discharges: a nurse, a pharmacist, a surgeon, and an administrator, each from a different department. What type of team is this?
options: A functional team, because they all work in healthcare
A self-managed team, because no supervisor attends
A working group, because they only meet monthly
A cross-functional team, because it joins people from different functions on one shared project
questionBank.explanation: A cross-functional team draws members from different departments or functions to work on one project — the same pattern OpenStax's Introduction to Business describes when matrix structures bring people from different functional areas together for a special project.
questionBank.skill: Identifying team types from a workplace scenario

questionBank.prompt: A new product team spends its first three weeks agreeing on schedules, deciding how decisions will be made, and learning to work together. Which honest cost of teamwork does this represent?
options: Conflict that good managers could have prevented entirely
Coordination — building a team takes time that solo work does not
A leadership failure, because the task should have come first
Wasted effort, because teams should start working before agreeing on anything
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax notes that teams need rules of behavior, time together, and agreement on how the work gets done — and that this takes time. That is the coordination cost of teamwork, not a failure or a waste.
questionBank.skill: Naming the coordination cost of teamwork

questionBank.prompt: A manager says, 'I will put my five best employees in a room, and a great team will form by itself.' Based on this lesson's honest framing, what is wrong with that expectation?
options: Great teams need at least ten members
The best employees are usually too competitive to cooperate
A team is a machine that needs tuning — goal, roles, trust, and communication must be built deliberately
Teams only form when the employees choose their own leader
questionBank.explanation: The honest framing: a team is not magic. Talented people still need a clear goal, defined roles, trust, and working communication — the tuning a machine needs — and even then coordination takes time and conflict happens.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing why teams do not form by themselves

title: Team Development
in30Seconds: Team development is the process by which a group of people becomes a working team, moving through stages as it matures. The model in this lesson comes from Bruce Tuckman: forming, storming, norming, and performing, with adjourning added in 1977 for when a project ends. Real teams loop back and skip stages, and conflict in the early stages is normal, not failure. Leaders adjust their support to the stage the team is in.
whyItMatters: Anyone who has worked in a group has felt the stages: the polite first meeting, the arguments, the moment things finally click. Knowing the model changes what those moments mean. Early conflict stops looking like a broken team and starts looking like a normal step that can be worked through. A leader who knows the stages gives the team what it needs at each one: direction while it forms, patience and structure during storming, and room to run once it performs. Teams that understand development also recover faster when a new member or a new task knocks them back a stage.
learningObjectives: State the working definition of team development, attributed to Tuckman's model as presented by OpenStax's Principles of Management.
Name the five stages of Tuckman's model—forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning—with one line and one original example for each.
Explain why conflict in the early stages is normal rather than a sign of failure.
Describe how real teams loop back and skip stages, and name one event that can slide a team backward.
Explain how a leader's support changes as a team moves through the stages.
Describe how team development connects to performance: mature teams work more smoothly and need less direction.

collegeVersion.heading: What team development is: the working definition
collegeVersion.body: Team development is the process by which a group of people becomes a working team, moving through stages as it matures. The definition this lesson follows the model developed by Bruce Tuckman and presented in OpenStax's Principles of Management: teams and team members start from friendliness and excitement, and then the real work begins—and as they work, they move through recognizable stages. OpenStax is careful to call them stages, not ages: a team does not graduate from one to the next like a student moving up a grade. The stages describe how the group's relationships and its way of working change over time. The model has five stages in this lesson—forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning—because Tuckman added the fifth, adjourning, in 1977 to describe what happens when a team disbands at the end of a project. What a team is, how to resolve conflict, and how to communicate well each get their own topics.

collegeVersion.heading: The five stages: forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning
collegeVersion.body: Forming is the polite opening stage. Members are introduced, stay cautious, and focus on similarities; the group looks to the leader for structure and direction, and enthusiasm mixes with uncertainty about roles. Example: at Northgate, a regional grocery co-op, five coworkers meet for the first time as the online-ordering project team and wait for the store manager to explain what to do first. Storming is the conflict stage. Members assert their ideas, test roles and group processes, and clash over goals, tasks, and progress; OpenStax calls it the win-lose stage, and frustration builds. Example: at Northgate, the designer and the software developer argue for a week over whether checkout should work on phones, and two members start choosing sides. Norming is the settling stage: ground rules are agreed, roles become clear, responsibility is shared, and trust grows. Example: after the manager sets clear decision rules, the Northgate team adopts a weekly review and stops re-litigating settled choices. Performing is the self-directed stage: the team has confidence and momentum, needs little management direction, and focuses on results; the strongest teams, OpenStax notes, optimize both task and people relationships. Example: Northgate's team ships the system and handles new issues without daily supervision. Adjourning is the closing stage: the project ends, the team disbands, and members reflect on the work and the relationships they built.

collegeVersion.heading: Why stages matter: early conflict is normal
collegeVersion.body: The stages matter because they give a name to experiences almost every team has, and the most valuable name is storming. When a new team argues, members often conclude the team is broken. The model says otherwise: storming is where real differences surface—about goals, methods, roles, and control—and those differences need to surface before the team can genuinely agree. OpenStax describes storming as the stage when the attitude about the team and the project shifts negative and frustration builds around goals, tasks, and progress. Corporate Finance Institute adds the constructive side: conflict can be healthy when managed constructively, because it can lead to better decision-making and team cohesion. And Wikipedia's summary of Tuckman records that he described the phases as necessary and inevitable for a team to grow, face challenges, and deliver results. That is the honest insight of this lesson: early conflict is not evidence that the team is failing; it is evidence that the team has started doing real work together.

collegeVersion.heading: Stage versus reality: loops, skips, and slides
collegeVersion.body: The model is a map, not a schedule. OpenStax is explicit that the stages are not linear: when a team member is added, the change can disrupt the dynamic enough to cause a backwards slide to an earlier stage, and a new project task that creates confusion can do the same; the team has to re-group and will likely re-form and re-storm before getting back to performing. CFI agrees, noting that a new member can take a team working well at the norming stage back to storming, and that team development is not a linear process. Teams also skip: a group that has worked together before may pass through forming in a single meeting, and a routine task may never produce a real storm. The practical reading is simple. Watch for the stage the team is actually in, not the stage the calendar says it should be in. When a change arrives—a new member, a new task, a new leader—expect the team to dip back, and treat the dip as normal regrouping rather than a crisis.

collegeVersion.heading: The leader's role, and what maturity looks like
collegeVersion.body: Different stages need different support. OpenStax notes that a forming team looks to the leader for structure and direction, while a performing team is self-directed and needs little management direction. CFI fills in the middle: in forming, leaders provide clear direction and establish goals; in storming, they encourage open communication and mediate conflicts; in norming, they reinforce positive behavior; in performing, they step back and allow autonomy; and in adjourning, they acknowledge contributions and provide closure. The general practice, stated simply: give more structure early, more room later, and steady attention to the team's relationships the whole way. Maturity shows up as smoother work. A performing team does not necessarily work harder than a brand-new one; it works with less friction, because roles, norms, and trust are already in place. That is the performance connection: mature teams spend their energy on the task instead of on sorting out how to work together, and the strongest of them get results while preserving the relationships that let them keep performing.

vocabulary.definition: The process by which a group of people becomes a working team, moving through stages as it matures; the model in this lesson comes from Bruce Tuckman.
The polite first stage, when members are introduced, stay cautious, and look to the leader for structure and direction.
The conflict stage, when members assert their ideas, test roles and processes, and clash over goals and control.
The stage when the team agrees on ground rules, roles settle, and members begin to trust and respect one another.
The stage when the team is self-directed and focused on results, needing little management direction.
The closing stage, when the team disbands at the end of a project and members reflect on what they accomplished.
A slide back to an earlier stage of development, often triggered by a new member joining or a new task disrupting the group.
A team that has optimized both its task work and its relationships among members, maximizing performance and effectiveness.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Team development is how a group of people slowly becomes a real team. Most teams pass through the same stages. Forming: everyone is polite and figuring out who does what. Storming: people disagree, argue, and test one another. It feels bad, but it is normal, and it is how real issues surface. Norming: the team agrees on how to work, roles settle, and trust grows. Performing: the team runs itself and gets results. Adjourning: the project ends and the team wraps up. Real teams do not march through these stages in a straight line. They loop back, skip stages, and slide backward when someone new joins. Storming is a stage, not a failure.
eli10.analogy: Think of a band learning a new song. First rehearsal: everyone is polite, watching the sheet music, waiting for the singer to count in. Then the disagreements start; the drummer thinks the tempo is too fast, the bassist wants a different ending, and the singer is frustrated. That is storming. Slowly they settle on an arrangement and the song comes together; that is norming. By the night of the gig they play it without cues; that is performing. Then the set ends and they pack up; that is adjourning.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy has limits. A band's members usually know their instruments from the start, while a work team may form with people who have never worked together and whose roles are unclear. A band can also choose its members; many teams get no say in who joins, and one new member can knock the whole group back to storming. And bands rehearse a fixed song, while work teams keep getting new tasks, which is why the stages repeat.

workedExample: Follow Northgate, a regional grocery co-op, as it builds a new online-ordering system. The five-person project team forms at a first meeting where everyone is polite and the store manager lays out the schedule. In storming, the designer and the software developer argue for a week about whether the checkout should work on phones, and two members start choosing sides. After the manager sets up a weekly review and clear decision rules, the team norms: roles settle, and the group agrees on how to test new ideas. In performing, the team ships the system and handles problems without daily supervision. When the project ends, the team adjourns: members hold a wrap-up meeting, review what worked, and move to other roles.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading storming as failure.
commonMistakes.correction: Early conflict looks like a broken team, but the model says storming is a normal stage where real differences surface. The task is to work through it, not to declare the team doomed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting a straight line.
commonMistakes.correction: Teams do not reliably march through forming, storming, norming, and performing in order. A new member or a confusing new task can slide a team backward, and some teams skip stages entirely.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leading every stage the same way.
commonMistakes.correction: A forming team needs direction; a storming team needs open communication and mediation; a performing team needs autonomy. One style for all stages ignores what the team actually needs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Skipping closure.
commonMistakes.correction: Treating adjourning as an afterthought wastes the chance to acknowledge contributions and capture lessons that the next project could use.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing a mature team with a conflict-free team.
commonMistakes.correction: A performing team still disagrees; the difference is that disagreements get handled through the norms the team built instead of flaring into storms.

compareContrast.distinction: Forming is the polite, cautious opening stage, when members look to the leader and avoid conflict; storming is the stage when members assert ideas, test roles, and clash. Both are early stages, and one usually leads into the other.
Performing is the stage of self-directed, high-output work; adjourning is the closing stage when the project ends, the team disbands, and members reflect on the work and the relationships they built.

keyTakeaway: Team development is the process by which a group becomes a team, moving through forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning. Early conflict is a normal stage, not failure; teams loop back and skip stages; and leaders adjust their support to the stage the team is in.

Storming
Norming
Forming

Two members have started trading messages about the fight before meetings. What does this lesson say about what is happening?

The team is in performing, and these are routine disagreements

questionBank.prompt: Northgate's team reaches performing: the ordering system is live and the group handles new issues without the manager's daily input. Then the manager reassigns one member to another project and a new developer joins the team. What does the Tuckman model predict is likely to happen next?
options: The team stays in performing because the work itself is unchanged
The team moves straight to adjourning because a member left
The team slides back to an earlier stage as the group adjusts to the change
The team permanently skips norming and stays in storming
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax stresses that the stages are not linear: adding a team member can disrupt the dynamic and cause a backwards slide to an earlier stage, and CFI notes a new member can take a team back to storming. The team re-forms and re-storms before returning to performing.
questionBank.skill: Applying the non-linear regression idea to a staffing change

questionBank.prompt: A year after launch, Northgate's leadership decides the online-ordering project is complete and dissolves the team. The members hold a final meeting, review what worked, thank one another, and move to different roles. Which stage of team development does this describe?

Adjourning
Storming
Performing
questionBank.explanation: Adjourning is the closing stage, added to Tuckman's model in 1977, when a team disbands at the end of a project. CFI notes that leaders help by acknowledging contributions and providing closure, which is exactly what the final meeting does.
