title: Power and Influence
in30Seconds: Power is the capacity to influence others — to change what people do, decide, or believe. Social psychologists John French and Bertram Raven identified five classic bases of power: legitimate (from a role), reward, coercive, expert (from knowledge), and referent (from admiration). Some bases attach to a position; others attach to the person. People spend that capacity through influence tactics like persuasion, consultation, coalitions, and exchange. And here is the honest part: power is borrowed. It works only as long as the people around you keep granting it.
whyItMatters: Almost every goal in an organization — getting a project approved, changing a process, winning support for an idea — requires moving other people to act, and power is the engine behind that movement. Understanding where power comes from helps you read situations clearly: who can grant what, whose expertise carries weight, and why some people are followed even without a title. It also guards against misuse. Power used carelessly breeds resentment and resistance; power used thoughtfully builds trust and gets work done. Later lessons on leading and ethics build directly on this foundation, so the clearer your picture of power, the better you will understand leadership, negotiation, and teamwork.
learningObjectives: Define power as the capacity to influence others, and explain why power is attributed rather than owned.
Identify the five classic bases of power — legitimate, reward, coercive, expert, referent — and give an original example of each.
Distinguish position power from personal power, and explain why a title alone does not guarantee influence.
Name four common influence tactics — persuasion, consultation, coalitions, and exchange — and recognize them in everyday situations.

collegeVersion.heading: What Power Is
collegeVersion.body: Power is the capacity to influence others — the ability to change what people do, decide, or believe. That working definition comes from the management tradition: the OpenStax Introduction to Business text defines power as the ability to influence others to behave in a particular way. Two details matter. First, power is potential. Having it means you could change someone's behavior, whether or not you ever act on it. Second, power is attributed, not owned. A request carries weight only because the people hearing it decide that it does, which is why the same sentence from two different people lands completely differently. The best-known map of where this capacity comes from was drawn by social psychologists John French and Bertram Raven, whose classic study of the bases of social power still anchors how organizations talk about influence. This lesson teaches the five bases from that tradition; some later treatments add a sixth base, informational power.

collegeVersion.heading: The Five Bases of Power
collegeVersion.body: French and Raven's five bases name the five things people respond to. Legitimate power comes from a role: people accept that the position carries the right to make certain requests, so the shift supervisor who assigns workstations is obeyed because of the title. Reward power comes from control over things others value — the manager who approves raises, schedules, or public recognition. Coercive power comes from the ability to impose negative outcomes, such as formal warnings, demotions, or lost overtime. Expert power comes from knowledge others trust and need, like the chemist whose judgment settles a dosage question. Referent power comes from admiration and respect: people follow the veteran technician because they want to work like her. Most people hold several bases at once, and which base works best depends on the situation and on the person being influenced.

collegeVersion.heading: Position Power and Personal Power
collegeVersion.body: The five bases divide into two families. Position power is attached to the role: legitimate, reward, and coercive power travel with the title, which is why the same request weighs more from a manager than from a colleague. Personal power is attached to the person: expert and referent power depend on what you know and how people see you, not on where you sit in the org chart. Management texts draw exactly this contrast — managers commonly derive power from the position they occupy, while leaders more often derive it from followers' perceptions of their expertise, personality, and relationships. The distinction explains a familiar puzzle: why some managers with full authority struggle to win cooperation, while a well-liked specialist with no title can move an entire project team.

collegeVersion.heading: Influence Tactics
collegeVersion.body: Power is the capacity; tactics are how it gets spent. An influence tactic is a specific move in a specific situation, and the research tradition lists a small set that covers most of what happens in organizations. Rational persuasion argues with facts, data, and logic — the most commonly used tactic of all. Consultation asks the people involved to help shape the plan, which gives them a stake in the outcome. Coalitions join forces: two departments backing the same proposal are harder to ignore than one person. Exchange trades something of value — support now for support later. None of these requires a title. That is why influence is not reserved for managers: a junior analyst can persuade with evidence, consult a colleague, build a coalition, or trade favors exactly as well as the department head can.

collegeVersion.heading: Power, Ethics, and Leadership
collegeVersion.body: Power can be used well or abused. Used well, it clears the way for work — a respected supervisor who rewards good effort and explains decisions builds trust. Abused, it turns into pressure, favoritism, or punishment used as a weapon, and people stop cooperating. The full question of when influence is ethical belongs to the ethics lesson; the honest note here is that power keeps working only while the people around you keep granting it. That is also the link to leadership: influence is the currency of leading, and leadership is at bottom a social influence relationship — the leading lesson takes it from there. The reality check closes the loop: power is borrowed from followers. It can be lent, and it can be taken back.

vocabulary.definition: The capacity to influence other people, changing what they do, decide, or believe.
Influence that comes from a role or position whose right to make certain requests others accept.
Influence based on control over things others value, such as raises, schedules, or recognition.
Influence based on the ability to impose negative outcomes, such as warnings, demotions, or dismissal.
Influence that comes from knowledge or skill that others trust and need.
Influence that comes from admiration and respect, so people want to please or emulate the person.
Influence attached to a job title or role rather than to the person holding it.
Influence attached to the person — their expertise, character, and relationships — rather than to a title.
A specific action used to carry influence in a particular situation, such as persuasion or exchange.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Think of power like being the person everyone wants on their team at recess — except the wanting is the power. Nobody hands you a crown that makes people listen. People listen because of what you can offer, what you know, whether you can make things hard for them, or simply because they like and respect you. That is the whole list: position, rewards, punishments, know-how, and likability. French and Raven wrote it down as five bases of power, and every situation you will ever face uses one or more of them.
eli10.analogy: A library card is a good picture of power. The card lets you borrow books — but you do not own the books, and the library can revoke the card. Influence at work works the same way: people lend you their cooperation, and they can take it back. The card itself is position power; the way you treat the librarians is personal power. Both matter, and neither survives if people stop honoring it.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks down because power is less formal than a library card. There is no central office that issues or revokes influence. People grant it bit by bit, in each interaction, and it can fade gradually without any single decision.

workedExample: Consider Rina, a bakery assistant who has worked there for nine years. She holds no title, yet when she suggests a new dough schedule, the bakers try it. Her legitimate and reward power are minimal — she cannot assign work or grant raises — but her expert power is strong: she has kneaded every recipe in the shop, and her judgment has been right before. She also holds referent power: new hires want her approval. When Rina needs the team to shift to an earlier start, she does not order it. She explains the numbers and asks the bakers what they think — persuasion plus consultation — and the team agrees.

commonMistakes.mistake: Power equals title
commonMistakes.correction: Assuming that a manager's authority automatically changes behavior. A title confers position power, but people still decide whether to comply, and expert or referent power often does the real work.

commonMistakes.mistake: Coercive power is the strongest base
commonMistakes.correction: Reaching for threats and penalties as the default tool. Coercion produces compliance that disappears when the threat does, and it breeds resentment. It is one base among five, not the strongest.

commonMistakes.mistake: Influence is only for leaders
commonMistakes.correction: Thinking tactics like persuasion or coalitions are off-limits to people without authority. Most influence tactics work from any position; consultation and exchange are available to everyone.

commonMistakes.mistake: Power is permanent
commonMistakes.correction: Treating influence as a possession that stays with you. Power is attributed and borrowed; it erodes when trust erodes, so it has to be maintained through the same behaviors that earned it.

compareContrast.distinction: Position power rides with the title and can be assigned to someone; personal power rides with the person and cannot be transferred.
Legitimate power rests on the right of the role; referent power rests on admiration for the person.
Power is the capacity to influence; tactics are the specific actions that spend that capacity in a given situation.

keyTakeaway: Power is the capacity to influence others. It comes from roles and from people, it is spent through tactics like persuasion and exchange, and it is always borrowed from the people who grant it.

questionBank.prompt: Priya supervises the night shift at a bakery. When she asks a baker to move from the ovens to the packaging line, he does it because company policy gives supervisors the right to assign stations. Which base of power is at work?
options: Coercive power
Expert power
Legitimate power
Referent power
questionBank.explanation: Legitimate power comes from a role whose right to make certain requests others accept; Priya's request carries weight because the position of supervisor carries the right to assign stations. Coercive power (A) would rest on threats of negative outcomes, expert power (B) on trusted knowledge, and referent power (D) on admiration — none of which the scenario describes.
questionBank.skill: Identifying a base of power from a workplace scenario

questionBank.prompt: At a community clinic, nurses and residents routinely follow Dr. Okafor's medication protocols even though she holds no supervisory role. They trust her judgment because of her eighteen years of clinical experience. Which base of power explains her influence?
options: Legitimate power
Reward power
Coercive power
Expert power
questionBank.explanation: Expert power comes from knowledge and skill that others trust and need, which is exactly what Dr. Okafor's eighteen years of clinical experience provide. Legitimate power (A) requires a role or position, reward power (B) requires control over things others value, and coercive power (C) requires the ability to impose negative outcomes — none of which the scenario gives her.
questionBank.skill: Applying the five bases of power to a real situation

questionBank.prompt: Two clerks want the library to adopt a four-day workweek. They collect attendance and productivity data, present it to the board together, and ask other staff to sign the proposal. Which influence tactics are they using?
options: Persuasion and coalitions
Coercion and legitimating
Exchange and pressure
Consultation and reward
questionBank.explanation: Persuasion uses facts and logical argument — here the attendance and productivity data — and a coalition joins several people behind one goal, which is what presenting together with staff signatures does. Coercion and legitimating (B) would lean on threats or formal authority, exchange (C) trades favors, and consultation (D) means asking others to help shape the plan itself, which the scenario does not describe.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing influence tactics inside a scenario

questionBank.prompt: The five bases of power are often grouped into position power and personal power. Which pairing belongs to personal power?
options: Expert and referent
Legitimate and reward
Coercive and legitimate
Reward and coercive
questionBank.explanation: Personal power is attached to the person: expert power comes from knowledge and referent power from admiration and respect. Legitimate, reward, and coercive power attach to the role and are grouped as position power, which rules out B, C, and D.
questionBank.skill: Classifying the five bases into the position and personal families

questionBank.prompt: Maya leads a project team of specialists even though she holds no formal authority over them. They follow her because she knows the work deeply and treats them with respect. What does this situation show about power?
options: Power comes only from formal titles
Personal sources of power can produce influence without position power
Coercive power is the only reliable base
Influence requires controlling rewards
questionBank.explanation: Maya's influence rests on expert power (deep knowledge) and referent power (respect), both personal bases that work without a title — exactly the point of the position-versus-personal distinction. Option A contradicts the lesson's core claim, C overstates coercion, and D ignores that expert and referent power need no control over rewards.
questionBank.skill: Interpreting a situation using the lesson's framing of power

title: Ethics
in30Seconds: Management ethics applies principles of right and wrong to business decisions — how we apply our values to how we do business. Ethics is not the same as compliance: the law is a floor, and doing right can demand more than staying legal. Workplaces constantly produce ethical dilemmas — two goods or two wrongs in tension, with no clearly clean option. Ethics matters because trust, reputation, and long-run survival ride on it. One practical test: would you be comfortable if this decision were public? Leaders set the ethical tone — ethics is the price of staying in business long.
whyItMatters: Every work decision has an ethical dimension, and most of them are small: whether to round up an expense, whether to tell a customer the truth about a delay, whether to look the other way when a coworker cuts a corner. Small choices stack up into a reputation that customers, employees, and communities either trust or distrust. When trust breaks, business gets harder and more expensive — and in the worst cases, the company does not survive. Ethics also shapes your own working life: you will be asked, pressured, or tempted to compromise your standards, and knowing where your line is before you need it makes the moment easier. That is why this lesson treats ethics as a practical management skill, not a philosophy lecture.
learningObjectives: Define management ethics as the principles of right conduct applied to business decisions, and attribute that working definition.
Distinguish ethics from compliance — doing right versus staying legal — using an original example.
Describe an ethical dilemma as two options in tension, two goods or two wrongs, and work through an original example.
Explain three reasons ethics matters: trust, reputation, and long-run survival.
Apply the publicity test — would you be comfortable if this decision were public? — to a workplace decision.
Explain how leaders and the surrounding culture set the ethical tone in an organization.

collegeVersion.heading: Management ethics: a working definition, attributed
collegeVersion.body: Management ethics is the principles of right and wrong conduct applied to business decisions. OpenStax's Principles of Management defines ethics as involving how we act, live, and treat others — our choices, our decision-making, and the moral principles and values that govern what we treat as right and wrong — and calls business ethics applied ethics that asks how we should apply our values to the way we conduct business. Three features matter. First, it is practical: it lives in real decisions, not abstract theory. Second, it is a standard, not a mood: it judges choices as right or wrong, which means it can be reasoned about and argued over. Third, it belongs to everyone: a cashier, an accountant, and a chief executive each face ethical choices in their own work. The philosophy subject studies the deep theories behind ethics; management studies what to do with them on the job.

collegeVersion.heading: Ethics versus compliance: doing right versus staying legal
collegeVersion.body: The law and ethics overlap but are not the same. OpenStax notes that ethical principles generally get codified into laws when society reaches broad agreement that something is wrong — laws against theft and fraud are ethical judgments written into rules. Following those rules is compliance: staying within the laws and regulations that apply to your work. Ethics is wider. CFI points out that some business practices sit in grey areas that are not illegal but are ethically questionable — paying a supplier's negotiator a lavish hotel weekend, for example, may not break any law and still looks like an attempt to buy a favorable deal. So the honest summary is simple: compliance asks "is this legal?" Ethics asks "is this right?" The law is a floor, not a ceiling, and the most dangerous ethical failures are often perfectly legal ones.

collegeVersion.heading: The ethical dilemma: two goods or two wrongs in tension
collegeVersion.body: An ethical dilemma is a situation where the options are in tension and neither choice is clearly right. OpenStax defines ethical dilemmas as situations in which there is no optimal choice between two options — neither one resolves the issue in a fully ethical way. Dilemmas usually take one of two shapes. In a two-goods dilemma, you must choose between things that are both valuable, like keeping a promise to one person or helping another. In a two-wrongs dilemma, every option does some harm and you must pick the lesser damage. Original example: Tessa manages a bookstore's delivery team. A longtime driver, Omar, asks for overtime beyond the company's safety cap on driver hours because he needs the money to keep his house. Approving it helps a loyal employee but breaks a rule that exists to keep tired drivers off the road. Refusing it protects the rule but may cost Omar his home. Either way, something valuable is damaged — that tension is what makes it a dilemma rather than a simple question.

collegeVersion.heading: Why ethics matters: trust, reputation, and long-run survival
collegeVersion.body: Ethics matters for three concrete reasons. Trust: OpenStax notes that even small companies increasingly emphasize ethics to restore trust among customers and the community, and cites an Ethics & Compliance Initiative survey finding that 22 percent of workers worldwide report pressure to compromise their standards — trust eroding from the inside. Reputation: OpenStax's Introduction to Business observes that poor business ethics can create a very negative image for a company, and that image damage is expensive. Long-run survival: the same source notes that ethical failures can result in bankruptcy and jail time for the offenders. Businesses rarely run out of good products; they run out of trust. A reputation takes years to build and can be spent in a single decision.

collegeVersion.heading: The ethical decision test: would you be comfortable if this were public?
collegeVersion.body: Because ethical choices are often pressured and rushed, a quick test helps. The Markkula Center for Applied Ethics at Santa Clara University, in its framework for ethical decision making, suggests asking: if I told someone I respect — or a public audience — which option I have chosen, what would they say? The publicity test, stated simply: before deciding, imagine your reasoning explained to a room of people whose respect you want, or printed where anyone could read it. If the thought makes you flinch, that is information. The test does not decide for you — some right choices are awkward to explain — but it catches the decisions we hide because we know they are wrong, and hiding is a strong signal.

collegeVersion.heading: Ethics and culture: leaders set the tone — and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Individual choices do not happen in a vacuum. OpenStax observes that a person's ethical stance at work is affected by peers, supervisors, and the organizational culture, which can support ethical action or quietly encourage the opposite. Leaders set the tone: Introduction to Business notes that organizations shape ethical conduct by educating employees about standards and, above all, by leading through example — people watch what their managers tolerate. A manager who praises results reached by cutting corners teaches a different lesson than one who asks how the results were reached. The full story of how shared values form and change belongs to the sibling topic organizational culture. The honest framing: ethics is the price of staying in business long. Not the cost of doing business — the price of remaining in business at all. Every shortcut cashes in a little of the trust the company lives on.

vocabulary.definition: The principles of right and wrong that govern how people act, live, and treat others.
The principles of right conduct applied to real business decisions — how a company applies its values to the way it conducts business.
Following the laws and regulations that apply to your work; the legal floor beneath ethical behavior.
A situation where someone must choose between actions that may be ethical or unethical.
A situation where two options are in tension and neither choice is clearly right.
A situation where a personal interest could improperly influence a professional decision.
The decision heuristic of asking whether you would be comfortable if your reasoning and choice were made public.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Ethics is the sense of right and wrong that guides how a business treats people. Compliance is following the rules the law sets. A business can follow every law and still do wrong — and the hard part is rarely spotting the crime, it is spotting the choice. Every day, people at work face decisions where both options look partly right and partly wrong; that is an ethical dilemma. Studying ethics is not about memorizing answers but about building the habit of asking "is this right?" before acting. One quick question helps: would I be comfortable if everyone knew?
eli10.analogy: Think of a school bake sale run by two friends. The rules say the money goes to the school — that part is compliance. But the rules do not say what to do when the last tray of brownies is broken and a teacher offers to buy it half price for the staff room. Keeping the tray for regular customers or selling it cheap both feel okay in different ways, and nothing is written down. The friends have to decide what is fair — and that judgment, what is right when no rule covers it, is ethics. The bake sale runs on trust: once the school sees the friends pocketing favors, nobody buys brownies again.
eli10.analogyLimits: The bake sale is small and its rules are few; a real business faces thousands of decisions under laws, contracts, and deadlines, and the right choice is often expensive or unpopular. A bake sale's fairness question settles in a minute, while workplace dilemmas can hurt or help many people at once. Still, the core holds: rules set the floor, and trust is earned by what you do above it.

workedExample: Rafael manages a family restaurant and orders produce weekly from two suppliers. A sales representative from his current supplier offers him a free weekend at a lake cabin — "a thank-you for your loyalty" — right before Rafael compares that supplier's new prices against a cheaper competitor. The gift is legal, and the restaurant has no written policy against it. Rafael runs the decision through the lesson's tools. Legal? Yes. Ethical? The cabin is a personal benefit that could steer a professional decision — a conflict of interest. Publicity test: would he want the owner and the kitchen staff to know the cabin trip played any part in choosing a supplier? He would not. Rafael declines the gift, tells the representative he will choose on price and quality, and mentions the offer to the owner so nothing looks hidden. He keeps the trust he needs for next season's contract talks — and the restaurant keeps a reputation for honest purchasing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating "legal" as the same as "ethical" — if nothing in the rulebook forbids it, calling it fine.
commonMistakes.correction: Compliance is the floor, not the ceiling. CFI's grey areas — legal but ethically questionable — show that the law's silence is not a green light; ethics asks what is right, not just what is allowed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting ethical problems to announce themselves as dramatic, headline-style scandals.
commonMistakes.correction: Most are small and ordinary — rounding up an expense, softening a delay, ignoring a shortcut. Small choices, repeated, are what build or burn trust.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming an ethical dilemma means both options are equally wrong, so any choice is as good as another.
commonMistakes.correction: Dilemmas are hard but not lawless: the better option is the one that best protects the people affected, and the publicity test helps you find the defensible choice rather than a free pass.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating ethics as top management's problem — a code of conduct on a website — with no connection to what managers actually tolerate.
commonMistakes.correction: Leaders set the tone through what they reward and overlook, and every employee faces ethical choices. Culture carries ethics, but individuals live it — the culture story itself is a sibling topic.

compareContrast.distinction: Compliance asks whether an action is legal — whether it follows the laws and regulations that apply. Ethics asks whether an action is right — a wider question that can demand more than the law does. Most laws started as ethical judgments, but the law's silence is not a verdict.

An ethical issue is any situation that calls for a choice between actions that may be ethical or unethical — often with a clear right answer that is hard to carry out. An ethical dilemma is the harder case where two options are in tension and neither choice is clearly right.

compareContrast.b: The ethical tone leaders actually set
compareContrast.distinction: A code states the standards on paper. The tone leaders set is what people observe in what managers reward, tolerate, and do themselves — and it usually wins when the two disagree, which is why leading by example matters more than posters.

keyTakeaway: Ethics is the principles of right and wrong applied to business decisions — and the price of staying in business long. The law is only the floor; trust, reputation, and survival are built by doing right, one decision at a time.

title: Diversity and Inclusion
in30Seconds: Diversity at work is the mix of identities, backgrounds, and perspectives employees bring — identity-based differences such as race and ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, and age, in OpenStax's working definition. Inclusion is making sure that mix actually participates: employees are accepted and treated fairly. Organizations pursue both for talent, better decisions, markets, and fairness. In the United States, law sets a floor: the EEOC enforces anti-discrimination protections for defined groups. Unconscious bias is real. Building inclusion takes listening, equitable practices, and accountability.
whyItMatters: Every team you join is a mix of people who grew up differently, think differently, and see the world differently. Whether that mix helps the team or quietly divides it depends on inclusion. A diverse team where only a few voices get heard is paying for diversity and getting none of its benefits. This matters for two reasons. Workplaces are diverse now and getting more so, so the mix is not optional. And the difference between a team that merely hires a mix and a team that actually works as a mix is something you can recognize — and something you can practice — in any group you belong to, from a shift crew to a volunteer committee.
learningObjectives: Define diversity at work as the mix of identities, backgrounds, and perspectives employees bring, and attribute that working definition.
Define inclusion as making sure the mix actually participates — employees accepted and treated fairly — and explain why diversity without inclusion falls short.
Name four reasons organizations pursue diversity and inclusion: talent, better decisions, markets, and fairness.
State the U.S. legal floor: anti-discrimination law protects defined groups, and the EEOC enforces it.
Explain what unconscious bias is and how it can affect hiring and promotion.
Describe three general ways organizations build inclusion: listening, equitable practices, and accountability.

collegeVersion.heading: A working definition of diversity, attributed
collegeVersion.body: Diversity at work is the mix of identities, backgrounds, and perspectives employees bring. OpenStax's Principles of Management defines diversity as identity-based differences among and between two or more people that affect their lives as applicants, employees, and customers — differences that include race and ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, and age. Notice what the definition includes and what it leaves out. It is about identity, not taste: the college you attended or the music you like is not diversity in this sense; the groups you belong to, and how they shape your life, are. OpenStax adds a useful distinction: surface-level diversity is what you can see — age, body size, visible disability, race, or sex — while deeper differences in experience and outlook matter just as much. When a manager says the team needs more diversity, they are talking about who is in the room.

collegeVersion.heading: A working definition of inclusion, attributed — and the honest gap
collegeVersion.body: Inclusion is what the mix does once it is in the room. OpenStax defines inclusion as the degree to which employees are accepted and treated fairly by their organization, and presents it as one way companies demonstrate that they value diversity. Plainer still: diversity is who shows up; inclusion is whether everyone actually gets to participate — to speak, to be heard, to be considered for the interesting work and the promotions. The honest gap is common. An organization can hire a diverse workforce and still run meetings where the same few voices dominate, still promote from a narrow network, still leave some employees feeling like guests. That is diversity without inclusion: the mix exists, but it does not work as a mix. CFI describes the organizational response — diversity management is the deliberate set of actions, policies, and programs that promote the inclusion of employees from different backgrounds.

collegeVersion.heading: Why organizations pursue both: talent, decisions, markets, fairness
collegeVersion.body: Four reasons appear again and again. Talent: a company known for valuing diversity attracts a larger applicant pool — OpenStax reports that women and minorities have stronger job-pursuit intentions toward employers that promote diversity in recruitment — and diverse organizations also see lower turnover among women and minorities. Decisions: OpenStax summarizes the Cox and Blake business case, which finds that diverse groups bring enhanced creativity and better problem solving, because different perspectives catch what a uniform group misses. Markets: a workforce that reflects its customers understands them, which is why the same framework lists greater marketing ability among the advantages. Fairness: beyond any business benefit, treating people fairly is its own reason — and it is the reason the law gets involved.

collegeVersion.heading: The legal floor: anti-discrimination law, U.S. context
collegeVersion.body: In the United States, the law sets a floor beneath all of this. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) enforces federal laws that make it illegal to discriminate against a job applicant or an employee because of race, color, religion, sex (including pregnancy, transgender status, and sexual orientation), national origin, age (40 or older), disability, or genetic information. Most employers with at least 15 employees are covered — 20 in age-discrimination cases — and the laws reach hiring, firing, promotions, harassment, training, wages, and benefits. The foundation is Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which makes it an unlawful employment practice to refuse to hire, to discharge, or to discriminate against someone in compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. This is the floor, not the ceiling: the law prevents defined harms, while inclusion is a broader, ongoing practice. This lesson describes the law generally; it is not legal advice.

collegeVersion.heading: Unconscious bias: the honest note
collegeVersion.body: Part of why inclusion needs deliberate effort is that people carry automatic judgments. Unconscious bias is the tendency to feel comfortable with people who think, act, and look like us, and to let that comfort shape decisions without realizing it. SHRM describes how this shows up at work: in hiring, people gravitate toward those inside their own group, and subjective comfort — often discussed as 'fit' — can override what should be an assessment of objective qualifications. The same dynamic affects promotions, where people tend to favor those who look like 'leadership material.' Naming this is not an accusation; it is a factual note about how human judgment works, and why structured, fair practices matter.

collegeVersion.heading: Building inclusion: listening, equitable practices, accountability
collegeVersion.body: Inclusion is built, not declared. Three general levers appear across the sources. Listening: CFI lists creating safe avenues for dialogue — employee resource groups and open channels where people can raise concerns — as a best practice, and OpenStax urges managers to seek feedback from employees rather than assume. Equitable practices: fair, consistent processes for hiring, promotion, and assignments — the same criteria applied to everyone — are the practical shape of fairness. Accountability: CFI puts commitment from top management first, and OpenStax notes that diversity programs can fail or backfire when they are not managed well; someone has to own the results, review the data, and follow through.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing: diversity is the mix; inclusion makes the mix work
collegeVersion.body: Here is the reality check that holds the lesson together. Diversity is the mix — who is in the organization. Inclusion is making the mix work — whether the people in it are accepted, treated fairly, and actually participate. A team can have one without the other. The mix without participation is a poster; participation without a mix is a comfortable club. Organizations pursue both because the mix is worth having and only works when it is made to work.

vocabulary.definition: The mix of identities, backgrounds, and perspectives employees bring; the identity-based differences among people that affect their lives as applicants, employees, and customers.
The degree to which employees are accepted and treated fairly by their organization, so that the mix actually participates.
Visible differences between people, such as age, body size, disability, race, or sex.
A collective of people who share a characteristic such as race, ethnicity, gender, or age.
Automatic judgments people make from comfort with those who think, act, and look like them, often without awareness.
The traits that U.S. anti-discrimination law names as illegal grounds for employment discrimination, such as race, religion, sex, and disability.
Fair and consistent processes, such as the same hiring and promotion criteria applied to everyone, that make fairness operational.
The practice of assigning ownership for results, so that diversity and inclusion goals are reviewed and followed through.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Diversity is the mix of people on your team — different identities, backgrounds, and ways of seeing things. Inclusion is whether the mix actually works together: whether everyone gets to talk, gets heard, and gets fair chances at the good assignments. The honest truth is that a team can have one without the other. You can hire a mix of people and still let the same few voices run every meeting — that is diversity without inclusion. That is why organizations work on both at once: the mix is worth having, and it only pays off when everyone in it actually participates.
eli10.analogy: Think of a pickup basketball game. Diversity is the players who show up — different heights, speeds, and styles. Inclusion is whether the ball actually moves: whether the quiet player gets passed to when she is open, whether the new player learns the plays instead of standing at the edge of the court. A game with a great mix of players where one player holds the ball all afternoon is not a good game — it is a mix that never became a team.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks down because a basketball game lasts an hour and its rules are simple. An organization lasts for years, has complicated rules, and decisions like hiring and promotion happen slowly. Making a mix work at work takes ongoing effort — listening, fair practices, and follow-through — not just one good pass.

workedExample: Riverbend Community Bank runs a branch in a neighborhood where many customers speak Spanish or Somali at home. For years the branch hired through one recruiter's network, so the staff looked little like the customers. After complaints, the managers tried a different approach. They posted openings at community colleges and local job fairs, and they changed the interview process so every candidate answered the same questions, scored on the same rubric. They started an employee resource group where staff could raise concerns, and a manager now reviews hiring and promotion data every quarter and reports back to the whole branch. Eighteen months later, the branch's staff mix changed, participation in meetings broadened, and the branch — once last in customer surveys — now scores highest. The mix grew, and the mix was made to work.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating diversity and inclusion as the same thing.
commonMistakes.correction: Diversity is the mix of identities and backgrounds on the team; inclusion is whether that mix actually participates. A team can be diverse and still exclude — that is the honest gap.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking that hiring a diverse team finishes the job.
commonMistakes.correction: Hiring only creates the mix. Without inclusive practices — listening, equitable processes, accountability — people stay silent or leave, and the mix never pays off.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating the legal floor as the whole goal.
commonMistakes.correction: Anti-discrimination law sets a minimum: it protects defined groups from defined harms. Inclusion is a broader, ongoing practice that goes beyond what the law requires. (General information, not legal advice.)

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming bias means deliberate prejudice only.
commonMistakes.correction: Unconscious bias is automatic — people gravitate to those who think, act, and look like them without realizing it. The usual remedy is structured, fair practices, not blame.

compareContrast.distinction: Diversity is the mix of identities and backgrounds on the team; inclusion is whether the mix actually participates. A team can have the first without the second.
The law forbids discrimination against defined groups and sets the floor; inclusion is the broader, ongoing work of making everyone accepted, treated fairly, and heard.
Being hired puts someone in the mix; being heard — having input sought and considered — is what makes the mix work. Organizations need both.

keyTakeaway: Diversity is the mix of identities, backgrounds, and perspectives employees bring; inclusion is making that mix actually work — through listening, equitable practices, and accountability. The law sets the floor; inclusion is the work.

questionBank.prompt: In the United States, the EEOC enforces federal laws that make it illegal to discriminate against an applicant or employee based on which of the following?
options: Whether coworkers personally like the person
How long the person has worked at the company
The person's hobbies and outside interests
Race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age (40 or older), disability, or genetic information
questionBank.explanation: The EEOC's overview states that its laws protect race, color, religion, sex (including pregnancy, transgender status, and sexual orientation), national origin, age (40 or older), disability, and genetic information. The other options are not protected traits.
questionBank.skill: Recalling which characteristics U.S. anti-discrimination law protects

questionBank.prompt: A software studio posts a diversity statement every year, yet over five years all senior roles went to people from one recruiting pipeline, and exit surveys mention feeling unheard. Which response best reflects building inclusion as described in this lesson?
options: Listening to employees' input, making hiring and promotion practices equitable, and holding managers accountable for results
Posting a longer, more detailed diversity statement next year
Hiring an outside firm to redesign the company website only
Removing the diversity statement so nobody feels singled out
questionBank.explanation: This lesson names three levers for building inclusion: listening, equitable practices, and accountability. A statement without follow-through changes nothing — which is why the other options do not build inclusion.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing a case and selecting the inclusion-building response: listening, equitable practices, accountability

quickCheck.prompt: The working definition used in this lesson, drawn from OpenStax's Principles of Management, describes diversity at work as what?
options: The number of employees an organization hires in a given year
Identity-based differences among and between people that affect their lives as applicants, employees, and customers
A legal requirement that every team include people from every background
A training program that teaches employees to be polite to one another
quickCheck.explanation: OpenStax defines diversity as identity-based differences — such as race and ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, and age — that affect people's lives as applicants, employees, and customers. Option A is headcount, C is a misunderstanding of the law, and D describes training, not the definition.
quickCheck.skill: Recalling the attributed working definition of diversity

quickCheck.prompt: A food co-op's staff reflects the city's mix of backgrounds, but in team meetings the same three people do the talking, and a new cashier's suggestion gets noticed only after a manager repeats it. What is happening here?
options: The co-op has both diversity and inclusion because the staff is a mix
The co-op has inclusion but not diversity, because not everyone speaks up
The co-op has diversity but not inclusion — the mix exists, but it does not actually participate
The co-op has neither diversity nor inclusion because the staff is small
quickCheck.explanation: The staff is diverse — a mix of backgrounds is present — but the mix does not participate: few voices dominate and new ideas get heard only when repeated. That is the honest gap this lesson names: diversity without inclusion.
quickCheck.skill: Applying the diversity-versus-inclusion distinction to a workplace situation

quickCheck.prompt: A regional grocery chain wants to serve neighborhoods with many first-generation immigrant families. Which reason from the lesson's business case supports pursuing diversity and inclusion?
options: A workforce that reflects those customers can improve decisions and marketing — what to stock and how to serve
A diverse workforce guarantees the chain can pay lower wages
Inclusion removes the need to follow anti-discrimination law
Diversity matters only when a company serves customers outside its home country
quickCheck.explanation: The Cox and Blake business case, summarized by OpenStax, lists greater marketing ability and better problem solving among the advantages of a diverse workforce — a team that reflects its customers understands them. The other options misstate the case.
quickCheck.skill: Applying the business case — talent, decisions, markets — to a company scenario

provenance.rightsStatus: reference-only sources; EEOC government facts restated in original prose with attribution recorded; OpenStax facts (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) restated in original prose with attribution recorded; no source prose adapted
provenance.transformation: The attributed working definitions of diversity and inclusion (OpenStax Principles of Management 12.1: identity-based differences affecting applicants, employees, and customers; inclusion as the degree to which employees are accepted and treated fairly), the surface-level/deep-level distinction (12.1), the business case (12.3, Cox and Blake: talent acquisition, creativity and problem solving, marketing ability, cost advantages, flexibility), the challenges of diversity initiatives (12.4: lower organizational attachment, misunderstandings, workplace discrimination), the U.S. legal floor (EEOC overview: protected characteristics, employer coverage, scope of laws; Title VII text via EEOC, corroborated by OpenStax 12.4), the diversity-management frame and best practices (CFI: policies and programs, top-management commitment, new talent pools, safe dialogue), and the unconscious-bias note (SHRM: gravitation toward similar people, 'fit' overriding objective qualifications) were synthesized into original prose. All examples are original (food co-op meetings, regional grocery chain, Riverbend Community Bank, pickup basketball game). Ethics, organizational culture, and employee engagement are referenced only as sibling topics; the legal content is general U.S. information, not legal advice.
